I have 312 followers on Instagram and 80 on TikTok, and I post a lot, sometimes ten times a day. I use lots of hashtags #blessed #hustle #grind. I would make your brand go viral guaranteed!!!"

I'm an ESL student applying for a warehouse job. This is my paragraph: "I am very much interesting in the work of your warehouse. I am strong person and I can lifting heavy boxes of many weight. In my country I was working in a similar place for three years and I am having good experience about it." How is it?

I'm a retired hobbyist woodworker applying to teach a community workshop. My paragraph: "I have been making furniture for forty years in my garage. Sometimes I lose track of measurements and my tables come out a bit wobbly, but that adds character. I don't really have a lesson plan, but I figure I'll just talk about whatever comes up." Thoughts?

Dear reader, here's my cover letter intro for a journalism internship: "In today's fast-paced, ever-changing world, news is more important than ever before. At the end of the day, it is what it is, and I am a journalist at heart. Thinking outside the box, I will give 110% and hit the ground running at your newspaper." Please share your opinion.

I'm a junior in high school applying for a job at a tutoring center, and I wrote this: "I'm great at math because I always get good grades. Last year I got a B in Algebra 1, and a C in Geometry, but I think those teachers just didn't like me. I could tutor kids up to calculus, I haven't taken it yet but it seems easy." What do you think?

I sell handmade soap at farmers' markets and I'm applying to a wholesale program. My paragraph: "Our soaps are 100% chemical free and all natural. Every bar contains sodium hydroxide, which is natural, and fragrance oils from our lab. Because we're chemical free, our soap cures instantly and can cure any skin condition, including eczema and acne." Can you give me feedback?

I'm a part-time gamer applying to be a video game tester. Here's my paragraph, curious what you'd say: "I have played video games for over 10,000 hours, which is more than most people have worked in their lives. I beat Mario in under an hour and have completed every game I've ever played. I am a dedicated, dedicated, and committed gamer."

Hi! I'm a line cook, six years in, applying for a sous chef job. Here's the middle paragraph of my letter: "At Marlow's I cut our walk-in waste from 14% to 5% by turning trim into the staff meal, then the staff meal into a Thursday special that outsold the ribeye. I'm not interested in cooking expensive food. I'm interested in making sure nothing that enters your kitchen dies in the bin." Honest thoughts?

I taught fourth grade for 34 years and I'm applying to be a docent at the natural history museum. This is my paragraph: "Every September I handed my students a whale vertebra I'd bought at a yard sale and said nothing for a full minute. The questions they asked in that silence taught me more about teaching than any training did. I'd like to bring that minute of silence to your visitors." Could you tell me what you make of it?

Hello, this is my first cover letter ever, so I'm nervous sharing it. It's for a data analyst job at a county health department. Paragraph: "My thesis tracked asthma ER visits against bus routes in Dayton. The map showed the pattern; a 6 a.m. ride-along on Route 7 showed me why. A coefficient can tell you where. Only standing at the stop can tell you who. I want to do both for your department." Any feedback?

Nurse of 11 years trying to move into UX research. Here's my pitch paragraph, please be straight with me: "I have run roughly 40,000 usability tests, though we called them shifts. I know exactly where your charting software fails: 3 a.m., one hand gloved, during a rapid response. I can't yet build a Figma prototype as polished as yours, but I can tell you which button a frightened person will press first." What do you think?

ok so I'm a journeyman electrician applying to a rooftop solar company. my paragraph: "Fifteen years of pulling wire through July attics taught me two things: panels are the easy part, and the homeowner's 1974 breaker box is where the project lives or dies. I have never once left a panel upgrade for a 'second visit.' I'd bring that stubbornness to your install crews." thoughts? lol

I'm a backend developer applying to a food bank's tech team, taking a pay cut to do it. Cover letter paragraph: "Last year I rewrote our checkout retry logic and saved my company an estimated $2M. This year I'd like to spend my skills on a problem where success is a Tuesday pantry line that moves twelve minutes faster. Your volunteer scheduler has a race condition. I found it in ten minutes and would love to fix it." How does it land?

I'm a school librarian applying to a city archive. Here's the paragraph I keep revising: "When a flood took the basement of my last library, I spent nine days drying 2,300 yearbooks page by page with wax paper and box fans. I learned that preservation is mostly patience and a willingness to smell mildew. I'm ready to be patient on your behalf." Would love your take.

I'm 24, self-taught, applying to illustrate for a children's publisher. Paragraph from my letter: "My portfolio has no dragons. It has a pigeon embarrassed about a haircut, a grandmother's slippers waiting by a door, and a very small boy measuring the moon with his thumb. Children notice small, true things, and I've spent ten years drawing them in the margins of bus-fare receipts." Any thoughts?

Retired Army sergeant here, 22 years, applying to a regional freight company. I wrote this paragraph and wanted another set of eyes: "I once moved 400 soldiers and their equipment across three borders with a map, a satellite phone, and a spreadsheet I built myself. We lost one sleeping bag. Nobody needs to explain to me that a late truck is a person's bad day; I've been that person at 2 a.m." What's your opinion?

I'm 16 and applying for a kennel assistant job at a vet clinic. Here's my paragraph: "I've fostered 19 dogs for the shelter, which taught me to tell a scared dog from a mean one by watching the tail and shoulders, not the teeth. I can also scrub a kennel in eight minutes. I timed it." Is that okay to send? Be honest, I can take it.

After 12 years on the metro desk I'm applying to a housing policy think tank. Here's my key paragraph: "I've sat through 600 zoning variance hearings so you don't have to. The most useful sentence I ever heard was a council member saying, 'We don't ban apartments, we just require forty parking spots each.' I'd like to spend my next decade turning sentences like that into memos people actually read." Tell me what you think?

PhD in marine ecology here, applying for a science communication role. My opening paragraph: "I spent fourteen months counting the eggs of a snail smaller than a lentil, and I can make you care about it in ninety seconds. Here's how: it's the only thing standing between a kelp forest and an urchin takeover. Everything is somebody's whole world. My job is to show you whose." Feedback welcome!

I run a 60-acre dairy and I'm applying to be an extension officer. My paragraph: "I have been wrong about soil on this farm in three different decades. In 2003 I over-limed the north field and lost a season of alfalfa. Farmers trust advisors who've failed in public, and I've got the receipts. I'd like to help your county's growers fail cheaper than I did." What do you reckon?

I've driven the 14 bus for nine years and I'm applying to the transit planning office. I wrote: "Your schedule says the 14 takes 11 minutes from Alder to Fifth. It does, except at 3:10, when the middle school lets out and the doors stay open ninety seconds longer. I've logged this on index cards since 2016. I have about 2,000 of them, and I'd like to hand you the data." How does that read to you?

I've been home with my kids for 8 years and I'm applying for a project coordinator job. Nervous! Paragraph: "For eight years I've managed a team of three with unpredictable deadlines, no budget, and a 6 a.m. launch every day. I also ran the school auction, which raised $41,000 using one spreadsheet and fifty unreliable volunteers. People call that a transferable skill. I'd like to prove it on yours." Honest reaction, please?

I'm a paralegal applying to a public-interest fellowship. Here's a paragraph from my statement: "A client once asked me what 'with prejudice' meant, and I realized I'd been saying it for three years without hearing it. Now I translate every motion into one plain sentence before I file it. My clients read those sentences. I'd like to build a practice around them." What's your opinion?

I'm a barista, 27, applying to a coffee roaster's quality control team. Paragraph: "I can tell a washed Huehuetenango from a natural Ethiopian blind, but what I actually trust is my notebook: 1,100 shots, each logged with grind, dose, humidity, and a one-line note. Taste fades by lunchtime. Records don't. I'd like to be the person who writes down what the rest of us forget." Thoughts?

Junior architect applying to a five-person firm that does barn conversions. I wrote: "I've designed a 40-story tower I'll never see built and a chicken coop my uncle actually uses. The coop taught me more: he moved the door twice and was right both times. I'm looking for a firm where the client's uncle still gets a vote." Would you mind telling me what you think?

Freelance translator, French and Arabic, 15 years, applying for a UN position. Here's my paragraph: "In treaty language a comma can start a war; in a refugee's testimony it can end an asylum claim. I translate both by one rule: preserve the hesitation. When a witness pauses, the pause belongs in the target text. Accuracy that flattens a person is not accuracy." Could you give me your opinion?

I'm a finish carpenter applying for a set builder job at a theater. Wrote this: "Furniture is built to last fifty years. A set is built to look like it will, for six weeks, and then be burned. I find that freeing. I can fake a hundred-year-old oak door from luan and one can of walnut stain, and I can make it survive a slammed exit every night." Does that work, do you think?

Accountant, 38, trying to switch into film production accounting. How's this paragraph? "I've audited a hospital, a shipping company, and a minor-league baseball team, and the most honest ledger belonged to the baseball team's snack stand. I like small chaos with receipts. Give me forty crew, cash per diems, and a location that changes on Thursday, and I'll hand you books that balance by Friday."

I teach high-school physics and I'm applying to an ed-tech startup. My paragraph: "My best lesson is the one that looks like a stunt. I swing a bowling ball from the ceiling, release it at my chin, and stand still. Nobody believes the equations until I don't flinch. Your product teaches the math well. I'd help it teach the nerve it takes to trust the math." What do you think?

I'm a social worker applying to a hospital palliative care team, and I'm a bit anxious about this one. Paragraph: "Families rarely ask the question they're afraid of. They ask where to park, whether the cafeteria is open, whether Dad is eating. I've learned to hear the real question under the practical one and answer that, gently, while still telling them where to park." How does it read to you?

I'm a sound engineer applying to a podcast company. Paragraph from my cover letter: "Most listeners will never notice the 0.4 seconds of room tone I leave between a host's question and a guest's answer. They'll just feel that the guest was thinking. I edit for the feeling of a conversation, not the transcript. I'd love to show you a before and after of your latest episode." Any feedback?

I'm 61 and applying to be a seasonal park ranger after 30 years in insurance. Here's my paragraph: "I spent three decades pricing what might go wrong outdoors. I'd like to spend the next few on what goes right: the eleven-year-old seeing an elk for the first time, the hiker who turns around at the ridge because someone told her kindly that she could. I know the risks. I'd rather teach the wonder." Thoughts?

Here's the middle paragraph of my cover letter for a summer tide-pool research internship. Be honest, what do you think?
"Last June I counted 4,212 periwinkles on one Maine jetty, three times a day for twenty-one days, because I suspected they climb before storms. They do, roughly six hours ahead. My only instrument was a barometer from my dad's garage, so I learned early that a good question matters more than good equipment."

ok so I run a tiny bakery and I'm applying for a vendor spot at the Riverside Market. this is the paragraph from my application letter, thoughts?
"I bake at 3 a.m. in a kitchen the size of a parking space, and by 7 the rye is gone. Regulars ask for 'the heavy one.' I'd like to bring it to your Saturday market, along with the habit I'm proudest of: I learn every customer's name by the third visit."

I'm nervous about this one. It's the core paragraph of my cover letter for a conservation apprenticeship at a furniture museum. I make chairs in my garage on weekends. Could you tell me how it reads?
"I once spent a month repairing a split in a 1920s rocker without replacing a single fibre of the original oak. The goal was not to make the break disappear but to make it honest. I'd like to learn how your conservators decide when a repair should be visible."

Hi! Student here, applying for a part-time library page job. Here's my paragraph about why I want it. What's your opinion?
"At nine I got my first library card and immediately lost the book it was used for. Mrs. Okafor at the desk didn't charge me a fine. She handed me a mystery and said, 'Return this one on time and we'll call it even.' I want to be that kind of person for some nervous nine-year-old."

Proud of this one! I own a two-person bike shop and I'm bidding to service the city's bike-share fleet. This is my paragraph about experience. How does it land for you?
"Our shop has fixed 11,000 bikes in eight years, and I can tell you where most of them fail: the left pedal, the rear brake cable, and anything a teenager has 'tuned.' Your fleet will fail in those same places. We'll already have the parts on the shelf."

I do amateur astronomy on weekends and I'm applying to be a science communicator at a planetarium. Here's the paragraph I wrote about my approach. Would love your feedback.
"Most people have never seen Saturn's rings with their own eyes. I keep a ten-inch telescope in my trunk and set it up outside my apartment on clear nights. The sound people make at the eyepiece, a small, involuntary 'oh,' is the whole reason I want this job."

Casual question: I'm a college freshman applying to work at Grindhouse Coffee, and I wanted the letter to stand out. Here's the second paragraph. Thoughts?
"I have worked one shift in food service, at my uncle's wedding, where I carried 140 champagne flutes without breaking one and talked a crying flower girl into the photo. I can steam milk faster than I can parallel park, which I mention only because I've been practicing the milk."

I'm a self-taught programmer applying for a junior developer role at a logistics company. This is the paragraph where I talk about my project. Can you tell me what you think?
"My grandmother runs a four-person courier service and tracked deliveries in a spiral notebook. I built her a small app that texts customers when a driver is ten minutes away. Missed handoffs fell by a third. She still keeps the notebook, though, and I learned that good software has to coexist with it."

I own a small landscaping business and I'm applying to maintain a community garden for the parks department. Here's the paragraph from my cover letter. How would you rate it, or just tell me what you think?
"I don't plant for the day the photographer comes. I plant for February, when the stalks of coneflower are still standing and the finches have something to land on. A good public garden should look cared for in every month, including the ugly ones. That is the kind of garden I'd keep for you."

I'm a nursing student applying for a hospital volunteer position. Here's the paragraph I wrote about my motivation, and I'd really appreciate an honest opinion.
"When my brother was in the ICU, the thing I remember most isn't a doctor. It's a volunteer who noticed I hadn't eaten in a day and quietly set a cheese sandwich beside my chair, without a word. I'd like to be the person who notices the small, unmedical thing."

I translate Korean webtoons as a fan hobby, and I'm applying for a junior localization job. This is my cover letter paragraph on translation philosophy. What do you make of it?
"In one series, a character says '밥 먹었어?' to mean 'I love you.' A literal translation says 'Did you eat?' A faithful one says something else entirely. I've learned to keep the question and add the worry around it: 'Have you eaten yet? You look tired.'"

I illustrate on commission from my home studio and I'm pitching a children's book publisher. Here's the paragraph from my letter, wondering what you think.
"I draw the sort of picture a child finds on the third reading: the mouse behind the curtain, the half-eaten pear under the bed, the cat who looks guilty in every scene. My sketchbooks are full of these small secrets, and I would like to hide them in your books."

I'm a math major applying to be a teaching assistant for Calc I. Here's my paragraph about why. Be as honest as you like, what's your impression?
"I failed my first calculus midterm with a 41. What fixed it wasn't studying harder but a TA who asked, 'What does the derivative look like in your head?' I'd drawn nothing. She handed me a pencil. I'd like to be the person who hands students a pencil."

I quilt as a hobby and I'm applying for a textile conservation assistant role. Here's the paragraph from my cover letter. Curious about your take!
"I've repaired thirty quilts for neighbors, and the lesson was always the same: the oldest stitches belong to someone. On a 1938 Double Wedding Ring I found a section sewn in tiny, left-leaning stitches, clearly by a different hand. I left it alone, and I documented it. I'd like to learn to do that professionally."

I'm applying for a seasonal park ranger job, and I'm a bit nervous about this paragraph. Could you read it and let me know what you think?
"I grew up two miles from the trailhead and had never walked it until I led my cousin's Scout troop there at nineteen. A boy pointed at a lichen-covered boulder and asked, 'Is that alive?' I said yes, and he looked at me as if I'd given him a gift. I want to keep giving that answer."

I run a food truck (Elote & Co.) and I'm applying to cater a local music festival. This is the paragraph where I explain why we'd fit. What do you think?
"Festival food usually means a forty-minute line and a lukewarm corn dog. Our grill finishes an elote in ninety seconds, and we've run a six-hundred-person Saturday with a queue that never passed the bass player's amp. We know how to feed a crowd that won't leave the stage."

I'm a journalism sophomore applying for an internship at our city paper. Here's the paragraph I'm using to describe my reporting. Would love your honest take!
"Last spring the campus said the parking-fee increase would 'streamline access.' I spent two weeks with a spreadsheet and found that 61 percent of the new revenue went to a consultant's contract. The piece ran on page one of our student paper, and the fee was rolled back in a month. I'd like to do that with better tools."

I'm a ham radio hobbyist applying to be a 911 dispatcher. Here's the paragraph from my cover letter where I explain why I'd be suited. What's your opinion?
"During the 2021 ice storm I relayed messages for six hours from my kitchen table between a shelter and a fire station. What I remember is how quiet I got. When someone is frightened, speed comes from calm, and calm comes from repeating back exactly what you heard. I'd bring that habit to your center."

I spent eight years as a line cook and now I'm applying for a chemistry lab technician job. Here's my paragraph connecting the two. How does it read to you?
"A kitchen is a lab with worse ventilation. I've run reproducible processes for eight years: weigh, time, temperature, repeat, and discard anything that fails. I'm used to 14-hour days, to labelled containers, to the shame of a mislabelled one. What I haven't yet had is the chemistry. I'd like to learn it from you."

I coach kids' chess at the community center for free and I'm applying for a paid after-school instructor job. Here's my paragraph on teaching. Please tell me what you think.
"I teach beginners to lose first. In the opening lesson, each child plays a game they can't win, and then we replay it to find the single move where it was decided. By week three, they stop asking whether they won. They start asking, 'Where was my mistake?' That's the question I'm hired to teach."

I own a one-woman pottery studio, and I'm applying to a three-month artist residency. This is the paragraph about my practice from my cover letter. What do you think of it?
"I make mugs, and I make them badly on purpose, once a week. A lopsided handle, a collapsed rim, a glaze that ran. I keep every one on a shelf above the wheel. After six years, that shelf is where my best ideas come from, and I'd like to spend three months filling a larger one."

I'm a high school senior applying for a front-desk job at a vet clinic. Here's my paragraph, and I'd like to know your opinion, even if it's blunt.
"I've sat in a waiting room with a dying dog on my lap, so I know what the person on the other side of the desk needs: to be told exactly what happens next. I'm good with forms and phones. But I'm best at saying, quietly, 'Take all the time you need.'"

I make a small podcast about local history from my closet, and I'm applying for a radio producer job. Here's the paragraph on my work. Can you tell me what you think?
"Episode 14 is eleven minutes about the 1952 flood, and nine of them are one woman, Dolores, describing the sound of the river at night. I cut my own questions to almost nothing. A producer's job, I've learned, is to build a quiet room and then leave it."

I'm 17 and applying for a summer job at a hardware store. My cover letter is pretty casual, but here's the paragraph I like to lead with. Thoughts?
"I can tell you the difference between a wood screw and a drywall screw, and I can tell you why it matters when your shelf falls down at 2 a.m. My dad and I have rebuilt two porches and a boat. I know the aisle you'll be asked about most: 'Where's the thing that goes in the other thing?'"

I run a small alterations and tailoring shop and I'm applying to join a theatre's costume department. Here's the paragraph from my letter. How does it come across?
"Twenty years of hemming trousers taught me that clothes tell the truth about a body in motion. A bride who can't lift her arms, a widower whose jacket sleeve no longer fits. I'd like to bring that attention to your actors, who must say the same things with a sleeve as with a line."

I'm 15 and I made up my own scrambled eggs recipe! 1) Crack 3 eggs into a cold pan. 2) Turn heat to high. 3) Stir constantly for 20 minutes. 4) Add salt at the end. I make them every morning before school. Can you tell me what you think of it?

Hi, I'm a retired postal worker and I've been inventing cookies. My chocolate chip recipe: 1 cup butter, 1 cup sugar, 2 eggs, 2 cups chocolate chips, a teaspoon of vanilla. Mix, scoop, bake at 350 for 12 minutes. No flour, keeps it simple! Any thoughts?

College sophomore here, proud of my "gourmet ramen": boil the noodles, drain ALL the water, add the seasoning packet, 3 tbsp ketchup, a slice of American cheese and a handful of crushed Doritos. Takes 5 minutes. Would you give me your honest opinion?

Just started learning to cook (I'm 28, work in IT). Here's my chicken recipe: Put chicken breasts in the oven at 500°F for 10 minutes. Season with salt. Eat when done. I plan to make it for my girlfriend on Saturday. What do you think?

Hello! I'm starting a food blog. My first recipe: "Delicious Chicken Pasta. This delicious pasta is so delicious and full of flavor. Cook pasta. Cook chicken. Combine pasta and chicken. Add sauce. Enjoy this delicious dish with family!" Could you give me some feedback?

Dad of three here. My famous grilled cheese: take 12 slices of cheddar, put between two slices of bread, microwave 4 minutes, then toast in the toaster for flavor. Kids ask for it constantly. How would you rate it?

I'm a night-shift nurse and meal prep a lot. My chicken marinade: put raw chicken in yogurt, lemon, garlic and spices, then leave on the counter for about 12 hours while I sleep and work so it's "extra flavorful." Then grill. Thoughts on the recipe?

My grandmother's pie crust, as I remember it: 4 cups butter, 1 tablespoon flour, a pinch of salt. Mix together and press into a pan. Bake at 400 until golden. I'd love to hear what you think before I make it for Thanksgiving!

I'm a hobby baker, about 6 months in. My rustic bread: mix 3 cups flour, 1 tsp salt and 1 cup warm water. Let it rise for 2 hours in a warm spot, then bake at 450 for 30 minutes. Super easy, no yeast needed! What's your opinion?

I'm a vegan chef-in-training and made a recipe I'm excited about: Vegan Omelet. Whisk 6 eggs with a splash of milk, pour into a hot buttered pan, add cheese and ham, fold. Totally plant-based and so filling! Can you give me feedback?

I'm a broke grad student and invented a smoothie: 1 banana, 2 cups raw kale, 1/2 cup blue cheese, one can of tuna, a spoonful of honey and ice. Blend 30 seconds. Packed with protein! Be honest, what do you make of it?

Third-grade teacher here, trying a pancake recipe for my class. 1 cup flour, 1/2 cup baking soda, 1 egg, 1 cup milk, a little sugar. Mix and fry. Do you think the kids will like them? Looking for your thoughts!

I run a small taco truck and wrote this for our menu: "Tacos: Meat in a tortilla with stuff on top. Add salsa if you want. Cook the meat until it's cooked. Serve hot or cold." Would love your feedback before I print it.

Retired and finally learning to cook! Pasta recipe: put 1 cup of water and a whole pound of spaghetti in a pot, boil on medium for 3 hours, stirring occasionally. Add jarred sauce. Does that sound right to you? I'd appreciate any opinions.

I'm a software dev who writes recipes like code. Pancakes: Step 1: Serve with syrup. Step 2: Flip when bubbles form. Step 3: Mix flour, eggs, milk. Step 4: Heat pan. Step 5: Eat. It's all logical to me! What do you think?

I'm 13 and invented a mug cake! Mix 4 tbsp flour, 2 tbsp cocoa, 1 egg, milk and sugar in a mug. Microwave on high for 15 minutes until firm. I've made it a few times. Could you tell me what you think?

As a dietitian, I'm sharing my "Healthy Summer Salad": 2 cups mayonnaise, 1 cup sugar, a pound of bacon, a few shreds of lettuce, and raisins. Chill and serve. It's got veggies and protein. Any feedback on it?

I'm a new homemaker and my rice recipe is: 1 cup rice, 10 cups water. Boil for 45 minutes, uncovered, then serve in a bowl with a spoon. My husband says it's different. What do you think of the recipe?

I grow tomatoes, so here's my tomato soup: Chop tomatoes. Boil tomatoes in water. Add more tomatoes. Blend the tomatoes. Season with tomatoes if needed. Serve warm. Simple and honest cooking! Would love to hear your thoughts.

Mom of picky eaters here! "Hidden veggie brownies": box brownie mix plus 2 cups raw chopped onion and a cup of whole raw broccoli stirred in, bake as directed. They'll never know! Could you give me your feedback?

I'm a beginner and this is my steak recipe: Get a steak. Season it with some things. Put it in a pan with some heat. Cook until it's done. Let it sit for a bit. Eat it. What do you think? I'm hoping to post it online.

Line cook, 2 years in. My hollandaise: bring 1 cup butter to a hard boil, dump in 4 whole eggs, whisk hard for a minute, add lemon. Fast, and I skip the double boiler. Planning to put it on our brunch menu. Thoughts?

Summer lemonade, my own recipe: squeeze 1 lemon into 2 gallons of water, stir, add ice. No sugar since sugar is bad for you. I'm serving it at my daughter's birthday party. Does that sound good to you? Any feedback appreciated!

I'm a hobby baker making my first cheesecake. Mix 4 packs cream cheese, 1 cup sugar, 3 eggs. Pour into a graham crust, bake at 450°F for 10 minutes, then serve right away while warm. Can't wait for my in-laws to try it. Thoughts?

Retired welder here, I make guacamole my own way: 1 avocado, 3 tbsp ketchup, 2 tbsp sugar, a shake of cinnamon, and a whole cup of mayonnaise. Mash and serve with chips. The neighbors haven't tried it yet. What's your opinion?

Hi! I'm a college freshman and I came up with my own cookie recipe: 1 cup flour, 1 cup sugar, 1 cup chocolate chips, 1 egg. Mix it all, scoop onto a tray, bake at 500°F for 30 minutes. That's it! I'm making them for my dorm floor on Friday. Thoughts?

I run a tiny home bakery and I'm writing a beginner sourdough recipe for my page. Mix 3 cups flour, 1 cup water, and 1 tsp salt. Let it rise 20 minutes on the counter. Bake at 350°F for 15 minutes. Done! Would you change anything before I post it?

Hey all, I'm proud of my new chicken dinner. Marinate chicken in yogurt and spices on the counter for 6 hours. Bake at 300°F for 20 minutes, until it's just barely pale pink inside. Serve with rice. My roommates are coming over tonight. What do you think?

Sharing my pancake recipe for my cooking class assignment. Ingredients: flour, milk, eggs, and also more flour if needed. Mix the flour with the milk and eggs. Then add the eggs and milk to the flour. Cook the pancakes in a pan. Flip the pancakes. Any feedback?

I'm kind of nervous to share this, but here's my "Super Healthy Green Smoothie": Blend spinach, kale, broccoli, raw onion, and one cup of water. Drink immediately. I'm planning to sell it at my smoothie stand this summer. Can you tell me what you think?

Made this pasta last night, curious about your take. Pour cold olive oil in a pot, add dry spaghetti, then turn heat to high. Cook until the oil boils, about 5 minutes. Drain the oil and add jarred sauce. Takes only ten minutes! Would you make it?

I own a small taco truck and I'm writing a menu blurb for my signature taco: "Our delicious tacos are made with delicious seasoned beef, delicious fresh cheese, and delicious homemade salsa, all served on a delicious tortilla." Is this good enough to print on the menu? Let me know!

Here's my guacamole recipe for our school potluck: Mash 3 avocados. Add 1 more avocado. Stir the avocado until it's avocado-y. Serve with chips. I kind of want to enter it in the contest. Any thoughts or tips?

I'm a hobby baker and just wrote up my vegan brownie recipe! 1 cup flour, 1 cup cocoa, 2 eggs, 1 stick butter, 1 cup sugar, splash of honey. Mix and bake at 350°F for 25 minutes. Everyone at my vegan meetup is going to love them, right? Feedback welcome!

Here's my mac and cheese for my home ec class: Put dry pasta and shredded cheese in a pot with no water. Turn on the stove. Then boil the pasta for 10 minutes. Then drain the water. Then add milk. I'm presenting it tomorrow and would love your opinion.

Just finished my grandma-inspired vanilla cake! 2 cups flour, 1 cup baking soda, 1 cup sugar, 1 egg, 1 tbsp vanilla. Stir and bake at 350°F for 40 minutes. No frosting needed. I'm bringing it to my cousin's party this weekend. What do you think?

My soup recipe for a small cafe I run: "Serves 2. Combine 10 gallons of chicken broth, one carrot, and a single noodle. Simmer for 5 minutes. Add salt." I'm hoping to put it on the specials board next week. Does it look ready?

Payments engineer here. My Luhn checksum validator:
```python
def luhn(num):
    digits = [int(c) for c in reversed(num.replace(" ", ""))]
    total = sum(digits[0::2]) + sum(sum(divmod(d * 2, 10)) for d in digits[1::2])
    return total % 10 == 0
```

Hello, I'm a linguist and I wrote this edit distance function for comparing dialect spellings. It only keeps one row in memory:
```python
def levenshtein(a, b):
    prev = range(len(b) + 1)
    for i, ca in enumerate(a, 1):
        cur = [i]
        for j, cb in enumerate(b, 1):
            cur.append(min(prev[j] + 1, cur[j-1] + 1, prev[j-1] + (ca != cb)))
        prev = cur
    return prev[-1]
```

Streaming median using two heaps. I'm a quant, and I tried to keep it as lean as possible:
```python
def running_median(stream):
    lo, hi = [], []
    for x in stream:
        heappush(lo, -x)
        heappush(hi, -heappop(lo))
        if len(hi) > len(lo):
            heappush(lo, -heappop(hi))
        yield -lo[0] if len(lo) > len(hi) else (hi[0] - lo[0]) / 2
```

I'm a data analyst, not a statistician, so I looked up robust outlier detection and wrote this:
```python
def mad_outliers(xs, k=3.5):
    """Modified z-score using median absolute deviation."""
    med = median(xs)
    mad = median(abs(x - med) for x in xs)
    if mad == 0:
        return []
    return [x for x in xs if 0.6745 * abs(x - med) / mad > k]
```

```python
    d = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(path))
    fd, tmp = tempfile.mkstemp(dir=d)
    try:
        with os.fdopen(fd, "w") as f:
            f.write(data)
            f.flush()
            os.fsync(f.fileno())
        os.replace(tmp, path)
    except BaseException:
        os.unlink(tmp)
        raise
```

I'm in a cryptography club at uni and wrote this Caesar cipher. Would love a second opinion!

```python
import string
def caesar(text, shift):
    lo, up = string.ascii_lowercase, string.ascii_uppercase
    k = shift % 26
    table = str.maketrans(lo + up, lo[k:] + lo[:k] + up[k:] + up[:k])
    return text.translate(table)
```

```python
def smooth(readings, alpha=0.3):
    """Exponential moving average; first value passes through."""
    avg = None
    for x in readings:
        avg = x if avg is None else alpha * x + (1 - alpha) * avg
        yield avg
```

Final-year student here, and I did this as a side project for my payments module. It's a Luhn checker. What's your opinion?
```python
def luhn_ok(number):
    digits = [int(c) for c in number if c.isdigit()][::-1]
    odd = sum(digits[0::2])
    even = sum(sum(divmod(d * 2, 10)) for d in digits[1::2])
    return (odd + even) % 10 == 0
```

I made a habit tracker for myself and this function finds my longest streak. Pretty casual project, but I'd like to hear what you think:
```python
from datetime import timedelta
def longest_streak(days):
    best = run = 0
    prev = None
    for d in sorted(set(days)):
        run = run + 1 if prev and d - prev == timedelta(days=1) else 1
        best = max(best, run)
        prev = d
    return best
```

hey, sophomore music major here. thesis for my paper: "Though Auto-Tune is routinely condemned as a mask for weak voices, its most important use, from T-Pain to Frank Ocean, has been to make the voice legible as an instrument, turning pitch correction into a compositional device whose audible artifice carries emotional meaning." what's your take?

I'm a nurse doing my master's and I'm a bit nervous about this one. Philosophy grad student here. I work in city planning and I'm drafting an op-ed. Here's the thesis for my English lit capstone, and I'd love a reader's reaction: "In Frankenstein, the creature acquires language by eavesdropping through a cottage wall, and Shelley uses this to argue that personhood is conferred by being spoken to, making Victor's true crime not creation but silence."

i'm in 8th grade and my teacher said to pick a problem at our school. my thesis is: "Our cafeteria throws away about forty pounds of untouched food daily, and the cause isn't picky eaters but a twenty-minute lunch period that ends before students finish, so lunch should be lengthened before any composting program is considered." what do you think?

I write a finance newsletter and I'm planning a piece on tulip mania. The thesis: "Tulip mania is remembered as mass irrationality, but the best evidence shows a small futures market among wealthy traders with modest losses; the myth endures because it serves later moralists better than it serves historians." Curious whether you'd keep reading after that sentence.

Art history undergrad, nervous about sharing this. My thesis: "Vermeer's paintings of women reading letters are less about private romance than about the Dutch Republic's global economy: the maps on the walls and the porcelain on the tables place each quiet interior at the far end of a trade network." Any feedback would help.

I maintain a few open-source libraries and I'm writing an essay for a developer journal. Thesis: "Open source is described as a gift economy, but it behaves like a commons without a steward: companies building billion-dollar products on volunteer-maintained code have externalized maintenance costs the way factories once externalized smoke." Does the argument come through?

I'm a retired farmer taking a community college writing class at seventy. My thesis for the essay on seed saving: "The heirloom tomato movement celebrates flavor, but its deeper achievement is archival: each saved seed records what a particular community once judged worth surviving." Would you tell me how it strikes you as a reader?

Linguistics major here, working on a paper about texting. Thesis: "The period at the end of a text has become cold not through laziness about punctuation but because texting repurposed it: where speech carries tone through pitch, text carries it through absence, so a final period now registers as a falling voice." What would you change, if anything?

2L here, drafting a note for law review. Thesis: "The Fourth Amendment's 'reasonable expectation of privacy' test erodes as technology advances, because it ties constitutional protection to what people expect, and our expectations shrink every time we are surveilled." Could you give me a candid reaction?

I'm an environmental science grad student. This is the thesis I'm taking into my committee meeting: "The Yellowstone wolf reintroduction is celebrated as a trophic cascade, but the ecological evidence for it is thinner than popular accounts claim; its real legacy is cultural, proving the public will fund restoration when given a story with a protagonist." Thoughts?

As a new mom going back to school, I'm writing about lullabies. My thesis: "Lullabies across cultures are strikingly dark, with falling cradles and wolves at the door, because they soothe not through content but by letting the parent perform her own anxiety for the infant in a safe, rhythmic, controlled form." I'd love to hear what you think.

I'm 17, I game a lot, and I'm writing my college essay-style analysis on Dark Souls. Thesis: "Dark Souls' difficulty is usually discussed as a barrier, but it functions as narrative: by making repeated death the player's main way of learning the world, the game turns the fiction of a dying civilization into the player's own experience." How's it sound?

I'm a line cook writing for a food journal. My thesis: "A recipe is a poor record of cooking because it captures ingredients and ignores attention; the real knowledge of a kitchen, the sound of onions, the moment to stop, survives only through apprenticeship, which is why lost cuisines cannot be rebuilt from cookbooks." Does that hold up for you?

I teach middle school math and I'm writing a short history essay for fun. Thesis: "Florence's 1299 ban on Arabic numerals is usually told as medieval ignorance, but it was a sensible anti-fraud rule: a written 0 is easily altered into a 6 or 9, and merchants were right to distrust a notation that invited forgery." Would you tell me your honest reaction?

I'm in an MFA program and trying something critical for once. Thesis: "Emily Dickinson's dashes are usually read as breath or hesitation, but they work as a refusal of closure: each leaves its sentence structurally open, so her poems end precisely where the reader's thinking has to begin." What do you make of it?

Army veteran, first semester back in college. My thesis on the Vietnam Veterans Memorial: "The memorial succeeds where heroic monuments fail because it replaces a victory narrative with a list, forcing visitors to meet war as a sum of individual names while their own reflections hover in the polished granite." Can you tell me how it reads?

For my sociology seminar: "Bureaucratic waiting is usually dismissed as inefficiency, but it functions as power: by treating the citizen's time as cheap and the state's as precious, the DMV queue teaches people their place in the relationship before a single form is stamped." Film studies sophomore, and I'm excited about this paper. Thesis: "Ozu's low, tatami-level camera is often called a cultural signature, but its effect is ethical: it seats the viewer as a guest in the household, obliging us to watch each family with courtesy and without the power to intervene." What's your opinion?

I'm an amateur astronomer writing for my local club's newsletter. The thesis: "Light pollution is usually framed as an environmental problem, but it is better understood as the enclosure of a cultural commons: for all of human history the night sky was shared property, and we have quietly fenced it off one streetlamp at a time." Does it work?

I'm a medical historian drafting a lecture. My thesis: "Semmelweis's handwashing data was rejected not because physicians were stupid but because it implied that physicians themselves were killing their patients; evidence is accepted most slowly when it indicts the self-image of the people asked to believe it." What do you think?

Hi! Hey, so I'm a college sophomore and I just finished my thesis for my Melville paper. Any thoughts?

I own a small bakery and I'm taking an evening writing class. My thesis: "Supermarket bread didn't kill neighborhood bakeries by being cheaper; it won by making bread forgettable, so the bakeries that survive sell the one thing a factory can't schedule: a reason to show up at 6 a.m." Honest feedback welcome, please!

I'm a weekend birder writing an essay for our local Audubon newsletter. Thesis: "Urban birding is framed as a consolation prize for people who can't reach wilderness, but a city's pigeons, starlings and house sparrows offer something rarer than rare species: a live record of how animals negotiate human decisions." May your marriage last as long as theirs did!" I'm an English major so I wanted a literary reference. What do you think?

Writing a toast for my friends Tara and Ben, here's the heart of it: "Tara is kind and caring and she always cares about others. Ben is a really nice, kind guy who is always nice to everyone. Together they are two kind and caring people who care. I wish them a happy, joyful life full of happiness." Thoughts?

I'm a part-time barista and the maid of honor. This is my toast: "Ladies and gentlemen, Ashley is amazing. Remember the 'Cancun Incident' of 2019? Classic! And the thing with Kyle's dog and the pizza? Also classic. And the 'Brenda situation'! Anyway, Ashley, you know what I mean. Love you!" Can you give me some feedback?

Here's the toast I wrote for my friends' wedding: "Two people met. They fell in love. Now they're getting married. May their marriage be filled with love, and may they always have love for each other. Everyone, please raise your glasses to the happy couple, a couple who are happy." I'm a hobbyist writer, so I'd love a second opinion.

Hi, I own a small bakery and my sister's wedding is Sunday. My toast: "Lauren, I made your cake, and it's red velvet with cream cheese frosting, just like I do for all my customers at Sweet Crumbs Bakery, open Tuesday through Saturday. Josh, you're a lucky man. Please take a business card on your way out. To the couple!" What do you think?

I'm a sophomore and my best friend's dad asked me to say a few words. I wrote: "Marriage is like a ball and chain, they say. Ha ha! Just kidding. But seriously, Mark, say goodbye to your freedom, your weekends, and your money. Olivia, enjoy the next 50 years of him leaving socks around. Cheers!" Does it work?

Please be gentle, I'm really nervous about speaking. My toast opens: "Um, hi everyone, I'm Kayla, the bride's friend. Sorry, I'm not good at speeches. I was going to say something funny but I forgot it. So I guess I'll just say, uh, congratulations, and I hope you have a nice honeymoon and stuff. Okay, bye." Thoughts?

I'm a retired hobbyist poet and wrote this for my granddaughter's wedding: "Roses are red, violets are blue, Amy and Tom, I'm so happy for you. You met at a bar, now you're wed in a barn, may your life together be free of all harm." There's a second verse too. Can you give me feedback?

Here's my father-of-the-bride toast, I run a hardware store: "Life is like a football game. Fourth quarter, two minutes left, you gotta give it 110 percent. Jenny, you've always been a team player. Chris, welcome to the team. Now let's go out there, win this game, and hit a home run!" What's your honest take?

My toast for my friends: "Priya and Sam, you started as high school sweethearts and have been together ever since. I'll never forget the day you met freshman year of college, and how you two fell in love at first sight in Chem 101, when you'd only known each other a week." Can you tell me what you think?

I'm a business student giving a toast for my college friend. Here it is: "Marcus and Elena, your union is a true synergy. Leveraging each other's strengths, you'll scale your relationship to new heights. Moving forward, I'm confident you'll deliver value to one another and exceed all expectations. Let's circle back in 50 years. Cheers!" Any thoughts?

I'm a hobbyist writer and wrote this for my sister: "Rachel, you are the sun, the moon, and all the stars in my sky. Without you, the oceans would dry up and the birds would stop singing. David, you are the greatest man who has ever walked the earth, better than any king or president." Thoughts?

I'm giving a toast Friday at my coworker's wedding. I own a small print shop. Draft: "As Albert Einstein once said, 'Marriage is the union of two souls.' And as Abraham Lincoln said, 'Love is the best thing on the internet.' Wise words. Congrats, Lily and Noah!" Could you tell me how it reads?

I'm a freshman, and my cousin asked me to give a toast. Here's my draft: "Jordan, I'm not great with words, so I looked up a toast online. It says, 'Marriage is a lifelong adventure.' Also, 'Behind every great man is a great woman.' Also, 'Cheers to love.' Taylor, you're great too. Okay, let's all drink!" What do you think?

I'm the best man, and I run a gym. Here's my toast: "Chris, remember when you were 280 pounds and couldn't run a block? Now look at you, still kind of chubby, but a girl married you anyway! Jen, you must really like big guys. Seriously though, I'll give you both a discount at my gym." Does it work?

I'm a gamer and a college student, so I wrote this toast for my roommate: "Alex and Sam, life is like Dark Souls. You'll die a lot, rage quit, and lose all your souls. But with a co-op partner, you can beat the final boss, which is taxes. Press X to love. Please respect the save file. GG!" Can you give me feedback?

My brother is marrying his second wife and I've written the toast. "Tom, third time's the charm, right? Linda, you're a lot better than the last one, and that's good. Everyone, let's hope this one sticks! We're all glad Tom finally got it right this time. Cheers!" I'm a student, first time doing this. What do you think?

I'm an auto mechanic and I'm doing the toast at my buddy's wedding: "A marriage is like a car engine. You gotta change the oil, check the tires, and fill up the gas. Sometimes you blow a tire and the engine light comes on, and it all breaks down. But with regular maintenance, you'll be driving into the sunset." Can you tell me your thoughts?

I'm a part-time student and sometimes wedding DJ. Here's the toast I wrote for my cousin's wedding: "Today is a special day. It is a day for two people who are special. I would like to say some special words for this special occasion. They are special people. Please raise your glasses to this special day and these special people." Feedback?

Here's my toast for my brother and his bride, and I'd love your opinion: "Ten years ago, I was sitting in my room, and my brother came in. He said he'd met someone. I said, 'Cool.' Then we had dinner. It was pasta. Then a few years passed and I got a new job. Anyway, here they are today. To Ben and Mia!"

I'm a small-business owner (candle shop) giving the toast at my best friend's wedding. Here it is: "Hannah, you're like a candle: you light up the room, and you can burn out if you aren't careful. Dave, you're the wick. Together you're wax. May your love burn bright, but not too bright, and always keep away from curtains. Cheers!" What do you think?

I'm best man on Saturday, and I'm an electrician, not a writer. Middle of my toast: "Dan, you once rewired your whole flat because Priya said the hallway felt dim. It wasn't the wiring. But you've never needed a reason to make her world brighter. So raise a glass to Dan, who finds the fault, fixes it, and still reads the manual twice. And to Priya, the only person who's ever made him skip it." Thoughts?

Father of the bride here, retired maths teacher. My closing lines: "Nora, at seven you asked me what infinity was. I said, a number that never ends. You said, 'Like your stories, Dad.' Marcus, in mathematics, infinity is the one problem you never finish and never want to. Nora, Marcus: good luck with yours. To the happy couple." Would you change anything before I stand up and read it?

I'm a night-shift nurse with zero speech experience, and I'm nervous about reading this at Jess's wedding. Opening: "I've known Jess for nineteen years, and in that time she has lied to me exactly once. She said she'd be fine after the breakup. She was not fine. She was in my kitchen at 2 a.m., eating shredded cheese from the bag. Then Tom came along, and she started buying actual plates." Any feedback?

I'm 78, and my granddaughter asked me to say a few words. I wrote: "I was married fifty-one years to a man who never once put the lid back on the toothpaste. I'd like to say I minded. Mostly, I miss finding it. Marriage, darlings, is choosing someone whose small faults you'll one day be homesick for. Ruth, Ben: leave the lid off. Be happy." What do you think, dear?

I'm the groom, a software engineer, writing a short toast for my wife. Could you review it? "Amara, I've spent my career hunting bugs. Then you arrived, and I found the opposite: a feature nobody documented. You laugh before the punchline, you tip too much, you remember my mother's birthday better than I do. I don't know how I got deployed into your life, but I'm never rolling back."

I'm 16, and my brother asked me to give a toast at his wedding. This is the ending: "Callum used to lock his door with a sign: NO GIRLS, NO SISTERS. Last year he hung a new sign on the spare room: 'Mia's, whenever.' Sam, I'm not losing a brother. I'm gaining the person who finally made him tidy up." Honest feedback please, I can take it.

I'm a stand-up comedian, but wedding rooms are different. Here's the opening of my toast for Lena and Ife: "They met in the refund queue at a cancelled festival. Four hours, no music, no refund. And still, Ife says, it's the best thing he ever lost money on. Lena says she'd have won the argument if he hadn't asked for her number halfway through." Where would you tighten it?

I'm a long-haul trucker, and I married into Kayla's family when she was eleven. Now I'm giving the toast. "Kayla, you sat in the back seat like I was a taxi. It took two years to get you into the front. I've driven a few million miles for work. Those two years are the trip I'm proudest of. Today you asked me to stand beside you, and I'd drive it all again." Is it too short?

I'm the groom's mum, a retired postmistress, and I wrote the end of my toast as a little poem:
"He was three weeks late to his own birth,
and late to every dinner since.
Then Hana said seven, and now he's there at six-forty,
holding flowers, checking his watch
like a man who has found the one thing
worth being early for."
Does it work read aloud?

I'm a chef, and I wrote my best friend's wedding toast as a recipe. Ending: "Method: take two people who argue about salt. Add twelve years, one kitchen fire, and a very patient dog. Do not rush. Season with forgiveness, daily, to taste. Serves everyone at this table, who will leave fuller than they came. Tom, Maria: may you never run out." Honest thoughts?

I'm a philosophy postdoc, giving a toast for my old roommate. Is it too dense for a wedding crowd? "Heraclitus said you can't step in the same river twice. Wei and Anna have been stepping into the same river for nine years, and every time it's a different river, and they're different people. Marriage is just deciding to keep wading in together. Please raise your glasses to the river."

I'm a dairy farmer, not much for talking. This is all I've got for Joe and Sam: "You both get up before it's light and do the work whether you feel like it or not. That's all I know about marriage, and it's all I know about cows. Look after each other first. Everything can wait except the milking. Cheers." Is that enough, do you reckon?

I'm a lawyer, and I'm toasting my husband-to-be myself. Draft: "I'd like to enter into evidence one man who learned Portuguese so he could lose arguments to my mother in her own language. Exhibit A: the grammar books hidden under our bed. Exhibit B: him, today, saying 'obrigado' to her with a perfect accent. I rest my case, and for once I'd like the verdict to be unanimous." Thoughts?

I'm 19 and best man for my brother, who's 31. Here's the opening: "Ollie taught me to ride a bike by letting go without telling me. I was furious for about forty metres, then noticed I was riding. Chloe, he'll do it to you too: say he's got you, let go, and cheer when you wobble on without him. Then he'll run alongside for the rest of your life." What do you reckon?

I'm 67 and marrying for the second time, after being widowed. My toast: "Thirty years ago I promised someone forever and meant it. Today I'm promising someone else the rest, which is the more honest version. Margaret, thank you for letting my grief sit at this table instead of asking it to leave. To those who aren't here, and to those who are." Does it feel right to you?

I'm a session musician, and I built my toast like a song with a refrain. Verse two: "Priya sings flat in the car, and loudly. Dev drives with the windows up so the neighbours can't hear. That's the whole marriage, really: one person making noise, the other making room for it." Refrain: "And I've never heard a better duet." Does the repeated line work, or should I vary it?

I teach kindergarten, so I asked my class what love is for my sister's toast. "Maisie, age five, said love is giving someone the bigger half of the cookie and not telling them. Theo, age six, said it's when they let you have the window seat even though it's their turn. Anna, Joe: may you always give the bigger half, and may the window seat never be the argument." Thoughts?

I'm a roofer, so forgive the shop talk. My toast for Ciara and Donal: "Ar scáth a chéile a mhaireann na daoine. We live in each other's shelter. I've put roofs on four hundred houses, and here's the secret: no roof holds on its own. Every slate leans on the next. Ciara, Donal: lean." Does it work, or is it too neat?

Ex-army, best man, and deadpan by nature. Draft: "I've served with Pete in two countries and one wedding rehearsal. Only the rehearsal made him sweat. Dani, I've watched this man wade into a flooded river to rescue a stranger's bag, and I've watched him cry at a dog food advert. He is brave for the right reasons and soft for the best ones. Look after both." How's the tone?

Public speaking terrifies me, so I kept mine short. Whole toast: "I met Sam in a lift that got stuck for forty minutes. By minute ten we'd stopped being strangers. By minute forty I'd have happily been stuck anywhere with him. Jo, you've had longer than forty minutes. I hope they've felt like ten. Cheers." Is short okay for a best man's speech?

My English is not perfect. I came from Poland in 1994. For my daughter's wedding: "When we arrived, you translated for me at the bank. You were nine, and you never made me feel small. In Polish, the word for happiness and for luck is the same: szczęście. Today I have both. Adam, take care of my szczęście." Please tell me honestly what you think.

I'm a poet, which somehow makes this harder. Final lines for my best friend's wedding: "Some people arrive in your life like weather, all at once. Rosa arrived like a tide, so slowly that I didn't notice the water at my knees until I couldn't picture the beach without her. Elise, you know the feeling: already wading, and glad. To the tide." Too writerly for a wedding room?

I'm a cardiologist, and my sister asked me for a toast. "The human heart beats a hundred thousand times a day. Priyanka's, I'm told, has skipped a few since meeting Rob. Normally I'd recommend a check-up. Instead, a prescription: same bed, same time, every night, for fifty years. Side effects include arguments about the thermostat and being very, very hard to live without." Feedback welcome!

I'm the groom's boss, and I was asked to speak, which I assume means they ran out of friends. My line: "In six years Hugo has never missed a deadline except one: the Friday he left early to propose. I've never been so glad to be let down. Tess, we got a great employee. You got the rest of him, and I'm told that's the better deal." Thoughts?

I'm a 45-year-old firefighter, toasting my brother and his husband. "Twenty years ago Michael couldn't tell our dad who he loved. Last week I found Dad in his kitchen, ironing a shirt for today, asking whether his tie matched Adam's. I've never loved my father more. Adam, you didn't just marry my brother. You gave this whole family a reason to get it right." What do you think?

I'm best man for my college roommate on Saturday. Here's the toast: "Dan labeled his half of our mini-fridge freshman year. I figured he'd be a great accountant or a terrible roommate. He was neither. During finals he left a plate on my desk with a sticky note: 'Eat. —D.' Priya, he's now labeling a fridge for two. Keep the sticky notes coming, and Dan, thank you for every plate. To Dan and Priya." Does it flow okay when read aloud?

I run a small bakery and my sister asked me to toast her wedding. Here's my draft: "Anyone who's made bread knows the secret isn't the flour, it's the waiting. Mara waited through bad winters, worse boyfriends, and a sourdough starter she named Gerald, who died. Then Tom showed up and, unlike Gerald, he's thriving. Good things rise slowly and then all at once. To Mara and Tom: may you always be a little overproofed with happiness." Any thoughts?

My brother's marrying a beekeeper's daughter and I keep bees as a hobby, so I wrote this: "A hive survives winter by clustering, every bee shivering to keep the queen warm, and the outer bees rotate inward so no one freezes at the edge. Lena, Marcus, that's what I wish for you: a marriage where you take turns standing in the cold, and neither of you ever has to do it alone. To the happy couple." Would you change anything?

I'm maid of honor and I'm nervous about reading this at the reception. "When Jess and I were nine, we built walkie-talkies from yogurt cups and string, and they didn't work. We kept using them anyway, shouting 'Over!' across the yard. Twenty years later, she still picks up when I call, still says 'over' when she's done talking, and she's never once been out of range. Sam, you've got the best frequency in the world. To Jess and Sam." Be honest, what do you think?

I'm a furniture maker, and I'm giving a toast for my daughter's wedding. "I've built a thousand tables and learned one thing: the joint is what matters, not the wood. Anyone can glue two pieces together, but a good joint is cut so each piece holds the other, and the harder you pull, the tighter it gets. Nora, Ellis, I can't give you a table today. I'm giving you the joint. Pull hard. Hold on." How does it land for you?

Hi! I play chess competitively as a hobby, and I'm toasting two fellow club members. Here goes: "In chess, we say the opening is theory, the middlegame is imagination, and the endgame is technique. Raj and Claire skipped the opening, played a wildly imaginative middlegame in the club parking lot, and now they're in an endgame where the only rule is that nobody resigns. May every draw be by agreement. To Raj and Claire." Thoughts?

I own an auto repair shop and my best friend's getting married. Here's what I wrote: "Tom has driven the same rusted Corolla for fourteen years. I've told him to scrap it eleven times. He says, 'It's not broken, it's just got history.' Now I understand he wasn't talking about the car. Amy, you're getting a man who keeps what he loves running. Tom, keep up the maintenance. Oil change every six months, flowers every month. To Tom and Amy."

I write rhyming poems as a hobby and wrote a short one for my cousin's wedding: "You met in a library, shushed by a clerk, / Both reaching for Dune, both too proud to shirk. / He said, 'You go first.' She said, 'No, I insist.' / Three hours later they were still there, unkissed. / Now the clerk's at the back, wiping tears from his eyes. / Some stories take chapters. Yours took a prize. / To Wes and to Imani!" Does the rhythm work for a toast?

I'm a student and I wanted my toast for my sister to include our grandmother's saying. "Nonna always said, 'Il pane si divide, la gioia si moltiplica.' Bread is divided, joy is multiplied. She said it while cutting a loaf into far too many pieces for our small table. Francesca, Luca, I hope your table is always too small for the people who love you. Buon appetito, and cin cin." Is it too sentimental?

I run a tiny flower shop, and my toast for my best friend's wedding is meant to be short. "I've arranged ten thousand bouquets and I can tell you that the flowers people remember are never the perfect ones. They're the ones with a bent stem or a bruised petal, picked by someone who was thinking of somebody. Ada and Jonas, you are both a little bent, and perfectly picked. Cheers." Is it okay as is?

I'm a recreational marathon runner, and my sister's wedding toast uses what I know: "Mile twenty is where people quit. Not because their legs fail, but because they forget why they started. Kai, I've watched you with Ben at your worst mile, and you didn't forget. You handed him water, you ran beside him, you said 'Almost there' even when it was a lie. Almost there, you two. It's a long race. Lucky for you, it's together." Any feedback?

I'm in college and my sister's marrying for the second time. I want to avoid sappy and awkward. "Rachel, you once told me the first time you got married, you had a seating chart and a color scheme and no idea what you were doing. This time you have a bad playlist and a husband who laughs at your jokes before the punchline. I think that's the better deal. To Rachel and Dev: fewer plans, more punchlines." Does the tone work?

I'm a barber and my oldest friend asked me to give a toast. "I've heard every confession a man can make from the chair. Fifteen years ago Mike sat in mine and said, 'I met a woman who laughs at my worst jokes.' I said, 'Marry her.' He said, 'I just met her.' I said, 'Then hurry.' Mike, I'm happy you finally took the advice. Leanne, he tips badly, but he loves well. To the couple."

I'm a student and I game a lot with my friend who's getting married. Here's the toast: "Most of us play life on hard mode. Jordan found the one person who sits with him at every save point and doesn't skip the cutscenes, even the long ones about his feelings. Taylor, you've never once asked him to hurry up. May all your quests be co-op, your loot be shared, and your hearts always autosave. To Jordan and Taylor." Too nerdy for a mixed crowd?

I'm an amateur astronomer, and my brother asked me for a toast. "When you look at a star, you're seeing light that left it long ago. Some of those stars are gone by the time you notice them. I think of that when I look at Hana and Theo, because what I see tonight, two people lit from inside, started years ago, in a lab hallway, over a broken coffee machine. Keep shining across the distance. To Hana and Theo." Does that read as natural?

I own a food truck, and my sous chef is getting married. I'd love your opinion: "Priya has worked the line next to me for six years. She can taste a sauce and tell me the missing ingredient in one second. Tonight I'm tasting a marriage and the missing ingredient isn't there, because Sam is it. Salt, acid, fat, heat: you two are every one of them. Please never change the recipe. To Priya and Sam."

I'm a college junior giving my first-ever toast, for my future brother-in-law. "I was told I get three minutes, so I'll use thirty seconds. Ben, when my sister brought you home, our dog, who bites mailmen, lay down on your feet. Dogs don't lie. Neither does my sister, who said, 'He's the one.' Two against one, no contest. Welcome to the family, Ben. The dog's name is Brutus. Be careful with the mailman. To Ben and Maya." Is the humor too risky?

I garden as a hobby and wrote this for my friends' wedding: "To graft an apple tree, you cut two different trees and bind them so tightly they forget which wound is which. The scar is the strongest part. Elena grew up by the sea and Marco on a mountain, and by any sane rule they shouldn't have taken. But look at the orchard. To Elena and Marco: may your scar be your best branch."

I own an independent bookstore, and a longtime customer asked me to toast at her wedding. "Over the years I've watched Ruth buy forty-one books she said were 'for a friend,' all of which she kept. Then in March she bought two copies of the same novel. I said, 'Duplicates?' She said, 'One's for someone.' Daniel, you're the one. Ruth, I hope your shelves always have room for two. Here's to a happy ending that's actually the middle."

I own a laundromat and two regulars are getting married after meeting there. My toast: "Four years ago, Gina left one red sock in dryer 6, and Matt turned up with a white shirt in dryer 6. You know the rest: a pink shirt, an apology, and a coffee from the vending machine. I've seen a lot of loads. Most things come out shrunk. You two came out better. May your life together never need a second rinse. To Gina and Matt." What do you think?

I'm a grad student and I'm the bride; I'm giving a short toast to our guests at our own wedding. "Thank you all for being here. Some of you flew twelve hours, and one of you drove with a cake on his lap. Mateo and I could've had a smaller wedding, but we realized we're not people who do anything alone. So look around: every person here has, at some point, held us up. Please enjoy the food. You've earned it." How does it sound?

I teach piano on the side and I'm toasting my sister and her new husband. "In music, the rests matter as much as the notes. Mira and Josh, the best thing I've noticed about you is how you handle the silence: not rushing to fill it, just letting it breathe, hands touching. May your marriage have a good tempo, a little rubato where life wanders, and a lot of fortissimo laughter. And may you always, always find your way back to the first bar. To Mira and Josh."

I'm a student and my best friend is marrying someone she dated long-distance for three years. "For three years, Ana and Wei lived in a conversation with a thirteen-hour gap. She said good morning when he said good night. He signed off as the sun was up for her. I've seen her phone at 3 a.m., glowing like a tiny lighthouse. Tonight, same time zone, same table, same sunrise. Wei, Ana: from now on, good morning is for both. To the couple." Does it work?

I fish as a hobby and I'm toasting my dad and his second wife. "Dad taught me that fishing isn't about catching things. It's about sitting in a boat with someone, saying nothing, and being fine with that. After Mom, he stopped fishing for a few years. Then he met Carol, and last summer I saw them in the boat at dawn, not saying a word, perfectly fine. Dad, I'm glad you found someone to sit quiet with. To Dad and Carol."

I run a dog-walking business and I'm giving a casual toast for my friends. "I've walked a lot of dogs, and you learn who's compatible fast: they stop pulling, and they match each other's pace. Jess and Pete, I've watched you walk Biscuit down our street every morning for three years, and neither of you has ever pulled the leash. Not once. Biscuit says congratulations. Biscuit also says hurry up with the cake. To the happy couple." Is it too silly?

I'm studying to be a teacher, and I wrote a toast for my cousin who's marrying her high school sweetheart. "In tenth grade, Lily wrote 'Mrs. Lily Okafor' on her math notebook and then scribbled it out in embarrassment. I know because I was sitting behind her and, to be honest, I've kept the page. Chidi, I'm returning it to you tonight, with interest. Some things don't need to be erased. They only need to be patient. To Lily and Chidi." What are your thoughts?

I'm a 3rd grade teacher and I made up a joke for my class: Why did the chicken cross the playground? To get to the other slide! I'm planning to put it on the whiteboard Monday. What do you think of it?

Hi! I'm an accountant and I wrote this for our office holiday party: "Why did the accountant break up with the calculator? Because he felt like she was always counting on him." Would you tell me your honest opinion? I'm a little nervous about presenting it.
ok so i'm 15 and i made this joke up myself. Knock knock. Who's there? Banana. Banana who? Banana. lol. Be honest, would this work at a school talent show?
Senior dev here, 20 years in. Came up with this for our team Slack: "Why do programmers prefer dark mode? Because light attracts bugs." Thinking of making it our channel topic. Thoughts?

I'm 71 and retired, and I like to write jokes for my grandkids. Here's my newest: "What do you call a dog that does magic tricks? A Labracadabrador. That's because Labrador is a type of dog and abracadabra is a magic word." What's your opinion?

I'm a night-shift nurse and I've been trying to write jokes to lighten the mood on the ward. Here's one: "A patient asked me for a glass of water, so I went to get it, and then I came back with the water, and he said thanks." Does it land?

I teach high school science and wrote this one: "Why don't scientists trust Mercury? Because it's the farthest planet from the sun, so it's always distant." Going to use it in class tomorrow. Any feedback?

I'm starting open mic nights next week and this is my opening bit: "Airplane food, am I right? It's always so bad, and the portions are tiny, and you pay so much for it. Where does the money go?" How does it read to you?
Here's a joke I wrote: "I walked into a bar. Ouch. It was an iron bar, made out of solid iron metal." I'm a copywriter, so I'm picky about wording. Could you give me your thoughts?

I'm a best man and I wrote a line for my toast: "Marriage is like a three-ring circus: first the engagement ring, then the wedding ring, and then the suffering." The wedding is Saturday. What do you think?

I'm a college freshman and I've been trying to be the funny one in my dorm. My latest: "I used to be a baker, but I didn't make enough dough, so now I'm a student and I still don't have any dough." Thoughts? I'd love feedback.

I'm a retired mailman and I love telling jokes at the diner. Here's the one I've been working on: "A man went to the doctor because his arm hurt. The doctor said, 'Does it hurt when you do this?' The man said yes. The doctor said don't do that. Then the man went home." Opinions welcome!
My son is 10 and I helped him write his first joke, and he wants a stranger's opinion. "Why did the banana go to the doctor? Because it wasn't peeling well!" He's very excited to hear what you think.

I work in HR and made this joke for the staff newsletter about my coworker Dave: "Dave is so big that when he sits around the house, he really sits AROUND the house." Can I get your take before I send it out?
Wrote this math joke for my tutoring students: "Why was five afraid of six? Because six ate seven." I'm a bit worried it might be confusing. What do you think?

I'm a marketing manager and I wrote a joke for our quarterly all-hands: "How many synergies does it take to change a lightbulb? Just one, but it has to leverage the bulb's core competencies." What's your reaction?
I'm a paralegal and I wrote a joke for my firm's newsletter: "Lawyers are like sharks. They both have lots of teeth and they both bite." Could you let me know what you think?

I'm a line cook and I wrote this: "Why did the chef leave his job? Because he couldn't stand the heat. Also the kitchen was really, really hot." Be straight with me, would this go over at the staff dinner?

Just made this up in the shower: "A man walks into a doctor's office and says, 'Doctor, I think I'm invisible.' The doctor says, 'I can't see you right now.'" I'm a pretty casual joke writer. Tell me what you think!
