I work closing shifts at a cinema and made a suggestion to my manager. Here's the email:
"Hi Paula, closing takes us 55 minutes because we sweep each theater after cleaning the concession counter. If one person starts on the theaters while the other counts the till, I timed it at 35 minutes in a trial last Friday. It means everyone leaves earlier and the floors get cleaned while the popcorn is still warm. Can I show you the checklist? Thanks, Devon"
What do you think?

I wanted to thank my manager at the dog daycare and be specific about it. Here's my email:
"Hi Kelly, I wanted to say thanks for staying with me last Wednesday when Biscuit panicked at the gate. Your tip to crouch sideways and not make eye contact worked within a minute. I've used it twice since. It made my first month much less scary. Gratefully, Tess"
What do you think?

I'm a student who works at a climbing gym and want more responsibility. I wrote this to my manager:
"Hi Mateo, I've been running the Tuesday kids' belay check for three months with no incidents. I'd like to try becoming a route-setting apprentice. I've read through the setter handbook, and I could shadow Alex on Wednesday mornings before class. Can we discuss it at our next check-in? Thanks, Lila"
How does it come across?

I run a pet-sitting business and I'm emailing the manager of the kennel I partner with. Here goes:
"Hi Greta, over July 4th weekend, I'd like to reserve five overflow kennels for my regular clients. All five dogs are vaccinated, and I'll send their records by Friday. I'll drop off, feed, and walk them myself, so there's no extra work for your staff. I can pay $200 up front. Could you confirm by the 20th? Thanks, Marcus"
What do you think?

I sell empanadas from a food truck and I'm writing the market manager. I'm excited but a bit nervous:
"Hi Ms. Lindqvist, I've been at the Saturday market for 14 weeks and sold out by 1 p.m. every time. Could I move from the back lot to the corner near the fountain? The line currently blocks no one, but at the corner I could double the queue space. I'd also add a compostable-packaging pledge. Happy to chat. Warmly, Valentina"

Writing to my manager at the call center to ask about working remotely for a week while I'm on a university field trip. Here's my draft:
"Hi Nadia, I'll be at a geology field camp in Utah from Oct 7 to 13 and would love to take calls remotely in the evenings, 5 to 9 p.m. Mountain time, since the camp has Wi-Fi in the lodge. I've tested the VPN from there and it works. If that doesn't suit the team, I'll take the week off. Thanks, Khalid"
Thoughts?

I'm a student who works at a skate rink, and I spotted a hazard. This is my email to my manager:
"Hi Joan, the rubber mat by the rental counter has curled at one corner. Two kids tripped on it today, and nobody was hurt. I've put an orange cone on it and taken a photo, attached. A replacement is about $40 at the hardware store on Elm, and I can pick it up on my way in tomorrow. Okay to do that? Thanks, Sam"
What do you think?

I'm a hobbyist drone photographer and want to pitch a hotel manager. Here's the email:
"Dear Ms. Aoki, I'm a local photographer, and last week at golden hour I shot your hotel's rooftop terrace from above, attached. The frame shows the pool, the hills behind, and the sunset hitting the cabanas. I'd be glad to shoot a full set of ten images for your website for $250. I'm licensed to fly in this area. May I send a quote? Regards, Daniel"
What do you think?

I work at a record shop and send my manager a Friday recap. I tried something different this week:
"Hi Gina, quick recap. We sold 31 used LPs, mostly jazz, which is up from 19 last week. People kept asking for Alice Coltrane, and we had none. Can I put in a bid on the estate collection in Dunmore? I'll check the grading myself. I also fixed the sticky turntable in listening booth 2. Have a great weekend, Theo"
How does it read?

I'm a student who needs to change my work schedule at a pharmacy because of a new class. Here's my email to my manager:
"Hi Mr. Bhatt, my new statistics lecture is Mondays and Wednesdays from 3 to 4:30 p.m., so I can't work those afternoons. I can take Monday and Wednesday mornings instead, plus all of Saturday. That would cover the same 16 hours. Is it possible to switch starting the 9th? I can talk to Elena about trading shifts if needed. Thanks, Aisha"
What do you think?

I've been late three times this month at my job in a bakery, and I'm nervous about the email I wrote to my manager:
"Hi Colette, I want to apologize for being late on the 3rd, 10th, and 17th. My bus line changed its schedule, and I didn't adjust quickly enough. I've switched to the 4:40 bus, which gets me there by 5:05, ten minutes before my shift. If you notice any slip, please tell me directly. Thank you for your patience. Sincerely, Jamal"
How does it sound?

Hi! I'm 15 and wrote this for debate club: "School uniforms should be mandatory because humans have worn uniforms since the dawn of time. Uniforms make everyone equal, and equal is better than unequal. Also my cousin's school has uniforms and he got into college. Therefore, uniforms are better." Can you tell me what you think before Friday's round?

I'm a marketing manager and I'm pitching a 4-day work week to my boss. My key paragraph: "Iceland switched to a 4-day week in 1990 and became the richest country on Earth. Happy employees are happy, and happy people work harder because they are working. Our competitors haven't done it, which is why we should." Thoughts? Be honest-ish, I'm a bit nervous.

Retired science teacher here, 68. Sending this to the local paper: "Cell phones are ruining our youth. Anyone who disagrees is probably addicted to their phone and a fool. In my day we had no phones and everybody turned out fine. Ban them from all public places immediately, and the world will return to normal." What's your take?

This is the thesis of my first college essay: "Social media is bad because it has negative effects that are not good for people. Many people use social media, and it is used a lot, which makes it a problem in today's society." I wanted it to be persuasive. How's it looking?

Hey, I wrote this cold email for my software sales job: "Our software is the best software on the market. It is the number one top-rated best solution for all your needs. Don't miss out on this once in a lifetime opportunity that won't last long. Buy now, or regret it forever." Would you send it if you were me?

I'm 13 and trying to convince my parents to let me stay up until midnight. Here's my speech: "If I go to bed at 9, I will be tired. If I'm tired, I'll fail school. If I fail school, I won't get a job and I'll live in your basement forever. Also, everyone else gets to stay up. Please consider." Do you think it'll work?

I volunteer at an animal shelter and wrote our donation appeal: "Every single day, countless animals suffer in silence. Together, we can make a difference, one paw at a time. Be the change you wish to see in the world. No act of kindness is too small. Donate today!" What do you think? Any feedback welcome!

Law student here, mock trial closing: "Ladies and gentlemen of the jury, my client is innocent. He is so innocent. The prosecution says he was at the scene, but he was clearly somewhere else, probably. And honestly, would an innocent man look this nervous? Only an innocent man would." Can you give me your opinion?

I'm trying to convince my wife we should get a dog. My argument: "Dogs are cute. Cats are not as cute. Our neighbor has a dog and he seems happy. Also I'll walk it every day, definitely, and I've never forgotten anything in my life. Dogs also live forever, basically." Does this seem convincing to you?

I'm a startup founder, and this is the market slide of my investor pitch: "The global pet industry is worth $200 billion. If we capture just 1% of the market, that's $2 billion in revenue. We have no competitors, because nobody else has thought of an app for dog walking." What do you think?

I'm in my 40s and joined a debate league. My opening: "Nuclear power must be banned. Chernobyl happened, and Fukushima happened. Two disasters prove that every nuclear plant is a ticking time bomb. Nobody has ever been hurt by solar panels, so the choice is obvious." Thoughts on how it reads?

I own a pizzeria and wrote this for our flyer: "Best pizza in the world. Number one pizza in town. Our pizza is the very best pizza you will ever taste. Top quality, high quality, great quality pizza. Come try the best pizza today!" Would this make you want to come in? Just curious!

I'm a grad student writing an op-ed: "Humans only use 10% of their brains, so schools are wasting 90% of their potential. If we simply taught kids to unlock the rest, every student would be a genius. Obviously, the education system doesn't want you to know this." Could you tell me how persuasive it is?

I'm an ER nurse and I'm presenting to hospital admin for a better break room: "Nurses are tired. We are very tired. Tired nurses make mistakes, and mistakes are bad. A couch would help, and also a coffee machine, and maybe a mini fridge, and a nicer microwave, and plants." Can I get your reaction?

Hi, I'm 10 and I wrote a persuasive essay! "Pizza should be lunch every day at school. Pizza is yummy. Vegetables are yucky. If kids eat pizza they will be happy and if kids are happy they will learn more. My mom says I am right sometimes. The end." What do you think of it?

Senior dev here. Proposing to my team: "We should rewrite our entire 400k-line Java backend in Rust over the next two weeks. Rust is newer than Java, so it's obviously better. Also, everyone on Hacker News uses it. Downtime during the rewrite should be minimal." How does the argument come across?

Applying for jobs after being laid off. Here's the pitch from my cover letter: "I am a hard worker, a team player, and a people person who thinks outside the box. I am passionate, detail-oriented, and a fast learner with a go-getter attitude. Hire me, and you will not regret it." What's your honest opinion?

I'm a union rep and wrote this for our next meeting: "Management has never cared about us. Not once. They are all greedy, and every manager is the same. Unless we get a 40% raise, full stop, we should strike forever. There's no other option, and compromise is for cowards." How does it sound to you?

I'm a 5th grade teacher making the case to my principal for banning homework: "Studies show 100% of students hate homework. Finland has no homework, and they have the best schools, so homework causes bad schools. Kids need to be kids. I rest my case." Please let me know what you think!

I'm an environmental activist, and here's my flyer text: "If we don't ban plastic straws by next month, the oceans will be dead by Tuesday. Every straw you use kills a hundred turtles. Anyone who uses a straw is a murderer. Join us!" Would love your opinion on it!

I'm launching a Kickstarter for a smart water bottle. Pitch: "Water is essential to life. Our bottle holds water. It's smart, because it has the word smart in it, and an app. You deserve this bottle. Back us now because it's going to be huge, and you'll tell all your friends you were first." Thoughts?

Trying to convince my wife we should buy a boat. I said: "We've already spent $4,000 on boating gear we never used, so we'd be wasting that money if we don't buy the boat. Boats are fun, and fun is important in a marriage. Also, Dave has one." Do you think this will persuade her?

I'm running for city council and this is my flyer: "Vote for me because I'm the best choice. My opponent is not a good choice. I care about this city and the people in it, and I will do things. Change is coming, and change is good. Vote Mike Dawson!" What do you think?

I'm a high school junior writing about grades. My intro: "Grades don't matter. Einstein failed math, and he turned out to be the smartest person ever. Many successful people dropped out too, like Bill Gates, so school is useless. Teachers should stop giving grades so everyone can be a genius." How's my argument?

Hi! Here's the body paragraph from my persuasive essay on school uniforms: "School uniforms should be mandatory because they are good. Uniforms make all students look uniform, which is what uniforms are for. Also, everyone knows students in uniforms get better grades. In conclusion, uniforms are good and schools should have uniforms." Could you tell me what you think?

I just wrote this flyer for my bakery and I'm kind of excited: "Our cupcakes are the BEST cupcakes in town! Why settle for less when you can have the best? Nobody makes cupcakes as good as ours, which is why ours are the best! Come to Sweet Bites today!" Any thoughts before I print 200 copies?

Debate team tomorrow, here's my opening: "Homework should be banned because my cousin never did homework and now he's a millionaire. Also, homework causes stress, and stress is bad. If you support homework, you support suffering. Thank you." Be honest, how does it sound?

Writing a mailer for my new gym. "Are you tired of being tired? Studies show 100% of people who join our gym feel better. Our machines are the newest machines, and our trainers are very trained. Join now, because later is too late!" Does this work, do you think?

Here's the product description I wrote for my handmade candles on Etsy: "Buy my candles because they are handmade and candles are nice. Everyone needs candles. Store-bought candles are made by machines, and machines have no heart, so they are bad for your home." Thoughts? 😊

My civics teacher asked us to argue a position. Mine: "If we allow phones in class, students will text during tests. Then they will stop paying attention completely. Then they will drop out, and soon nobody will have a job, and society will collapse. Therefore, phones must be banned." Can you give me your opinion?

I'm applying to be a barista and wrote this for my cover letter: "I would be the perfect barista because I love coffee and I am a people person. I am a hard worker and a team player who works hard with teams. Coffee is my passion, and passion is what makes a great barista." What's your take?

Nervously posting this for the school newspaper: "The cafeteria should serve pizza every day because pizza is the most popular food in the world. I surveyed three of my friends and all three agreed, so it's basically proven. Students deserve pizza. That's just the truth." Would you read on?

I'm writing a petition for a dog park in our neighborhood: "Dogs are man's best friend, and since dogs are our friends, they deserve a park. Since the dawn of time, humans have loved dogs. A dog park would be good for dogs and also dogs' owners. Please sign." What do you think?

Here's the pitch on my lawn care van: "Hire GreenThumb Lawn Care! We cut grass so you don't have to. Our prices are low and our quality is high, which is rare, and also we are cheap. Your lawn is our lawn." Curious what you think, I'm getting it printed this week.

For my science paper I argued this: "Global warming is caused by the hole in the ozone layer, which lets extra sun heat in. That's why we need to ban aerosol cans immediately. If we stop using hairspray, the hole will close and the planet will cool down." Does this make a strong case?

Okay, my argument for the school board: "Teenagers naturally sleep until noon, which is science. Therefore school should start at noon. Teachers would also be happier at noon. Starting later has no downsides, and anyone who disagrees just hates teenagers." Thoughts? I'm presenting Friday.

Sending this to a potential sponsor for my podcast: "Hey! My show has like 40 listeners, but they're extremely loyal, so your brand will get massive exposure. Sponsor me for $2,000 per episode. You won't find a better deal. Let me know!" How does that read to you?

Here's the start of my speech about reading: "Webster's Dictionary defines reading as the act of reading. In today's society, reading is more important than ever. Books are like windows to other worlds. In conclusion, you should read, because reading is reading." Be gentle, I'm presenting it in English class!

Posting this on my gardening forum, wanted a second opinion first: "You should water your tomatoes with a splash of bleach every week. It kills all the germs, and germs are bad for plants. My neighbor does it and his tomatoes are fine. Trust me, bleach is the secret!" Does this sound convincing?

I wrote this Facebook ad for my dog grooming business: "Your dog deserves the best!!! We groom ALL dogs!!! Big dogs, small dogs, medium dogs!!! Cheap but also premium!!! Call now, your dog will thank you, maybe!!!" What do you think? I'm kind of proud of it honestly.

For my history class I argued: "Rome was the greatest empire because it lasted 1,000 years. Julius Caesar, the first emperor, built it up before Brutus killed him, which proves how powerful he was. Without Rome, there would be no pizza or modern Europe." Can you tell me what you think?

My persuasive essay intro: "Everyone should be vegetarian because animals are cute. Cows are cute, pigs are cute, and chickens are kind of cute. You wouldn't eat a puppy, so why would you eat a cow? Think about it." Feedback welcome! I'll be reading it out loud.

I'm trying to convince my friends to invest in crypto with me: "This coin will hit $1 million by next year because the number keeps going up. It's basically free money, you can't lose. Only losers wait. Send me $500 now and I'll buy it for you." Do you think this will convince them?

Here's what I plan to say to the city council about my bookstore: "Our bookstore should get a tax break because books are good and the city likes books. A city without books is like a city without pages. We have been here for two years, which is a long time." What's your opinion?

This is the opening of my college essay on why I want to attend: "Ever since I was a young child, I've dreamed of attending State University because it's a great school with great academics and a great campus. I am passionate about learning and want to make a difference in the world." Thoughts?

I'm trying to convince my D&D group to let me play my new character: "I should be allowed to play a dragon-vampire-angel because it's more fun for everyone. It's only overpowered if you're jealous. If you say no, you're ruining the game for the whole table." Does that sound persuasive?

Our class is debating zoos. My argument: "Zoos should be abolished because animals don't like being in zoos. We know they don't like it because they are in zoos. If animals liked zoos, they would not be in them. Zoos are bad, and bad things should end." What do you think?

Writing a proposal for a four-day school week: "A four-day week is better because there are fewer days. Some people say kids would learn less, but I disagree. Also, my uncle works four days and he's very happy. Five days is too many, and four is the right number." Any thoughts?

Here's my pitch to the festival organizers for my food truck: "Our tacos are tasty, delicious, and flavorful. You should let us in because food trucks are popular and tacos are popular. We are a taco truck. We make tacos. People like tacos, so they will like our tacos." Thanks for reading, curious what you'd say!

I wrote this to persuade my roommates to get a cat: "We should get a cat because cats are cats. They are soft and they purr. It won't cost much, since cats basically feed themselves. Also, cats never make a mess. If we don't get one, we'll regret it forever." What's your opinion?

I'm 16 and I'm speaking at city council Tuesday about the crosswalk outside my school. Here's my opening: "Council members, you've measured this intersection for traffic. Nobody has measured it for hesitation. Every morning, 400 students stand at that curb and do arithmetic: is the gap wider than my courage? We shouldn't make children gamble to reach a classroom. A $9,000 signal costs less than one ambulance trip." Does this land? I'm pretty nervous.

First letter to the editor I've ever written, as a retired ICU nurse: "The hospital charges $14 to park while your husband is dying. We call that a fee. The family in Bay C calls it the price of saying goodbye. An institution that bills grief by the hour shouldn't call itself a place of healing. Waive parking for critical-care families; it would cost less than the executive retreat." Would you run it if you were the editor?

Proposal to my team to kill our "smart suggestions" feature. Key paragraph: "Suggestions are used by 3% of users and generate 31% of our support tickets. Every feature is a promise to maintain it forever. We aren't deleting a feature; we're refusing a lifelong loan with a 3% return. Cut it, and move those two engineers to search, which 90% of users touch daily." Sending it Monday. Any thoughts first?

Mock trial closing, I'm a 2L and this is my big moment: "The defense wants you to believe in coincidence. The bakery alarm fails on the one night the ledger vanishes. Fine, once. Then the same man holds the only spare key. Then he books a flight for the morning after. Ladies and gentlemen, three coincidences isn't luck. It's a schedule." How does it read to you? Be straight with me.

I'm 63, been farming all my life, never given a speech. Tomorrow at the co-op I'll say: "Each of us owns a combine that sits idle 340 days a year. That's eleven machines, eleven loans, eleven rusting evenings. Buy one together and we each keep our money and lose only our pride. And my father's pride never once made a payment." Would that move you if you were sitting in the room?

Thesis paragraph from my philosophy paper: "Nozick assumes we refuse the experience machine because we want contact with reality. I think we refuse because we want to be answerable: to be the kind of person who can let someone down. A simulated life contains no one we can fail, and so no one whose forgiveness we can earn. That, not the missing real world, is what we'd mourn." Does the argument hold together?

Pitching our bookshop to the bank for a $40,000 loan. This is the core of it: "Amazon will always be cheaper. We don't sell books; we sell the eleven minutes a stranger spent telling you which one to read. No warehouse can ship that. Lend us $40,000 and we'll open Sundays, when people have the most time to be recommended to." I'd love an honest opinion on whether it would persuade a loan officer.

I'm 10 and I wrote a letter to my parents about getting a dog. "Dear Mom and Dad, I did research. A dog costs about $1,200 a year. I have $212 saved and will walk neighbors' dogs for the rest. You said responsibility can't be taught by talking about it. I agree. Please let me prove it." Do you think it will work on them? I want to give it to them Saturday.

I teach middle school and I'm presenting to the board about the proposed cut to orchestra. My closing line: "Cutting orchestra saves $38,000, which is 0.02% of our budget. It costs us the only room where sixty children learn to be wrong in public, together, and still be in tune by Friday." Is that the right way to end, or should I bring numbers back in? Curious what you think.

I'm a city planner arguing against parking minimums at tonight's meeting. Here's my draft: "Every required parking space is a small law declaring that a car deserves more room than a person does. Minimums didn't give us parking. They gave us distance: longer walks, wider roads, and a grocery store that's a mile from the nearest front door." Be honest, how does it sound out loud? I tend to over-explain.

I used to be a line cook and I'm applying for project manager roles. The paragraph of my cover letter that matters: "I've run a fourteen-burner line on a Saturday night with two cooks down. Your sprint deadlines don't frighten me; I have never missed a 7 p.m. seating. I can't write Python, but I can tell you which of your five blockers will be on fire by Thursday." Would you keep reading or toss it?

Drafting a grant request for a long-term beetle survey and trying a bolder opening: "We're asking you to fund the least glamorous work in conservation: counting. You cannot protect what you cannot number. Our twelve-year survey is the only reason we knew the wetland was failing years before the herons left. Counting is how we hear a warning while it's still a whisper." Does it work as a first paragraph for a funder?

Text I'm about to send my sister, who's been dodging Mom's 70th: "Come home. Not because you owe it, you don't. But in ten years you won't remember the meeting you skipped. You will remember whether Mom looked at the door when you walked in." I'm worried it's too much, or not enough. What do you think?

I'm a literary translator replying to a post claiming AI will make us obsolete: "Translation isn't swapping words. It's deciding what to lose. Every sentence of Chekhov costs something in English, and someone has to choose the price. A machine can hand you the menu. It can't tell you which dish to give up, or sit with you while you grieve it." Posting this tonight. Would you share it?

Telling a client why we removed the "Skip" button from their onboarding flow: "Skip is a promise that the next screen isn't worth your time. If you believe that, don't ship the screen. If you don't, don't offer the exit. Either way, the button is a confession." I get one email to convince them. Does the logic hold, and is the tone okay for a client?

I'm the mayor of a town of 6,000 and I'm campaigning for the library levy. Here's a section of my speech: "A library is the last place in town where you can walk in with no money and nobody asks why you're there. It costs the average household $41 a year. Ask yourself what else you can buy that's open to everyone, including the person you'd never think of." How does that sit with you?

I'm an accountant asking my boss to renew remote work. This is the core of my email: "Last year, in the two months I worked from home, I closed the books four days early both times. I'm not asking for a perk; I'm asking you to renew an experiment whose results you've already seen. The data is attached. If it fails, I'll come back in myself." Does that feel persuasive or pushy?

Scholarship essay opening, I'm 18 and writing about my grandmother: "Ask my grandmother what a good investment is and she'll point to a fig tree: nothing for four years, then fruit for forty. When people ask why I want to be a soil scientist, I tell them I'd like to spend my life on slow returns. Please fund the four years." Would this make a committee remember me?

I'm a pediatrician and I've been practicing this for a hesitant parent: "I won't tell you your fear is irrational. It's the right instinct pointed at the wrong target. You want to protect her from harm, and so do I. Measles just feels less threatening because it hasn't walked into your house yet. I've watched it walk into other people's." Does it come across as respectful, or does it risk sounding preachy?

Pitching my D&D group on the next campaign: "You're all accountants to the villains. Nobody swings a sword. Every fireball comes with an invoice, the dragon's hoard needs an audit, and the Dark Lord will be furious about Q3. Trust me, the most terrifying thing in any dungeon is a well-organized ledger." Would this get you to say yes, or should I tone down the absurdity?

Opening of an appellate brief on water rights: "This Court is asked to decide whether a river can be sold twice. The State sold its water to the mill in 1911 and to the town in 1987. Only one sale can have been valid, and the 1911 deed, read as written, conveyed the mill a use, not the river." I'm a few years out of law school. Any feedback on the framing?

I coach a high school soccer team that went 0-11 and the athletic director wants to cut it. I'm sending him this: "You're measuring the wrong scoreboard. Twenty-two kids who'd otherwise be home alone at 3 p.m. have shown up every day, in the rain, for a season of losing. I'd like to be the adult who tells them it counted. Give us one more year." How would you react if you were him?

Our neighborhood association wants to cut down the old oak beside the church to add 14 parking spots. I'm speaking against it: "That oak is 140 years old. Parking lots get repaved every twenty years; trees can only be cut once. You can always add spaces later. You can't add a hundred and forty years." I'm 71 and not much of a public speaker. Is it enough?

I'm a union rep making the case for a four-day week at a hospital laundry. My pitch to management: "Our turnover costs you $9,000 per replaced worker. Every Friday, someone leaves a job they're good at because they're exhausted. Give them Fridays and you're not subsidizing leisure; you're buying back experience at a discount." I'm used to bargaining, but writing's not my strength. How does it come across?

I'm 24 and I've written the first line of a donor email for our food pantry: "Hunger isn't a shortage of food in this town. It's a shortage of Tuesdays: the ones between paychecks, when the fridge empties before the rent clears. $30 buys a family a Tuesday." I'd really like to know if it makes you want to keep reading and give.

I run a small repair cafe and wrote this for our funding application: "A toaster thrown away is a decision made by a manufacturer and paid for by a landfill. We give people the chance to make a different decision for the price of a screwdriver and a cup of tea. Last year, 1,300 items stayed in use, and so did the people who fixed them." Does it make a strong case, in your opinion?

I'm a retired history teacher writing to my congressman to save our town's tiny railway museum: "You'll hear that we're a museum of old trains. We're really a museum of arrivals: where your grandparents stepped off with one suitcase and a surname the clerk misspelled. Cut our $18,000 and the building will stay. The surnames won't." Would a busy staffer read this and care?

Debate practice is tomorrow and this is my closing for "start school later." Feedback please: "My opponents say teenagers should just go to bed earlier. But biology isn't a habit. At puberty, the body's melatonin shifts about two hours later. Asking a sixteen-year-old to sleep at nine is like asking them to be taller. Don't blame the clock in their bodies. Fix the one on our wall." Does it land?

I'm putting this on the counter card at my bakery to get people to bring their own boxes: "Our croissants take three days to make. Their box takes three seconds to throw away. Bring your own container and we'll take 50 cents off, because anything worth waiting for deserves better than cardboard." Would this make you do it? Be blunt.

I'm writing to my HOA board about replacing my front lawn with native plants. Here's my key paragraph: "The bylaws ask for a yard that looks cared for. Mine will be: mapped, mulched, edged, and labeled with a small sign naming each species. A lawn takes forty hours of mowing a year; this takes four of weeding, and it feeds the bees that pollinate the neighborhood's tomatoes." Any thoughts before I send it?

I get two minutes at the school board meeting to save our Latin program. My opening: "Cutting Latin saves $41,000 once. Keeping it pays out in every unfamiliar word a student ever has to decode, on the SAT, in a biology textbook, in a legal contract. We're not preserving a dead language. We're funding a skeleton key." What would you change, if anything?

I run a small bike repair shop and my landlord wants a 30% rent increase. Core of my email: "Since 2019 my customers have parked outside your other tenants' doors about 11,000 times, and the café next door tells me Saturday is their busiest day because of us. A shop that brings foot traffic is the cheapest anchor tenant you'll ever have. I'd like to renew at 8%." Would you send it?

Trying to talk my D&D group into a one-shot instead of another six-month campaign. My pitch in the chat: "Forget the 40-hour commitment. One night. Four heroes, one sinking ship, ninety minutes before the tide takes the library. If you hate it, we've lost an evening. If you love it, we've got a story you'll tell for years." Thoughts?

Here's the opening of my op-ed for the school paper: "Every day, our cafeteria throws away about thirty pounds of untouched fruit. Students aren't rejecting apples. They have 22 minutes for lunch, and nine of them are spent in line. Lengthen lunch by ten minutes and the apples might finally get eaten." Does it work as an opening?

I'm asking our running club to start a 12-minute-mile group. This is what I'll say Thursday: "Every club says it welcomes beginners. Then the beginners show up, watch the pack vanish around the first corner, and never return. A group where nobody gets dropped isn't a lesser group. It's the one that will still exist in five years." Honest take?

I'm a wedding photographer, and this is a pitch email to a couple choosing between me and a cheaper option: "You'll forget the centerpieces and the playlist. In forty years, you'll want your grandmother's hands adjusting your veil, and your father's face a second before he walks you down the aisle. I take only twelve weddings a year, so I can be standing where those moments happen." Should I send it?

I'm 16 and speaking to city council on Tuesday about Sunday library hours. My ending: "Closing on Sundays saves $9,000 a year. But the kid in my building with no wifi still has homework due Monday. The savings show up in your budget. The cost shows up in his grade. Please don't make him pay it." Does this work for a three-minute speech?

Wrote this for our woodworking forum, arguing beginners should buy a hand plane before a table saw: "A table saw teaches you to fear the machine. A plane teaches you to read the wood. Fear makes you cautious; reading makes you good. Spend $60 on the plane, and save your fingers for the day you're ready for the saw." Feedback welcome!

For English we had to write a persuasive paragraph. Mine argues cooking should be required: "We make every student learn the quadratic formula, which most will never use, but not how to feed themselves, which they'll do about 20,000 times. Nobody has ever been stranded by a parabola. Plenty of people have been stranded by an empty fridge and ten dollars." What do you think?

I'm applying for a spot at our farmers market. Here's the paragraph from my application: "Other coffee vendors sell to people already walking past. I sell to the people who haven't arrived yet. My cart opens thirty minutes before the market, and those early customers stay to buy produce. Last season, three vendors told me their first sale of the day went to someone holding my cup." Is it convincing?

I'm emailing the city to ask that skyscraper lights go off during migration season. My main argument: "On two October nights I counted 212 dead warblers at the base of three downtown buildings. Each weighed about as much as two quarters. Switching off the lights from midnight to dawn for six weeks costs almost nothing, and spares them the one thing they navigate by." Would you change anything?

Persuasive speech for class, about weekend homework: "Adults protect their weekends and call it work-life balance. We have the same brains, the same need to rest, and a Monday test. If homework is practice, let us practice Monday through Friday. Give us Saturday, and I promise that by Sunday night I'll remember why I like learning." Any feedback on how persuasive it is?

I'm trying to get my neighbors to chip in for a shared backyard pizza oven. Flyer text: "Twelve households. $85 each. One oven. We already share a fence and a dozen opinions about parking. Let's share something that smells better." Honestly, would you show up to the meeting?

I'm putting this on my dog-grooming flyer: "Your dog can't tell you his ears hurt. He can only shake his head and look at you. A groomer sees mats, ticks, and lumps weeks before a vet appointment would. Book every six weeks and you get a clean dog and a second set of eyes." Does the tone feel right to you?

Here's the thesis paragraph of my philosophy paper: "Critics say our refusal to enter Nozick's experience machine is just status quo bias. But tell people they're already plugged in, and most still choose to unplug. A bias toward the familiar can't explain that. A desire for contact with reality itself can." Does the argument hold up?

Group chat message I'm about to send to convince my friends to try a co-op board game: "Every game night ends with one person happy and four pretending to be. Pandemic ends with five people shouting at the same board, and either we all lose or we all get to be insufferable about it. Try it once." Do you think it'd work on a skeptical crowd?

Writing to my principal to ask that the music room stay open at lunch: "Unlock one door, add a sign-in sheet, and I'll handle cleanup. It costs nothing. In return, forty kids stop eating alone in a hallway and start a band." Does this sound like something a principal would say yes to?

This is the new homepage copy for my plumbing company: "A $20 valve inspection is boring. A flooded kitchen at 2 a.m. is not. Most of our emergency calls started as a drip someone meant to look at. Book a yearly check, and the only exciting thing in your house will be dinner." Does it sound like a real person wrote it?

I'm applying for a historical marker for the old Delmar Bakery on 5th Street. Our statement opens: "For 41 years this building fed the neighborhood on credit. A ledger still hangs on the back wall, recording striking miners' debts the owner never collected. Towns are remembered for their monuments, but they're held together by their bakeries." How does it read to you?

Here are the last lines of my class president speech: "You've heard promises about vending machines and longer dances. I can't promise those. I can promise that every Friday at 3:15, I'll post what I asked the principal and what she answered, word for word. Vote for the person who'll show their work." What's your honest reaction?

I host a local hiking podcast with 800 listeners and I'm pitching an outdoor store for sponsorship: "Eight hundred is a small crowd. But every one of them has just spent forty minutes learning a trail they plan to hike this weekend. They won't skip your ad. They'll be standing in your parking lot Saturday morning, buying socks." Would this convince you?

I'm a florist pitching a hotel lobby contract. Here's my core paragraph: "Imported roses travel 5,000 miles to look the same in January as in July. Your guests won't remember them. Seasonal flowers grown within forty miles change every month, so regulars notice. A lobby guests mention is worth more than a lobby that's merely nice." What do you think?

Hi! I'm in 4th grade and my science fair project is: 'Which paper towel is the best?' I will test Bounty and another kind with water. My hypothesis is that Bounty will win because it costs more. What do you think?

My project: Does music affect plants? I'll play heavy metal to one plant and nothing to the other, in my room. I'll measure growth after 3 days. I expect the metal plant to die because sound waves hurt it. Can you tell me your opinion?

I'm a 6th grade teacher drafting a sample project for my class: 'Does the moon's phase change how fast ice melts?' I'll put one ice cube outside on a full moon night and one on a new moon night and compare. Would this work as an example for students?

My daughter (age 8) and I came up with: 'Can a potato power a house?' We'll connect one potato to a lightbulb and, if it lights, scale up to a house. We figure a few hundred potatoes should do it. Thoughts before we submit the proposal?

Um, hi, this is my first science fair. My question is 'Do plants grow better with water or soda?' I'll give one plant each water, Coke, Sprite, Mountain Dew and orange juice, and keep them in different rooms of the house. Is this okay? I'm kind of nervous.

For my intro bio fair, I'm proposing: 'Does hand sanitizer kill 100% of germs?' I'll swab my hands before and after, then look at the swabs with my eyes for germs. Conclusion: it kills 99.9%, like the bottle says. Feedback appreciated!

Retired engineer here, mentoring at the local fair. My idea is a perpetual motion machine: a wheel of magnets that spins forever once started. I'll leave it running for the judges. Materials cost about $40. Does this sound like a strong entry?
ok so my project is 'Does gum make you smarter?' I'm gonna have 3 friends chew gum then take a math test I made up, and 3 other friends not chew. Whoever scores higher wins. lol what do you think

My project is about volcanoes. I will make a volcano with baking soda and vinegar. Then it will erupt. Then I will make another volcano and it will erupt too. I will write down that it erupted. Any tips?

I'm a nurse and my son needs a science fair topic. I suggested: 'Does cracking knuckles cause arthritis?' He'll crack the knuckles on one hand for two weeks and leave the other alone, then check for arthritis. Do you think the judges will like this?

My title is 'Using Wi-Fi Signals to Cure Colds.' I'll seat a sick friend next to my router for a week and track symptoms. If they get better, Wi-Fi cures colds. I'm hoping to make it to state. How does it look?

Our homeschool co-op project is 'Why is the sky blue?' Our answer: the sky reflects the ocean, so it's blue. We'll demonstrate by pouring blue water in a bowl and pointing out it looks like the sky. Can I get your opinion before we print the poster?

I'm a software dev helping my niece. Her project: 'Which phone is fastest?' Code: import time; start=time.time(); for i in range(10): print(i); print(time.time()-start). We'll run it on each phone with a Python app and compare the times. Thoughts?

Project: 'The Effect of Sleep on Grades.' I will sleep 4 hours a night for one week and 10 hours the next and compare my grades. Hypothesis: more sleep, better grades. Conclusion: sleep is important. Please tell me what you think!

I want to find out if dogs like music. My dog Max is the subject. I played Taylor Swift and he looked at me. Then I played Beethoven and he fell asleep. So dogs like Beethoven more. Is this enough for an experiment? I'm 10.

I'm 68 and my grandson wants to enter a fair with my idea: a car that runs on plain tap water. Water has hydrogen, so the engine burns it. We'll pour water in the tank and drive around the yard. What's your opinion?

My project compares the strength of two magnets. Magnet A picked up 5 paperclips. Magnet B picked up 3 paperclips. So magnet A is stronger. I will also write that magnets are magnetic. The display board will be pink. Can you give feedback?

Does food color change taste? I'll give my family red, blue, and green mashed potatoes and ask which tastes best. I think blue will taste like blueberries. I'll only ask my mom so it's fast. Would you change anything?

My senior project: curing cancer with lemon juice. I read online that lemons are 10,000 times stronger than chemo. I'll grow cancer cells in my garage and add lemon juice. Do you think a judge would be interested?

Here's my abstract: 'This project is about plants. Plants are living things that need sun. I put plants in sun and not in sun to see what happens. The plants in the sun were greener. In conclusion, plants need sun.' Is that ready to submit?

Here's the Python for my fair's gravity simulator:
height = 10
while height > 0:
    height = height - 1
    print(height)
It shows a ball falling to the ground. I'm a bit nervous about showing it to the judges. Does this make sense?

Boiling vs. microwave: which heats water faster? I'll boil 1 cup on the stove and 2 liters in the microwave and time both. My son's hypothesis is the stove wins because it has fire. Does the setup look okay to you?

Do fish get bored? I will put 1 goldfish in a bowl with nothing and 1 goldfish in a bowl with a castle. Then I will watch them for 1 minute and see which looks more bored. I'm 9. What do you think of this idea?

I'm a barista taking night classes. My project: does more caffeine make you type faster? I'll drink 1 espresso, then 5, then 10 and test my typing speed after each, all within an hour. Curious what you think.

Project idea: 'Do boys or girls have better memory?' I'll test 2 boys and 2 girls with a list of 10 words. I'll pick the boys from my soccer team and the girls from my sister's choir. Please give me your honest opinion.

My science fair idea: I'm going to test if plants grow better with music. I'll play rock to one bean plant and classical to the other, water them the same, and measure which is taller after a week. My hypothesis is classical wins because it's more relaxing. What do you think?

Hi! I'm in 7th grade and my project is called "Why We Have Seasons." With a lamp and a globe I'll show that summer happens when Earth is closer to the Sun and winter when it's farther away. I'm kind of proud of it. Any feedback before I make my poster?

I own a small bakery and my daughter's class asked me to help with a project. Idea: "Which yeast brand is best?" I'll bake one loaf with each of three brands, taste them myself, and announce the winner. Would this work for a science fair? Curious what you'd say.

My project is a volcano. I'll make it out of clay and use baking soda and vinegar so it erupts, and add red food coloring so it looks like lava. The title is "How Volcanoes Work." Do you have any thoughts on it? Thanks!

I'm 15 and I want to build a perpetual motion machine for the fair. It's a wheel with magnets around the edge that keeps spinning forever and will power a small lightbulb. My budget is $20. Can you tell me your opinion on the idea?

I keep two beehives as a hobby and want to enter the county fair. I planted blue, red, and yellow flowers and counted bees one afternoon: 14 on blue, 3 on the others. Conclusion: bees prefer blue. I'd love to hear what you think of this project!

ok so my idea is to test which homemade water filter is best. I'll pour muddy pond water through a coffee filter, then sand, then a cotton ball, and then drink each one to see if it's clean. Pretty excited about it. Thoughts?

Here's my hypothesis and procedure. Hypothesis: If I put ice in the sun, then it will melt, because the sun is hot. Procedure: Put ice outside in the sun and watch it. Data: The ice melted. Conclusion: The sun melts ice. Could you give me your opinion?

For my science fair I wrote a Python program to average my reaction times:
times = [210, 250, 190, 300]
total = 0
for i in range(1, len(times)):
    total += times[i]
print(total / len(times))
It prints a number so I think I'm done! Any feedback?

My project shows that cell phones can cook an egg. I'll put a raw egg between two phones, call one from the other, and wait an hour. I read that the radiation gets really hot. I'm hoping to win a ribbon with it. What do you think?

I run a small candle shop and I'm sponsoring a table at our town's science night. My demo is titled "Candles Burn Because of Fire." I'll light candles in different colors and show that they all burn. Would you have any thoughts for me?

Hi, I'm kind of nervous about this. My science fair project is about "Space." I'll make a poster about the planets and glue a model of each one onto it, and write facts underneath. Can you let me know what you think?

I'm testing which fertilizer grows the biggest tomatoes. I'm using four fertilizers, but different pot sizes, and I'll put them in different spots in the yard. I'll water them whenever I remember. I can't wait to see the results! Thoughts?

My project proves that heavier objects fall faster. I'll drop a bowling ball and a feather off the roof, time them with my phone, and show the bowling ball hits first. That proves Aristotle was right! Would you give me your honest opinion?

As a hobby brewer, I want to do a project on fermentation. My hypothesis is that yeast eats the alcohol in the wort and produces sugar, which is why beer tastes sweet at the end. I'll show it with a jar and a balloon. What do you think?

My plan: train a neural network in one week to diagnose cancer from photos I find on Google Images. I'm aiming for 100% accuracy and I'll present it to real doctors at the fair. I've never coded before, but I'm really motivated. Thoughts on this idea?
ok so idea: does chewing gum make you smarter? I'll chew gum during my next math test and compare my score to my last test, which I took without gum. me vs me lol. what do you think??

Here's my abstract: "In this experiment, the experiment tested the pH of soda. Soda is acidic. The soda was tested using pH paper and the results were in the data. Soda is bad for teeth and that is why this is important." Could you let me know what you think?

I own a small gym and want a display for the school fair: "Protein Shakes Make Muscles Instantly Bigger." I'll measure my biceps before and after drinking one shake, and show the difference on a chart. Would love your thoughts!

My title is "The Amazing World of Magnets: Discover the Power of Attraction!" My question is: Do magnets stick to things? I'll test ten objects around my house and write down yes or no. I worked hard on the title. What do you think?

I have a fish tank hobby and want to show that fish grow bigger in bigger tanks. I'll put one goldfish in a 1-gallon bowl and one in a 50-gallon tank, and give the big tank fish extra food too. Can I get your opinion on this?

My project asks: does cup color change how fast hot water cools? I'll use a white ceramic mug and a black plastic cup, pour in the same hot water, and check the temperature after 10 minutes. I'm proud of how simple it is. Any thoughts?

For my project, I'll rub my hands on bread slices in bags: one after washing with soap, one after hand sanitizer, one with nothing. Whichever grows the least mold shows which kills the most bacteria. I'm excited to start! What do you think?

I'm in 8th grade and here's my science fair idea: Do kitchen sponges really get cleaner when microwaved? I'll cut one used sponge into 4 equal squares, treat them (60 sec microwave while wet, vinegar soak, dish soap rinse, untreated), then swab each, make serial dilutions, and count colonies on agar plates after 48 hours. I'll run it on 3 sponges from different homes. Does the design hold up? Anything I should change before I start?

Hi! I'm a high school senior and I'm planning to measure the inclination of Earth's magnetic field at our school. I'll wind a Helmholtz coil from magnet wire, drive it with a known current, and use a phone magnetometer to cancel the local field component along each axis. Then I'll compare my angle to the NOAA value for our zip code and report the percent error. I'd love your honest opinion on this plan.

I taught middle school science for 31 years and now help at our library's fair night. My idea: test Dolbear's law on local crickets. I record evenings at five spots with a phone and a clip-on thermometer, use a spectrogram to ID species by pulse pattern, then plot chirp rate against temperature separately per species instead of lumping them. My guess is the law's slope differs between species. What's your take on it?

I'm a night-shift nurse helping my daughter with this, and honestly the idea was mine: How long do you really need to wash hands? Volunteers press fingertips on agar after glowing-lotion contamination, then wash for 5, 10, 20, or 30 seconds with the same soap and water temp. I'll check each person with a UV lamp before plating, so I can separate technique from time. Could you give feedback on the setup?

I'm 10 and my project asks: do bean seedlings bend more toward blue light than red light? I'm making 4 cardboard boxes with one LED window each (blue, red, green, white), all set to 50 lux with my dad's light meter. 12 seedlings per box. I'll photograph them every 6 hours and measure the bend angle with a protractor on the photos. What do you think? Should I add anything?

I run a small vegetable farm and I want to enter our county fair's open science category. I'm testing whether tillage affects earthworm numbers. In 10 plots, I'll pour 5 liters of dilute mustard water per quarter-square-meter, count worms that surface in 10 minutes, then dig and hand-sort the same square to check the mustard method. Any feedback on whether that comparison makes sense?

I'm an electrician and I built a solar water heater from copper pipe in a window-box frame. I'm painting three identical absorbers (matte black, selective-coating paint, and flat dark green), logging inlet and outlet temperatures with thermocouples on an Arduino, and dividing by readings from a reference photodiode so cloudy days don't skew results. I'd like to know how this reads to you as a fair project.

I'm a software engineer and keep bees. My idea: point a Raspberry Pi camera at the hive entrance and use a trained model to count bees entering and leaving per minute. Then I'd log temperature, humidity, and light, and find the temperature at which foraging switches on in the morning, over a whole season. I'll share the code publicly. Does it sound like a good fit for a science fair? Please be honest.

I'm in 7th grade. My question: does road salt melt ice faster than sugar or sand? I'm using the same number of moles, not the same weight, of NaCl, CaCl2, and sucrose on identical ice discs. Chemistry says NaCl splits into 2 particles, CaCl2 into 3, and sucrose stays at 1, so I predict melt depth ratios near 2:3:1. Sand is my control. Can you tell me what you think of my design?

I'm a line cook who got curious about browning. I'll caramelize identical onion slices in solutions of baking soda at five different pH levels, then photograph each batch every 5 minutes next to a gray card and convert the pixels to L*a*b* color values. Then I'll plot how fast browning happens against pH. I'm a little nervous presenting at a science fair as a non-scientist. What do you think of it?

I'm 16 and I'd like to redo Eratosthenes. I teamed up with a student at a school 410 km due north of mine through an online club. On the same day at local solar noon, we each measure a vertical stick's shadow and compute the sun angle, then use the angle difference and the distance to estimate Earth's circumference. I'll also propagate the measurement uncertainty to see whether we can tell our answer apart from 40,075 km. Thoughts?

I'm a college sophomore volunteering as a mentor. Our student wants to count microplastic fibers shed by washing machines. She'll collect rinse water through three lint filters (none, mesh, and a ball), stain it with Nile red, shine a blue flashlight through an orange filter, and count the glowing fibers per liter under a USB microscope. Blank filters will check for contamination from the lab. I'd like feedback on her design.

I'm a grad student in plant science and I'm helping my little cousin make a project. We make alginate hydrogel beads at 0.5%, 1%, and 2% calcium chloride cross-linking, mix them into sand, and then plant radish seeds and water the pots on a drought schedule. We'll measure germination rate and root length on day 10. Could you let me know if the variables are cleanly separated? I'm worried I'm too close to it.

I'm a dad who loves physics, and my son and I are building a cloud chamber from dry ice, isopropanol, and a fish tank. We'll count particle tracks per minute with the chamber tilted at 0°, 30°, 60°, and 90°, then shield half the runs with lead flashing. We want to see whether the counts follow the cos² distribution cosmic muons are supposed to have. I'd love a reaction to the plan, especially the angle part.

I'm 68 and retired, and I'm sick of mosquito-repelling phone apps. For my grandson's fair, we'll build a two-chamber choice box with a screen divider, put in 20 fruit flies, and then play the app's tone on only one side. A blinded helper chooses the side with a coin flip. After 10 minutes we count the flies per side. Then we'll repeat it 30 times and run a binomial test. What's your opinion?

I'm in 6th grade and I'm testing paper airplane winglets. I made a launcher from a ruler and a rubber band pulled back to exactly 10 cm so every launch has the same speed. I'll fold 5 identical planes for each wing design (none, up, down, and split tips), throw each one 10 times, and record the glide distance from a fixed height. Then I'll calculate the glide ratio for each. Does this sound good to you?

I teach high school chemistry. My project idea for students is to turn red cabbage juice into a measuring tool. We photograph the juice in 8 buffers (pH 2-9) on a white card under the same lamp, build a calibration curve of the hue values, and then use it to estimate rainwater pH at 10 spots around town. We'll compare the estimates to a lab pH meter and give the error. I'd love your thoughts.

I'm a bike mechanic, and I'm turning a shop question into a project: how much does tire pressure change rolling resistance? I'll roll the same bicycle with the same rider down a ramp at 5 pressures (30 to 110 psi), and measure how far it coasts on a flat concrete floor. Five trials per pressure. I'll also do rough pavement. I'm hoping to show the curve flattens out. Any feedback?

I'm a psychology major working on a project for a youth science fair. Does music tempo change performance on the Stroop task? Sixty classmates will each do three counterbalanced blocks: silence, 60 bpm, and 120 bpm instrumental tracks matched for loudness and key. I'll record reaction times and errors, and use a paired analysis and a Latin square to cancel out practice effects. How does the design strike you?

I'm an ecology teacher and I want my students to do the Tea Bag Index at school. We'll bury green and rooibos teabags 8 cm deep in three schoolyard spots (mowed lawn, garden bed, and woodlot edge), then dig them up after 90 days, dry them, and weigh them. From the mass loss we get the decomposition rate and the stabilization factor for each habitat. I'd really like your take on whether it suits a fair.

I'm a first-year med student, and I'm planning a transmission model for a middle school class. I'll put UV powder on one 'index case' hand, track spread over a 20-minute class period through door handles, pencils, and handshakes, and count contaminated surfaces afterward. Then we'll fit the data to a simple SIR model and test whether adding hand sanitizer stations at 5 minutes slows it. I'd appreciate any feedback.

I'm 14 and I like music, so I'm doing Chladni plates. I'm bolting a 20 cm square aluminum plate to a speaker driver, sprinkling salt on it, and sweeping frequencies from 100 to 3000 Hz. I'll photograph each pattern at resonance, then compare the frequencies to the theoretical plate-mode formula to find which ones match. I'll also test how the patterns change when I clamp the plate at its center vs. its edge. What do you think?

I'm a civil engineering technician and I'm planning a mini concrete project for my niece. We'll cast 12 beams (4x4x16 cm) with 0, 1%, 2%, and 3% fibers by volume (hair, straw, or shredded plastic bags). Each beam is supported at both ends, and a bucket on the middle slowly fills with sand until the beam breaks. The failure load is divided by the beam's mass. All beams will cure 28 days. Does this seem like a solid project?

I'm in 9th grade and I want to find out if my school's two ponds differ in biodiversity. I'll take 5 water samples from each, 100 mL each, and count the organisms by group under a $40 microscope using a Sedgewick-Rafter-style gridded slide I made from a plastic slide and a laser-cut grid. Then I'll calculate the Shannon index for each pond. I'd like a candid reaction to the plan before I submit it.

I'm a retired machinist and now I do science fairs with kids. This year's project: does a pendulum's period change with amplitude as much as the equation says? We'll film a 1 m pendulum at 5°, 15°, 30°, 45°, and 60° with a 240 fps phone camera, extract the period frame by frame, and compare it to the small-angle formula and the elliptic-integral correction. We'd like to know how this comes across.

I'm a nervous 12-year-old, but here goes. I noticed my dog's water bowl gets slimy faster outside than inside. I'm going to put 6 identical bowls out: 3 steel and 3 ceramic, half in shade and half in sun, and swab a 1 cm square from each bowl every day for 5 days. I'll then streak the swabs on agar and compare how many colonies grow. Please let me know what you think of the idea.

Hi! My science fair idea: do fleece jackets shed more microplastic fibers in hotter washes? I'll wash three identical jackets at 20, 30, 40 and 60°C, five washes each, with a 25-micron filter on the machine outlet. Then I dry the filtrate and weigh it to 0.001 g. Same detergent, same load, and a blank wash as control. Prediction: shedding rises with temperature, but plateaus. What's your opinion on the design?

I'm 16 and nervous about this. My project uses Daphnia heart rate as a bioassay for caffeine. Concentrations: 0, 50, 100, 200 mg/L in spring water, 10 Daphnia each. I film them under a microscope at 30 fps and count beats frame by frame, after a 5-minute acclimation. I'll run ANOVA at the end. Could you tell me what you think of the setup?

I keep bees, and I want to enter our county fair with this: a hive on a $12 load cell and a microcontroller, logging weight every 15 minutes for a whole summer. I'll plot overnight weight gain against local bloom dates from a county phenology list to show nectar flow. Raw data and temperature are logged too. Any thoughts on it as a project?

I run a small bakery and I'm mentoring a student with this idea. Sourdough starter in identical clear jars, same flour and hydration, held at 18, 22, 26 and 30°C in water baths. Time-lapse photos mark rise height every 10 minutes. Then we compute peak-rise time and estimate Q10 for fermentation. Three jars per temperature. How would you rate the approach?

Here's my plan: road salt versus roadside grass. I'll germinate 50 native grass seeds per dish in NaCl solutions of 0, 1, 2, and 4 g/L, four dishes each. I'll count germinated seeds daily for 14 days and graph the curves, not just the final percentage, so delays show up. I also measure radicle length on day 14. Honest feedback welcome, please!

I make soap, and I want to test whether water hardness affects cleaning. I soil cotton swatches with a standard oil and carbon mix, wash them with the same soap bar in distilled, 120 ppm, and 300 ppm hard water, then photograph the swatches under fixed light. A grayscale app gives reflectance values. Ten swatches per condition. What's your opinion of this?

My project compares 3D-printed infill patterns: gyroid, grid, and honeycomb. Each test cube is adjusted to exactly 12.0 g (±0.1) so strength is per unit mass. I print five of each and load them with sand until they fail, recording the mass of sand at the crack. Same filament, same print temperature. Tell me what you think, please. I'm happy to take criticism.

Hey, quick one. For the fair I'm testing if people react faster to light, sound, or touch. I built an Arduino rig with an LED, buzzer, and small vibration motor, randomized delays of 2–6 s, and a button. 30 classmates, 20 trials per stimulus, with the first 3 trials discarded as practice. I'll compare the medians. Can you give me your take on it?

My friend in a city 400 km north and I are redoing Eratosthenes. On the equinox, we both measure a vertical stick's shadow at local solar noon, which we calculate from our longitudes. Shadow angle differences give us Earth's circumference. We'll also quantify the error from our stick leaning, using a plumb line. I'd love to hear what you think of it!

I teach pottery classes as a hobby, and I'm designing a project on crazing. Same clay body and same glaze on 18 tiles. I fire them together, then cool them at three rates by cracking the kiln lid at 900°C, 700°C, or leaving it closed. I count crazing lines per cm² after 24 hours and a week. What would you say about this?

For my project, I'm testing paper helicopters. I vary rotor length from 5 to 12 cm in 1 cm steps while keeping paper mass constant by adjusting width. Each design gets 10 drops from 3 m, timed with slow-mo video. I expect a peak, since longer rotors add lift but also weight. I'd like your honest opinion before I build the poster.

I garden in a community plot, and my idea is to map soil pH using red cabbage indicator. I take samples from 12 spots, mix each with distilled water at 1:2, and compare filtrate colors against a reference scale I calibrated with buffer solutions. Then I check results against a store-bought meter and the hydrangea bloom color. Would you tell me what you think?

My science fair project: which materials absorb sound best? A speaker plays pink noise at a fixed volume into a shoebox with a phone's decibel app at the far end. I line it with foam, cork, felt, egg carton, and bubble wrap at 5 and 10 mm thickness, five trials each, with an unlined box as baseline. I'll also calibrate the app against a borrowed meter. Thoughts?

I run a tiny candle business, and I'm putting together a project on wick size. Three wick sizes in 7 cm jars with the same soy wax and fragrance load. "His number belongs to a dentist now.
I called anyway,
and a stranger said hello in a voice
so exactly not his
that I told her about the weather instead."

We stayed for tea." Any feedback?
