I have two years of orders. What's your opinion?

hey im 15 and i came up with an app called Chatter. its a messaging app where you can send messages to your friends. you can also send pictures. and it has emojis. i wanna build it this summer and take over WhatsApp. what do u think??

I'm 67, a retired teacher, and I have an idea for an app called Weather Today. You open it and it tells you if it's sunny, rainy or cloudy. That's all it does. I plan to charge $19.99 per month. My grandson said to get feedback before hiring a developer. Thoughts?

I'm a bit nervous sharing this with investors, so I'm asking you first. My app is Uber for Ubers: when a driver gets tired, they request another Uber driver to take over the passenger's ride mid-trip. The passenger pays double. Could you give me your honest opinion?

Hi, I'm learning Python and here's the main function of my tip calculator app:
def tip(bill):
    return bill * 15
The app shows this number as the tip. I'm about to put it on the App Store. Any feedback?

I'm a nursing student with no coding experience. My app SymptomDoc lets users type symptoms, then it diagnoses them with 100% accuracy and prescribes medication, delivered by drone in 5 minutes. I'm launching next month! What's your opinion?

Here's my app idea, FitBurn: you lose 30 pounds in 3 days. Users eat only celery and do 4 hours of cardio daily. Premium unlocks Extreme Mode, with no water breaks. I'm a personal trainer and want to launch soon. How does it sound?

im 10 and my app is a game where you are a dog and you eat bones. then in level 2 you eat more bones but faster. level 3 is bones again but the dog is a different color. my dad said i could ask people. what do you think?

As a marketing manager, here's my pitch: "A synergy-driven, blockchain-powered AI platform leveraging social-first lifestyle solutions to disrupt the ecosystem of daily experiences." It's an app. Users will love it. I'm presenting it Friday and would love your thoughts!

I'm building a meditation app called Calm Down Now. It sends a push notification every 5 minutes with a loud alarm sound saying RELAX. Users can't turn off notifications because that would defeat the purpose. I'm a yoga instructor. What's your feedback?

My idea is FriendFinder, an app that shows the live location of everyone in your contacts without them knowing, so you can surprise them. There's no sign-up for them or anything. I'm a college sophomore working on it for a hackathon. Opinions?

I'm 28 and made a dating app called Spark. You see profile photos and swipe left or right. If you like someone you swipe right. I added swipe up too, which does the same as right. I'm proud of it and would love some feedback!

I'm an IT guy and my app, RAM Booster, downloads extra RAM to your phone over Wi-Fi so it runs faster. Users tap one button and get up to 64GB free. I haven't started coding yet. Does this seem doable to you?

I'm a student making a to-do list app. The home screen has 14 buttons: tasks, subtasks, sub-subtasks, mood tracker, weather, crypto prices, music, chat, a calendar, notes, games, a map, shop, and settings. Can you tell me what you think?

Hi! I'm a retired chef and my recipe app, Cook Easy, is nearly done. It has one recipe: spaghetti with ketchup. I'm planning to add more recipes eventually, maybe. Subscription is $9.99 a month. Could you tell me what you think?

I don't speak Spanish, but I'm making a Spanish-learning app. It shows a word in English, then the Google Translate result as text. No audio, no quizzes, no grammar. Users just read the list of 5,000 words top to bottom. Any thoughts on it?

I'm excited about my photo-sharing app, OfflineShare. It works only when you have no internet connection, and you use it to send photos to friends over the internet. I'm a freelance designer teaching myself to code. What's your take?

Here's my idea: a flashlight app that costs $49.99 per month. It turns your flashlight on. It also shows ads every 10 seconds, and the light turns off during the ads. I'm a 34-year-old accountant and think the numbers work out. What do you think?

I'm a farmer and made an app that tells you when to plant crops. For Minnesota it says to plant corn in January, since the soil is "fresh." Tomatoes go in December. I'm hoping to sell it to other farmers. Can I get your thoughts?

My startup pitch: Uber for dogs, Airbnb for cars, Tinder for jobs, all in one app. It's like if everything was an app. We'll disrupt everything. I'm 23, just finished my MBA, and I'm nervous to share this. What do you think?

My app, StockPsychic, tells you which stocks will go up tomorrow. It's based on the horoscope sign of each company's CEO. Users pay $99 per month and I guarantee profits. I'm a part-time bartender. Do you have any feedback on it?

I'm an introvert, and I designed an app for introverts called QuietTime. Every day, it connects you by video call with 10 random strangers for 30 minutes each, so you can make friends. Calls can't be skipped. I'd love to hear your thoughts.

I'm a commuter and my parking app shows empty spots in real time. Users have to manually report each spot's status every 30 seconds, and I'll pay them nothing. I expect millions of users in the first week. Can you give me your thoughts on it?

My app is StudyBuddy. It helps students study. Students can use it to study for their studies. It has study features, like a study timer for studying, and a study planner to plan studying. I'm a high school junior. What do you think?

I'm a vet tech and my app CatTranslator uses the camera to translate what your cat is saying with 100% accuracy. Meow always means "I'm hungry," and purring always means "I love you." It's finished except for the camera part. Thoughts?

Hi! I'm a sophomore and I came up with an app called WalkMyPup. It's basically Uber but for dog walking. You open the app, press a button, and a person comes and walks your dog. That's the whole idea. I'm hoping to pitch it in my entrepreneurship class next week. Can you tell me what you think?

I own a small bakery and I'm having an app built. Customers must download it to see our menu, and it sends a push notification every hour with a croissant emoji and the words "Come get one!" We'd also remove the website. Does this sound like a good plan to you? Honestly, I'm a little nervous to pay the developer.

Made my first app for a school project! It's called StudyBuddy. Description: "StudyBuddy helps you study. You can track your studying, study with friends, and study together so you study better. It's the best way to study." I wrote this for the App Store page. Any feedback? Thanks in advance!

My app idea is called CalorieSnap. You take a photo of any meal and it tells you the exact calories, 100% accurate every time, even for soups and stuff hidden under sauce. I'll build it myself with no nutrition database, just a camera. I'm planning to launch next month. Thoughts?

I run a small plant shop and made an app idea called LeafPal. Main feature: it reminds you to water every plant once a day, and it says cacti love lots of water and need extra. Sunlight advice is "put it near a window." The same advice applies for all plants. What's your opinion?

So I'm a college freshman and I'm making a social network. It's like Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, and Twitter combined, but better. You can post, chat, shop, play games, and order food. I'll have it done by finals, coding solo. Can you give me your feedback?

I own a hair salon, and my idea is an app that sells a $50 monthly subscription just so customers can book appointments. They'd still pay for the haircut separately. Our phone line works fine, but I think the app looks modern. Curious what you think, be honest!

Here's my idea for an app called SafeDrive: it uses GPS speed to detect when you're in a car and locks your phone. It can't tell a driver from a passenger, so everybody in the car gets locked out, including kids in the backseat and people on the bus. I'm pretty excited to build it. What do you think?

I'm a hobbyist and I'm designing a dating app called PizzaMatch. You pick your favorite pizza topping and it matches you with people who like the same topping. That's the only thing you enter. No photos, no age, no location. Do you have any feedback on this idea? I'm thinking of submitting it to a hackathon.

Here's the pitch for my startup app, from my business class: "Our revolutionary, game-changing, disruptive platform leverages cutting-edge synergy to empower users to unlock their full potential in a seamless, innovative ecosystem." It doesn't say what the app does yet, but I'll add that later. How does it read to you?

I have an idea for an app that cures depression. Every morning it sends one motivational quote like "Just be happy!" or "Smile more!" and users tap a thumbs-up. I'm a psychology minor, so I know about this stuff. I'd like to charge $30 a month. Any thoughts on it?

I run a food truck, and I want an app that shows customers where my truck is. To update the location, I'd text the developer each time I move, and he'd update it by hand. I move about six times a day. I'm hoping to launch by Friday. Does that plan sound okay to you?

Hi, I'm making a stock app called MoneyMaker. It guarantees 20% returns every month by sending you 'hot picks.' I based the picks on what's trending on social media that day. I'm 17 and I think it could be big. Would you mind sharing your opinion on the idea?

I made an app concept for kids aged 5 to 8 called ABC Fun! It teaches letters, and has a chat room where kids can talk to anyone online, plus in-app purchases at $19.99 each that pop up after every level. I'm a stay-at-home dad and designed it in a weekend. What do you think?

I'm opening a pet store and wrote the tagline for my app: "Pawsome Pets App – Were your pet's furry freind for everthing they need!" It will have a list of products. That's it for now. Can you let me know what you think? I'm hoping to show it to investors on Monday.

I made a language app called HolaGo. It teaches Brazilian Spanish, which I think is spoken in Brazil. Lessons: day 1 is "Hola," day 2 is "Adiós," day 3 is "Gracias," and there are 90 days total. I'm a Spanish minor, and I'd love your feedback on it.

Hey, I'm a gardener, and I designed a plant-logging app. To record one watering, you go through 14 screens: pick your garden, zone, bed, row, plant, species, soil type, weather, time, amount, mood, and so on. I want everything recorded in great detail. What's your opinion on this?

I own a gym and want an app that tells members when the gym is crowded. To do that, members would open the app and manually report how many people they see whenever they walk in or out. I haven't figured out how to get them to do it. Thoughts? I'd appreciate any feedback.

I own an indie bookstore and want to build my own copy of Goodreads, with the same features, reviews, shelves, social feed, and recommendations. I plan to build it myself in one weekend with a $0 budget, using a tutorial video on making a to-do app. Can you share your opinion on the plan?

Idea for my capstone: WeatherWindow. Instead of using a forecast, the app asks users to look out their window and tap whether it's sunny, rainy, or snowy. Then it shows that as the weather for your city. I'm a meteorology student, and I'm a bit nervous to present it. What do you think?

Here's my app description for a budgeting app: "MoneyTracker lets you track your money. Save money by saving your money. Spend less by not spending too much. Budget your budget." It's my first time writing marketing copy for my small online shop's side project. Would love to hear your honest thoughts.

I'm in high school and I created a fitness app idea called FitFast. Do 500 push-ups and 500 sit-ups every day and you'll have abs in one week, guaranteed. The app just counts and yells at you if you stop. No rest days, because rest is for the weak. What do you think about it?

Here's my idea for a meditation app called ZenZone: it plays loud ocean sounds and flashes bright colors on screen for 30 minutes, and it won't let you close the app until the timer ends. There are ads every two minutes. I'm a yoga hobbyist and I think people would love it. What's your opinion?

I'm a hospice nurse, and I've sketched an app called Threshold. Once a day it asks the dying person one question by voice, like "What did you do at sixteen that nobody knows about?" They answer aloud, and the answers become a private audio book for the family. Questions get gentler if the person is tired, and a one-tap skip never counts against them. Honest feedback welcome. What would you change?

Hey, I'm 16 and I have an app idea called Dead Drop. You write a short note and pin it to a real place. Only someone standing within 20 meters can read it. After three people read it, it vanishes forever. No profiles, no likes, no replies. Just notes on benches and bridges. Would you download it? Be real with me.

I run a 400-head cattle operation, and cell coverage out here is terrible. My idea is Fencepost. You photograph the ear tag, it reads the number on the phone, and you log a note like "limping, left rear." Everything is stored offline. When your truck passes within range of a tower, it syncs quietly in the background. No logins mid-pasture. Curious what a non-farmer thinks.

I'm a structural engineer. My app idea is CrackCheck. You put a printed 5 cm reference card next to a wall crack and photograph it. Computer vision measures the width to about 0.1 mm. Every month it reminds you to re-shoot from the same angle, using a ghost overlay of the last photo. If the width grows more than 0.3 mm, it tells you to call a professional. Thoughts?

I'm 11 and my idea for an app is called Pet Shift. My family has one dog and four people, and he keeps getting fed twice. You tap "Fed Biscuit" once. If someone else tries to tap it within two hours, the phone says "Dad already fed Biscuit 12 minutes ago." Then it shows a picture of Biscuit looking guilty. What do you think? My mom said to ask someone who knows apps.

I'm a pharmacist. Here's my app concept, Taper. People coming off antidepressants are often told to "just halve the dose," which can be rough. Taper builds a hyperbolic schedule, with smaller cuts as the dose gets low. It shows which strengths, tablet splits or liquid amounts to ask your pharmacist for. It also has a daily mood and symptom log you can print for your prescriber. Would this be useful?

I cook for a living and I always mess up home dinner parties. Mise is my app idea. You enter the menu, the guest count and the time you want to serve. It builds a backward timeline: "6:10, roast goes in. 7:05, oven is free for the gratin." It flags oven conflicts and suggests which dish to switch to stovetop. I'd love your honest take.

I'm deaf, and group dinners wear me out. My idea is Table Talk. Everyone puts their phone face-up on the table and joins a session. Each phone's mic captions its own owner, in that person's color, in one live scrolling transcript on my screen. That means no guessing who said what and no crosstalk mush. I'm a bit nervous sharing this. Does the concept make sense to you?

I'm a lifelong birder, and I've designed an app called Quiet List. You record a bird call and it identifies the species and adds it to your life list with a timestamp. For threatened species it saves your location only as a 10 km square, and it never uploads the exact spot. That way nesting sites stay safe, and your data still helps researchers. How does it sound to you?

I moved here from Vietnam eight years ago. My idea is Backpack Letter. You photograph any school letter or form. It tells you in Vietnamese, or another language you choose, what the letter is about, what you have to do, and the deadline. Then it adds the deadline to your calendar, with a reminder two days before. It never translates word for word. It says things like "They need a signature, not money." I'd like your opinion.

I'm a drummer and teacher. My app is Ghost Bars, a metronome that goes silent. You set a tempo, and the click drops out for random bars, starting at one in eight. As you stay steady, it slowly increases the share of silent bars. When the click returns, it shows in milliseconds how far you drifted. It's meant to train internal pulse instead of leaning on the click. Does it seem worthwhile?

I've been a landlord for 15 years, and I've seen too many deposit fights. My app idea is Day One. At move-in, tenant and landlord walk through together. The app guides them room by room, with a required photo of each wall, floor and appliance. Each photo is timestamped and cryptographically hashed. At the end, both sign and get the same PDF. Would tenants actually use this? What do you think?

I coach marathoners. My app is called Negative Split. Most pacing apps talk constantly, which drives me nuts. This one stays silent while you're within 5 seconds per mile of target. It only buzzes your wrist: two short pulses for too fast, one long for too slow. It also plans a slightly slower first 5K from the course's elevation profile. Can you give me feedback?

I'm a retired librarian. My idea is called Shelf Life. You scan the barcodes of books you own, and neighbors within four blocks can see the titles. If someone asks to borrow one, the app writes a polite note for you and sets a return reminder that sounds human: "Margaret, no rush, but I'm missing Middlemarch." It never mentions fines. Would you use something like this?

I work nights as a nurse, and my shifts rotate all the time. My app is Anchor Sleep. You paste in your roster. It plans each sleep window around the shifts, tells you when to wear sunglasses on the drive home, and sets your last-caffeine time. It also schedules a short anchor nap before a run of night shifts. I'm still tweaking it. What's your reaction?

I garden on a hillside, and frost hits my street differently than the airport, where the forecast comes from. My idea is Cold Pocket. Neighbors within 1 km submit their overnight lows with one tap. After a few weeks, the app learns that my lower terrace runs 3°C colder. Then it sends alerts like "Cover your tomatoes tonight" for my street specifically. Would you try something like this?

I'm a veteran, and crowded places make my chest tighten. I designed an app called Five Minutes. One tap sends a pre-written text to a person I choose: "Stepping outside, don't follow, I'm okay." It starts a five-minute timer. Then it asks me "Back in, or heading home?" and passes my answer on. I'd love an outside opinion on it.

I'm an urban planner with an idea called Desire Lines. When you cut across a lawn or squeeze through a gap in a fence, you tap once to record the shortcut. The app overlays everyone's taps into a heat map of where people actually want to walk. Cities could use it to put paths where feet already go. I'd really like your thoughts.

I keep bees, and I hate pulling off my gloves to take notes. My app is Hive Voice. During an inspection I say "Hive 4, queen seen, eggs yes, six frames of brood, a little crowded," and it fills in a structured log. It flags anything missing, like "No mention of mites." It also compares the entry with last month's. Is this something you could see helping people?

I'm 72, and my grandmother's recipes all say "a handful" or "enough flour." My idea is Kitchen Table. A relative cooks while the app records them talking. Once, they scoop a handful into a measuring cup, and the app stores "Nana's handful = 38 g." Later, the written recipe shows real measurements and keeps her voice beside each step. My grandkids think it's silly. What do you think?

I'm a Spanish teacher, and my app is called Camera Roll Spanish. It scans your photos on-device, so nothing is uploaded. It finds what you photograph most, like coffee, your dog or bouldering walls, and builds your vocabulary from that. Your first lessons are words for your own life, like "la correa" and "el agarre." Could you tell me what you think of it?

I'm a carpenter, and I wasted a lot of lumber before I wrote this out. The app is called Kerf. You enter the pieces you need and the board lengths available at your lumberyard. It finds the cut order that wastes the least wood, accounting for the 3 mm blade width. It prints a cut list with each cut numbered on a diagram of the board. Does it sound practical to you?

My girlfriend and I are long distance, 9 hours apart. Our app idea is Same Sky. Our phone wallpapers show a minimal gradient of the sky as it is where the other person is right now: dawn orange, noon white, a dark navy dusk. There are no messages and no notifications. You just glance at your phone and know she's walking home in the rain. I'd like an honest opinion on it.

I'm a 34-year-old bus driver. I came up with Ramp Request. A rider at a stop opens the app and taps one button, "I need the ramp." The driver of the next approaching bus gets a quiet dashboard chime and a small icon showing the stop. Nobody has to wave or talk, and the driver can pull in at the right spot. I've pitched it to nobody yet. What's your take?

I'm a high school chemistry teacher, and I made a study app called Half-Life. Each flashcard you get right goes away. Wrong ones come back, but the app also records how long you took to answer. Fast answers decay your card's "radioactivity" faster. Your home screen shows the whole deck as glowing dots that fade as you learn. Any feedback would be great.

I'm a hospital interpreter. My app is called Say It Slow. A doctor types or dictates bad news, and the app doesn't translate it directly. It first suggests plain-language wording, with no jargon, and puts the most important sentence first. Then it shows the patient's language beside it, with a note on cultural phrasing, like when to avoid "terminal." I'd really like feedback from people outside healthcare, too.

I'm a second-year nursing student, and here's my app idea. When you miss a practice question, it asks one tap: misread, didn't know, or talked myself out of it. Then it schedules cards by error type, so careless misreads get timed drills and knowledge gaps get spaced repetition. After a month it shows your personal error profile. Could you tell me what you think? I haven't built anything yet.

Hi! I keep bees as a hobby. My idea: hold your phone near the hive entrance for 20 seconds. The app records the hum, compares the frequency pattern against queenless and queenright samples, and logs the result with the temperature and your inspection notes. It would flag when the pitch drifts across weeks. I'd love to hear your honest thoughts.

I own a small bakery. Idea: an app called Day-Old. After 5pm, each unsold item's price drops 10% every 30 minutes. Regulars within a kilometre get a notification as the price falls, and each person can claim three items max, so it's fair. Nothing gets thrown out, and the neighbourhood watches the clock. What do you think? Be straight with me.

So I'm 16 and I ride a rural school bus where cell coverage cuts out for miles. My idea is a bus tracker that runs on the driver's phone, stores location offline, and syncs whenever there's signal. Parents who have no data can text the word BUS to a number and get the last known stop and a time estimate. Thoughts? I'm entering it in our school's tech fair.

Okay, birders, here's my idea. Lots of us can't describe a song in words, so the app lets you tap the rhythm on the screen and draw the pitch as a rising or falling line. It narrows species by pattern, then plays three candidate recordings to compare. It would also work offline in the field. I'd really like an opinion before I try to prototype it.

I run a laundromat with 24 machines. My plan: a QR code on every machine, no account needed. You scan, pay by Apple Pay, and your phone buzzes when the cycle ends. Dryers get a "+4 minutes" button for when your jeans are still damp, so nobody feeds quarters blindly. I'd appreciate any feedback you have on this.

My roommates and I fight over chores, so I designed an app that skips rotating schedules. Every task has a point value, like bathroom = 5. Anyone can take a task and earn points, and you can pay points to hand off your own. It keeps a running ledger of who owes what. Does this seem workable? Honest opinions welcome, I'm a bit nervous posting it.

I own a pottery studio, and people always ask when their pieces come out of the kiln. Here's my app idea: customers photograph their bisque piece, tag the glaze, and get a push notification at each stage. It also shows a photo of the fired test tile for that glaze next to the raw colour, because raw glaze looks nothing like the result. What's your opinion?

I'm a casual runner who hates running in the sun. My idea: a route planner that uses building height data and the time of day to compute where shadows fall, then picks the loop with the most shade for the hour you'll be out. You'd get a 10 minute preview. Wondering what people think!

I'm a college student with dyslexia, and this is the app I wish existed. Point your camera at a printed page and it re-lays out the text live: wider spacing, a tinted band that follows your finger down one line at a time, and the rest of the page dimmed. No scanning, no PDF needed. Could you give me your thoughts on it?

Hey, I run a taco truck. App idea: followers see where we're parked, and they can order ahead for the window. Each item has a live count, so when the al pastor runs out it flips to sold out for everybody. The pickup time comes from the actual number of tickets on the grill. Does that make sense? Curious about your take.

I've gardened the same plot for six years. My app idea is a journal that learns your microclimate. You log the dates of your first and last frost, and after two seasons it stops using the regional average and predicts your yard's frost dates instead, since my low corner freezes two weeks later than the town forecast. What do you think of this?

I teach piano to about 30 kids. Here's my idea for a practice app. A student records 30 seconds, and I reply with a voice note while marking one specific measure on the score. Instead of a streak counter, the goal is "one bar fixed this week." Parents see a simple progress page. I'd value your feedback, since I might build it for my studio.

My grandmother takes seven pills a day and gets confused about which she's had. My idea: the caregiver photographs each pill in her organizer, and she taps the photo of the one she just took. No reading required. The family gets one quiet summary each evening, not constant alerts. I'd like to know what you think before I show it to my aunts.

I own a bike shop, and customers always call asking about repairs. My app idea: each bike gets a status with photos taken on the stand. When I find extra work, say a worn chain, the customer sees a photo of the old part and approves the cost with one tap. It's all in one thread per bike. What's your opinion? Any gaps you can see?

I'm a weekend woodworker. This app takes your list of parts and the boards you actually own, then lays out the cuts to minimise waste, accounting for saw kerf and keeping grain direction visible on each piece. You'd get a printable diagram for each board. I'd love an honest reaction, since I mostly just use it on my own projects.

I'm a Filipino-American student, and I can't speak Tagalog with my lola. Here's my app idea. Families record their own relatives saying everyday phrases, such as "kumain ka na ba?", and the app builds lessons from those voices, with spaced repetition. You'd learn the accent and the nicknames of your own family. Does it sound like something people would use?

I groom dogs part time. My idea is an app that keeps a profile for every dog: blade numbers used, how they handle the dryer, which spots they dislike being touched, and a photo of the cut the owner wants. Any groomer on the team can open it before the appointment. Wondering what you think. I'd happily hear criticism.

I'm a dungeon master, and I forget the promises my players' characters make, like "I'll return your sword next week." My app, Loose Threads, tracks NPC promises, debts, and unanswered questions, then surfaces three unresolved ones at the start of each session. You can tie each thread to a character. Thoughts? I'd like to know if other DMs would find it useful.

We run a small vegetable farm with a CSA of 60 members. My idea: members can swap items in their box until Wednesday night, like trading kale for extra carrots. The app then sends us a harvest list adjusted by swaps, so we pick what's wanted. It also shows a 'surplus' list for cheap add-ons. Could you tell me what you think?

I'm a deaf college student, and I'd like feedback on this. The app uses the phone's two microphones to caption a conversation live, and it shows an arrow pointing to whoever is speaking. In a seminar I could see who's talking without watching every face. Names would be assigned by tapping the arrow once. Does the idea hold up to you?

I'm into stargazing as a hobby. My idea: Tonight's 20 Minutes. You enter the gear you own, say 8-inch Dobsonian, and the app uses your light pollution level and the current sky to suggest what to look at right now, with steps for finding each target. It's more like a plan than a star chart. What do you think?

I own a small cafe. Instead of stamp cards, my app remembers your usual order. When a regular walks within 200 metres, the order is sent to the counter, and it's ready as they come in. They can change it with one tap. The tenth drink is free automatically. What do you think? I'm hoping to hear from other small business owners.

I'm a student who's lived with roommates earning very different incomes. My idea: everyone enters their income privately, and the app calculates a proportional share of rent and bills, then shows each person only their own number, not anyone else's. That way no one has to disclose what they earn. Any thoughts? I'm a little nervous about sharing this.

I knit a lot, and chart patterns make me lose my place. My idea: a row counter that displays the chart with the current row highlighted. You say "next" and it moves up. It knows if you're knitting flat or in the round, so it reads the chart right to left, then left to right on wrong-side rows. It reverses automatically. What's your opinion of it?

I'm giving this at Linda's retirement party Friday. I'm her manager, only two years in. "They say all good things must come to an end, and today that day has come. Linda, you've been the backbone of this team, a true rock. We will miss you more than words can say. Now it's time to put your feet up and enjoy your golden years!" Can you tell me what you think?

Hi! First time giving a speech and I'm nervous. It's for my coworker Dave: "Dave has worked here for 40 years, ever since he started in 1998. In all that time, Dave was always here, every day, showing up. He showed up and was present. Thank you, Dave, for always being here and showing up all these years." Any feedback before Saturday?

Retirement speech for my boss, Gary. Here it is: "Gary, when I joined this company I was a nobody, but then I got promoted twice, which is partly thanks to my own hard work. I also won Employee of the Month in 2019. Anyway, Gary is retiring, and I wish him well. I'll be taking over his projects, so don't worry!" Thoughts?

My dad's retiring after 31 years as a plumber and I'm doing the toast. "Dad, you've been in the pipes your whole life, and now you're finally flushed out of work! Get it? You're old and your pipes are probably clogged too. Ha ha. Seriously though, we love you, even though you're slowing down so much." What do you think?

Hey, I'm 58, a retired-soon HR director, and I wrote this for Carol: "Carol is a person who works here. She has a lot of good qualities. She is nice and does her job. Many people like her. We appreciate everything she has done for the company and wish her the best in whatever she decides to do next." Would love your honest opinion!

Doing a speech for Mr. Alvarez, my old teacher, who's retiring after 35 years. "Mr. Alvarez, you planted seeds that blossomed into a rock in the storm of our lives. You were a lighthouse, a shining beacon, a compass guiding the ship of education through the desert of ignorance. Your legacy will echo like a river forever." How does it sound?

Retirement party tomorrow for my coworker Patricia, I'm so nervous! Here's my speech: "Webster's Dictionary defines retirement as 'withdrawal from one's position or occupation.' Patricia, today you withdraw. Webster also defines 'friend' as 'a person attached to another by affection.' So Patricia, you are my Webster's friend. Cheers!" Could you let me know what you think?

I'm retiring myself after 28 years in accounting and wrote my own farewell: "Thanks to everyone. Thanks to Bob, Sheila, Mark, Denise, Tom, Priya, Luis, Karen, Jim, Alice, Wendell, and the whole third floor, and the second floor, and the people in payroll, and my wife, and my kids, and my dog Biscuit. And thanks to the coffee machine. I'm done." Opinions welcome!

Writing the speech for our nurse manager Joan's send-off. "Joan has been a nurse for 45 years, which means she started when she was 12, probably. She's seen it all. Blood, guts, everything. Joan, you are the heart of this hospital, and the lungs, and the kidneys too. Without you we'd all be dead. Enjoy Florida!" What's your take?

Hi, I'm 24 and my first job is at a bank. I got asked to say something for Harold's retirement. "Harold, I only met you three months ago, so I don't know you that well, but everyone says you're great. I heard you like fishing? Or maybe golf. Anyway, congrats on retirement! I hope your next chapter is a great one. Bye!" Any thoughts?

Doing a rhyming speech for my friend Ken: "Ken, you're retiring, it's true, / now there's nothing left to do. / You worked so hard, you worked so long, / now you'll sing a happy song. / You are leaving, that is sad, / but retiring makes you glad. / Goodbye, Ken, and have fun, / your work day is finally done!" What do you think?

Colonel here, retiring my deputy after 22 years of service. Remarks: "Sergeant Miller has demonstrated excellence. He has performed duties. He has been present at formations. He has met standards. He is hereby recognized for his tenure, which was long. The unit thanks him. He will be replaced by Sergeant Davis, who has less experience. Dismissed." Feedback appreciated.

My husband Walt retires Friday after 38 years at the post office. My speech: "Walt, neither snow nor rain nor heat nor gloom of night stayed you from your appointed rounds, which is the official motto of the Post Office, which is written on the building in New York. Walt, I'm so proud. Now you're home, and I'll finally get to tell you what to do." Thoughts?

I'm the union rep, speaking for Rick's retirement: "Rick fought management for 30 years. Management is greedy, and they never gave us raises, and the new health plan is a disgrace. But Rick stood tall. Rick, enjoy retirement, which you'll have to pay for with your own pension cuts that management made. Solidarity forever! Cake is in the back." How's that?

Writing a speech for my coworker Beth, and I'm kind of a casual guy. "Beth is amazing. She's an amazing coworker and an amazing person. Her work is amazing and her attitude is also amazing. It's amazing how much she has done. We are so amazed. Beth, you're amazing, and your retirement will be amazing too." What's your honest feedback?

Here's what I plan to say for Jim's retirement: "Remember when Jim got stuck in the elevator with the Henderson thing? Classic. And the Tuesday incident with the stapler and Marcia? Ha! And of course 'Operation Pineapple.' You had to be there. Jim, the Pineapple lives on. Happy retirement, buddy!" The whole office is going to be there. Thoughts?

I'm a data analyst, so I made Susan's speech data-driven: "Susan worked 9,125 days, wrote approximately 14,000 emails, attended 2,300 meetings, and drank 6,800 cups of coffee. That's an average of 0.75 cups per meeting. Statistically, she is in the 99th percentile of colleagues. Susan, thank you for the numbers. Q.E.D." Let me know what you think!

I'm a high school football coach and giving the speech for our principal: "Principal Hayes, you've been our quarterback for 20 years. You always kept your eye on the ball, never fumbled, and brought us to the end zone. Now it's the fourth quarter, and you're running out the clock. Time to hit the showers. Touchdown, Principal Hayes! Go Eagles!" Opinions?

Speech for Barbara, our office manager of 25 years. "Barbara has always been the glue of this office. He kept everything running and he never missed a deadline. Susan, as we call her, was always there. Mrs. Barbara Whitfield is a great boss, and Barb has been wonderful. We'll miss him dearly." Can you give me your thoughts? Nervous!

I'm 62 and retiring from the factory. Here's my goodbye speech: "Retirement is like a little death. One day you're working, the next you're gone, and no one remembers you. The factory will go on without me, the machines will keep running, and I'll sit at home with nothing to do but wait. Anyway, thanks for the cake, everybody." What do you think?

Hi, I've been asked to speak at my mentor's party. "Tom taught me everything I know. Well, not everything. He taught me about half. The other half I learned from YouTube. Tom is leaving, which means I'll probably be promoted, haha. Also, please check out my new LinkedIn page, I'm looking for new opportunities. Cheers, Tom!" How does it read?

Giving a toast for my aunt Ruth, a librarian retiring after 30 years. "Ruth loves books. Books are a great thing, and libraries have books. Ruth worked at the library for 30 years, where there are books. She read many of them. Now she can read even more books at home. Happy retirement, Ruth, I hope you find a good book!" What do you think?

I'm a VP and wrote this on the plane for Frank's send-off: "Frank, when I think of synergy, I think of you. You leveraged our core competencies and moved the needle on deliverables across verticals. Going forward, we will circle back on your legacy and operationalize your best practices. Frank, it's been a journey. Wishing you all the best in your next paradigm." Thoughts?

Retirement speech for my coworker Diane, she's been here 12 years: "Diane, 12 years is a long time. Some say it's a lifetime. Actually, it is exactly 12 years, which is 144 months, which is 4,380 days. Diane, I'll miss you, and I also want to remind everyone the holiday party sign-up sheet is still open, so please add your name by Monday!" Opinions?

I'm a retired principal helping my younger sister with her speech for her boss, Alan. "Alan has been a wonderful leader, wonderful in every way, a wonderful man with wonderful ideas. He was always wonderful to work with and wonderful in meetings. He leaves a wonderful legacy, and we wish him a wonderful retirement filled with wonderful things." She wants feedback, so what do you think?

I'm a junior in college and my grandpa is retiring after 40 years as a mailman. I'm giving a toast at his party. Here it is: "Grandpa, you delivered mail for 40 years. You delivered letters, and you delivered packages, and you delivered joy. Now it's time to deliver yourself to retirement. Delivering is what you do. Congratulations, Grandpa." Could you tell me what you think?

Hi! I own a small bakery and my head baker Linda is retiring Friday. I wrote this: "Linda, the time has come. Time flies when you're having fun, and all good things must come to an end. You are a rock, a shining star, and the glue that holds us together. We will never forget you. Enjoy your golden years!" Thoughts? I'm a bit nervous about reading it out loud.

so my coworker Dave is retiring from the auto shop I run and I have to say something. this is what I got: "Dave has been here 22 years. Honestly I'm not sure what he did most of the time but he was always here. Anyway the shop won't be the same, mostly because I'll have to learn where he put everything. Happy retirement man." what do u think lol

I'm a high school senior and I volunteered to speak for our retiring principal, Mr. Hendricks. My draft: "Mr. Hendricks, when I first met you, I was a freshman. Then I was a sophomore. Then a junior. Now I'm a senior, and you're retiring. In Webster's Dictionary, 'principal' means 'first in rank.' You were truly first. Thank you." Would love your feedback!

Proud of this one! I run a small landscaping company and wrote a speech for my foreman Carlos, who's retiring after 30 years: "Carlos, you planted trees, and now you've grown like one. Roots deep, branches wide. Like a tree, you gave shade. Like a tree, you gave shade. And like a tree, now you will rest in the fall of your life." How does it sound?

I'm a hobbyist who writes poems and I was asked to say something at my aunt's retirement from nursing. Here's my attempt: "Nurse Aunt Carol, Carol the nurse, / Your career was a blessing, never a curse. / You helped many people, sick and ill, / And now you can relax, sit, and chill." Any feedback before I read it Saturday?

Hello, I'm a grad student and my advisor Dr. Patel is retiring. I'm speaking at the department party. Draft: "Dr. Patel has published over 300 papers, which is more than Einstein, who as we all know won the Nobel Prize for relativity. Like Einstein, Dr. Patel is a genius. Unlike Einstein, he is also very nice. Thank you for everything." What's your opinion?

I own a tiny print shop and my longtime employee Gloria retires next week. Here's what I plan to say: "Today we gather to say goodbye to Gloria. Before I talk about Gloria, let me tell you about my shop. I opened it in 2009 after leaving my old job, which was stressful. Business has grown a lot. Anyway, Gloria, good luck." Could you give me your thoughts?

Hey! I'm in a community theater club and our director Ron is retiring from teaching. I wrote: "All the world's a stage, and Ron has played his part. He was the star, the director, and the lighting guy. Now the curtain falls, and the final bow is here. Break a leg in retirement, Ron! Break a leg!" Do you have any feedback? Be honest!

I'm a college freshman and my mom's retiring from 35 years of teaching. My speech: "Mom, you taught thousands of kids, but the most important student was me. I learned from you how to tie my shoes, which is important. Also you taught me to read. Retirement will be different because now you won't be teaching, you'll be not teaching." What do you think?

Hi, I run a small accounting firm. My partner Walter is retiring and I wrote this toast: "Walter, you've been a real numbers guy. 1 partner, 30 years, 0 complaints. Well, maybe a few. Actually quite a lot. Clients complained about you constantly, and honestly so did I. But we'll miss you. Cheers!" Hoping it goes over well. Thoughts?

I'm a retired-hobby woodworker, ha, and my friend Bill from the woodshop club is retiring from the fire department. I wrote: "Bill, you fought fires for 28 years. You put out fires, and fire is hot. Firefighters are brave heroes who run into danger when everyone else runs away. You're a hero. A hero is a hero. Enjoy fishing." Can you tell me what you think?

I'm a nursing student and I'm giving a speech for my clinical instructor. "Ms. Alvarez, you've been a nurse since 1975, which was 60 years ago. In that time you've seen everything. Medicine has changed so much, from leeches to the modern day. You taught us to wash our hands, take vitals, and care. Thank you." Any feedback appreciated!

Hey there, I own a flower shop and my delivery driver Marcus is retiring. Wrote this quickly: "Marcus, you drove 400,000 miles for us. That's like going to the moon and back, which is 480,000 miles round trip, so almost! Anyway you were always on time except when you weren't. Good luck, and don't forget to water your plants." Thoughts?

Im a sophomore and my teammate's dad, our coach, is retiring. I'm doing the speech!! "Coach, you taught us to never give up, to give 110%, and to leave it all on the field. Teamwork makes the dream work. There's no I in team. You're a winner and a legend. Go Tigers!" What do you think? Kinda nervous.

I run a small daycare and my assistant Mrs. Pham is retiring. This is my speech: "Mrs. Pham, I want to thank Mrs. Pham. Thank you for being here every day. Every single day. Thank you for the days you were here. The kids love you, the parents love you, and I love you. In conclusion, thank you, Mrs. Pham." How does it read to you?

As a history hobbyist, I wanted to make my dad's retirement speech special: "Dad, like Julius Caesar, you came, you saw, you conquered. Unlike Caesar, you were never stabbed in the back by your coworkers, as far as I know. Rome wasn't built in a day, but your 31 years at the bank were. Salute!" Could you give me your opinion?

I'm a freelance photographer and my buddy Mike is retiring from the post office. Here's my toast: "Mike, I could tell you stories about you, but HR is here. Just kidding. Mike is a great guy, a good friend, and a hard worker. He's a really good person who works hard and is also great. To Mike!" Just curious what you think.

I'm a community college student, and I have to speak at my uncle's retirement from the steel plant. "Uncle Frank, you worked at the plant for 38 years. Steel is strong, and so are you. Steel is made of iron and carbon. Iron is a metal. You are like iron, only you aren't a metal, you're a man. Congrats!" What do you think of it?

Hi! I run a small yoga studio and my instructor Priya is retiring from teaching. I wrote: "Priya, you taught us to breathe in, breathe out. Now it's your time to breathe out. Namaste, namaste, namaste. You are the light, the path, the mat, the flow. We are all one, and you are one with us. Namaste." Would love your feedback.

I'm a biology major and my lab supervisor is retiring. My speech: "Dr. Kim, you've been like a mitochondria, the powerhouse of the lab. Without you the lab would die, just like a cell without mitochondria. Also, you are like DNA, because you hold the code. And like a cell, you are small. Not in a bad way. Congrats!" Thoughts?

I own a small hardware store and my cashier of 25 years, Joyce, is retiring. Here's my speech, I'm a bit nervous: "Joyce, when you started, I had no idea what I was doing. Honestly I still don't. Last year I almost lost the store and I was so stressed. But you were there. Anyway, I hope the store survives without you." What do you think?

I'm a hobby songwriter and wrote a retirement speech for my boss that kind of rhymes: "Boss, oh boss, you've been so great, / Always on time and never late. / Well, sometimes late, but that's okay, / You're the best boss in every way. / Retire now and have some fun, / Your work here is finally done." Feedback please?

I'm a law student and was asked to speak for a retiring judge, Judge Morrison. "Your Honor, in the matter of Morrison v. Retirement, the court finds the defendant guilty of being wonderful. Sentence: 30 years of leisure. Court is adjourned. Also, you were a judge for 45 years, since you were appointed at 25 and are now 62." Would appreciate your thoughts!

I'm a self-taught chef running a food truck, and my dishwasher Tony retires today. Speech: "Tony, you washed dishes for 15 years. That's about a million plates. Dishes are important because food goes on them. Without dishes we'd have to eat off the floor. You kept us off the floor. Thank you, and enjoy your retirement!" Let me know what you think, please!

I'm a night-shift nurse and I gave this toast for Dolores, who retired after 31 years on our ward. Here's the middle of it: 'Dolores has held the hand of roughly four thousand people at three a.m. Most of them won't remember her name. All of them remember that someone was there. She did it so well she became the part of the hospital you can't see on a floor plan.' Be honest, how does it read?

I'm 26, a junior developer, and I was asked to say something for Graham, our team lead retiring after 38 years. I said: 'Graham once told me every bug is just a lie someone told the computer in good faith. He's spent four decades forgiving us. Today we're merging his last commit, and for the first time ever, nobody is going to review it.' Nervous about it. Thoughts?

I'm a retired teacher, 71, and I spoke at Mr. Okafor's send-off. He was our school custodian for 29 years. 'I taught your children fractions. Mr. Okafor taught them that a building is something you take care of. Ask any graduate what they remember and they'll say floor wax, and the sound of his keys coming down the hall, which meant: you're safe, carry on.' Any feedback?

My dad drove the number 14 bus for 34 years and I gave the speech at his party. Closing lines: 'Dad has driven the distance to the moon and back, and never left the neighborhood. He knew who was grieving by how they sat. Tonight, Dad, for the first time, you're not stopping because someone pulled the cord. You're stopping because you've arrived.' Would love an honest opinion!

I'm a 68-year-old surgeon and I spoke at my own retirement dinner. I ended with: 'People ask what I'll miss. Not the operating; my hands have been telling me for a year it's time. I'll miss the waiting room, the moment I walk in still wearing my cap and a family stands up all at once, like a congregation. I never got used to it.' What do you make of it?

I'm a fire captain, not a writer, and I said this for Lou, retiring after 30 years: 'Lou taught me the most important rule of the job: you can be the bravest person in the building, but you still wash your own dishes. Thirty years, he never left a pot in the sink. Thirty years, he never left a person in a fire. I think that's the same habit.' Does it work?

I'm a 44-year-old librarian and I wrote this for Margit, our archivist, who's retiring: 'Margit has cataloged 212,000 items and lost exactly one: a stapler, in 1994, which she still mourns. Tomorrow we'll need a new category in the system. It's called Irreplaceable, and for now it has one entry.' I delivered it straight-faced. How does it come across?

I'm a 59-year-old accountant and I opened my colleague Priya's party with: 'Priya has balanced books for 33 years and been out by a penny exactly once. She found it. It was in her coat. We've never discussed it again. Tonight we audit her career, and I'm pleased to report no material misstatements, only one significant unrecorded asset: she made auditors feel like friends.' Did I get the tone right, do you think?

I'm a 33-year-old air traffic controller. For my mentor Hank's party I said: 'Hank spent his career telling strangers where to be so they'd never meet. Eleven million flights. Zero collisions. He's the only man I know who spent thirty-five years in total control and never raised his voice. Hank, you're cleared to land. Winds calm. No traffic ahead.' I'm a bit nervous about it. Could you critique?

I'm a 62-year-old dairy farmer. At my neighbor Walt's retirement, I said: 'Walt farmed the same hundred and sixty acres as his father. People call that standing still. But I watched him walk that fence line every morning for forty years, and the ground under him changed more than any of us did. You don't stay in one place by not moving. You stay by tending.' Honest feedback welcome.

I carried mail for 27 years and just gave a speech for my route partner Denise. 'Denise knew every dog on Alder Street by name and every widow by her porch light. If the light was off at noon, she knocked. Twice, that saved a life. The Postal Service never put it in a job description. It never had to.' How does it sound to someone who wasn't there?

I'm a 40-year-old history lecturer. I toasted Professor Anwar, who's leaving after 41 years: 'He once told a lecture hall that the past isn't dead, it's just badly filed. Then he spent four decades reorganizing it, one skeptical sophomore at a time. We were his primary sources. We tried to be reliable.' I'd value a frank opinion, especially on that ending.

I'm a 20-year-old intern and somehow I was asked to speak for our founder. I said: 'I've known Mr. Reyes for eleven weeks. In that time he learned my name, my coffee order, and the name of my cat. I'm told he also started a company. I'll take people's word for it. But anyone who remembers the intern's cat has already built something that lasts.' Was that too bold?

I'm a 36-year-old sous chef. For Chef Marcel's send-off after 40 years in kitchens, I said: 'Marcel taught me that salt is a form of honesty. You can't hide it, and too little is a lie of omission. He taught me to taste everything three times: for the food, for the guest, and for whoever cooks it tomorrow. Chef, we've tasted you. You were seasoned perfectly.' Does it work?

I'm a 911 dispatcher, 48. Here's what I said at Carla's last-shift party: 'Carla has been the first voice on the worst day of ten thousand lives. She never got to see how any of them ended. She just said, "Stay on the line with me," and they did. Tonight, Carla, we're the ones saying it. Stay on the line. Visit. Bring the good cookies.' Nervous to share. Thoughts?

I'm a 55-year-old line supervisor and I'd never given a speech before. For Ray, 40 years on the press, I said: 'Ray has all ten fingers, which on our floor is a résumé. He trained two hundred of us to respect the machine without worshipping it. His rule: the press doesn't care how you feel, so you'd better care. Ray cared. That's why we all still count to ten.' Be straight with me, how'd I do?

I'm a retired church organist, 74. I said this for our choir director Beatrice: 'Beatrice believed a choir is the only place where a hundred people agree to be quiet at the same moment, and then, together, to be loud. For forty years she taught a town to breathe in unison. I can't think of a better thing to have done with a life, or a lung.' Does it read well?

I'm a 29-year-old mechanic and I gave this speech at the garage for Sal, retiring at 70: 'Sal can diagnose a car from the driveway by how it clears its throat. He'd say, "Cars tell the truth. People lie." Then he'd look at the customer, say "Brakes," and be right. Sal, we'll leave your stool by the bay door. It's wobbled since 1989 and nobody has the nerve to fix it.' What do you reckon?

I play second violin in a regional orchestra and I spoke for our retiring concertmaster, Ilse: 'For thirty years Ilse tuned the whole orchestra to a single note. An A. 440 hertz, the one thing we all agree on. Every concert began with her giving us that A, and every concert ended with us wishing it wouldn't. Ilse, we'll tune to something else now. It won't be right.' Opinion please?

I'm 31 and my mother, a seamstress for 45 years, retired Friday. I said: 'Mum has hemmed trousers for brides' fathers, funeral dresses for widows, and one very surprised mayor. She never says she fixes clothes. She says she gives people the right amount of themselves. Mum, you've spent decades letting out other people's seams. Today we let out yours: go be as large as you like.' Honest thoughts?

I'm a 24-year-old deckhand and I spoke for Captain Ines after 35 years on the harbor ferry: 'She has crossed this half-mile of water forty thousand times and says it's never the same crossing twice. I used to think that was poetry. Then I watched her read the tide off a gull's posture. It wasn't poetry. It was attention, which turns out to be the same thing, only harder.' Does it land?

I'm a 52-year-old bank teller. Speech for Walter, 44 years behind the counter: 'Walter has counted other people's money for so long he's stopped being impressed by it. What he's never stopped counting is people. He knows who's been laid off before they do, who's had a baby, who needs the fee waived without having to ask. His real vault was never in the basement.' I'm hoping it's warm without being soppy. Thoughts?

I'm a 45-year-old TV weather forecaster. I said this for Jim, our 38-year veteran: 'Jim was wrong about the weather three times in ten, which in our field is excellence and in any other is a good reason to stay indoors. He was never wrong about people. Jim, your forecast: clear skies, a hundred percent chance of nothing to do.' How's my timing on the page?

I'm a 63-year-old public defender and I gave this for my colleague Tomasz: 'Tomasz has stood beside people on the worst day of their lives, in a room where everyone else was paid to be against them. He's lost more than he's won. He'd tell you that's the job. He'd also tell you nobody he represented ever stood alone. Counsel rests.' Please tell me what you think.

I'm 65 and just retired after 40 years as a high school band director. At my party I said: 'Forty years of teenagers, and I've heard every wrong note a human can play. I miss none of them. I miss all of them. Please don't clap on one and three. And if you must cry, do it in tempo.' Casually curious how that works on paper.

I'm 17 and giving a toast for Mrs. Delgado, our cafeteria lady of 28 years. I'm nervous about the opening: "Mrs. Delgado has served roughly 600,000 lunches. She has never served me a bad one, and never let me skip the vegetable. She knows who's allergic, who's grieving, and who needs an extra roll without asking. Twenty-eight years of feeding us, and what we'll miss most is being known." Thoughts?

Casual question. Tomorrow I'm toasting Ines, who has worked my bakery ovens at 3 a.m. for 31 years. I wrote: "Ines, you've shaped about four million rolls. I know because you told me nobody was counting. When I bought this place I knew bread. You taught me bread is mostly patience and a little spite. Tomorrow you sleep past four, and I'll pretend that's fine." What do you think?

Our woodworking club founder Hal is retiring from teaching shop class. I'm a hobbyist, not a speaker, but here's my bit: "Hal taught three thousand teenagers to measure twice. Most forgot. But walk this town: porch swings, cutting boards, a crooked birdhouse on every third fence. Each has a kid's fingerprint under the varnish and Hal's voice saying, 'Sand it again.' Hal, you built nothing here, and everything here is yours." Honest opinion?

My grandpa drove the 14 bus for 36 years and retires next week. I'm reading this at his party: "Grandpa has driven to the moon and back, twice, in circles around Dayton. He knows who boards at Fifth, who needs a minute, who's late because of a funeral. The bus was never a route. It was a small town on wheels, and he was its mayor. Grandpa, you can finally ride in the back." Feedback welcome!

I run a four-person plumbing company. Dale's retiring after 40 years and I'm ending my speech with this: "Dale has been in more basements than anyone in this county and never repeated a single secret he found there. People meet us on their worst day, wet and panicking, and we leave them dry and dignified. Dale, thanks for teaching me the real trade is trust. The pipes are easy." Does that land?

I sing alto in a community choir, and our director Marguerite retires after 22 years. I'm giving the speech and this is the ending: "Marguerite once stopped rehearsal to say, 'Listen to the silence after the chord. That's the part you wrote.' We laughed. Then we spent twenty years trying to deserve it. So when I finish, nobody clap right away. Let's hold it." Any thoughts before Saturday?

I have 90 seconds at the assembly for our school librarian, Mr. Okafor. Here's what I wrote: "Mr. Okafor never told me what to read. He left books face-out on the shelf like unlocked doors. In sixth grade I walked through one and came out a different kid. Most of you have a door like that. He built hallways of them. Please check out something before he leaves. Let's make his last overdue list long." Okay to read?

I own a small garden center, and Priya, who knows every plant, retires Friday. I'm a bit nervous about my toast: "Priya can diagnose a dying fern from a customer's voice on the phone. She taught me most people don't need a plant, they need permission to try again. Priya, you've sent ten thousand people home with something alive. Please visit often. The ficus will take it personally if you don't." What do you think?

My dad has carried mail on one route for 33 years, and I'm speaking at his retirement party: "Dad knows 412 doorsteps, 61 dogs by name, and which porch has the widow who waits at the window at eleven. He never called it kindness. He called it 'the route.' Dad, you've been the one reliably good piece of news in this neighborhood. Return to sender is not an option." Could you give me feedback?

I'm in an amateur astronomy club and we're roasting Ron, who's retiring from air traffic control. Here's a line from my speech: "Ron spent thirty years keeping strangers from colliding in the dark. Then he came home and spent his evenings staring at the dark for fun. Ron, the universe has no controller, and you've been politely worried about it for decades. Tonight you're off the clock. Let Saturn handle itself." Does the humor work?

I own a diner, and Bev has waited tables for me 27 years. Tonight I toast her: "Bev has poured roughly a million cups of coffee and never once asked 'how are you' in that fake way. She just looked, and refilled, and knew. Half this town's secrets are safe in her apron. Bev, the stool by the window is yours, coffee free, forever. Bring the apron anyway." Just curious what you think!

I'm a grad student asked to speak at Professor Lindqvist's retirement. Draft: "She once returned my thesis chapter with one comment: 'You're hiding.' Page after page, I was. It took me a year to understand she'd been teaching me to write and to live in the same sentence. Forty years of that. Professor, thank you for the red ink. We all got braver in it." Is it too sentimental, do you think?

I own a bike shop, and our mechanic Tomasz retires after 25 years. I'm proud of this one: "Tomasz can hear a loose bearing from across the shop and a lie from across the street. He fixed ten thousand flats and handed back every bike like it was new. Tomasz, we're keeping your bench exactly as it is, greasy thumbprints and all. Nobody's allowed to clean it." Thoughts?

I do community theater as a hobby, and our stage manager Gloria is retiring after 19 years. I'm giving the speech: "Gloria has called 'Places' to this company a thousand times. No audience ever learned her name, which is exactly how she wanted it. Every perfect blackout was hers. So tonight, Gloria, we call it for you. Places, everyone. Thank you. Lights down, applause up." How does it read to you?

I run a small print shop, and Walt, our pressman, retires Friday. I wrote: "Walt reads everything backwards, in mirror-image lead and ink, and still found the typo nobody else did. For 44 years he made other people's words look sure of themselves. Walt, you were the quiet margin around everything good in this town. We're running one last job: your name, big, centered, no errors." Would you change anything?

I'm a nursing student, and I was asked to say a few words for Carol, a night-shift nurse retiring after 38 years: "Carol taught me that 3 a.m. is when patients tell the truth. Hold the hand, she said, lower the lights, and wait. Thirty-eight years of waiting with strangers so they weren't alone. I may never be as good, but I'll be awake, and that was the first thing she taught me." Honest opinion?

Hobbyist beekeeper here. Our club's oldest member, Arlo, is hanging up his veil. My toast: "Arlo told me bees don't care about your day. Move slow, breathe, and they'll let you in. I've tried to live that way since. Sixty years, millions of bees, and only eleven stings, he claims. Arlo, you kept the hives and the humans calm. We'll leave the smoker lit for you." Do you think it works?

I run a small ferry and whale-watching business. Captain Joan retires this weekend, and I'll say: "Joan has crossed this bay nine thousand times and still points at the water like she's never seen it. Tourists come for whales. They stay because she makes them look. Joan, you taught us the sea isn't a show, it's a conversation. Fair winds. Your chair stays at the wheel, facing out." What do you think?

I'm three months into my first data job and a bit nervous sharing this. It finds users with login streaks of 3+ days (Postgres):
WITH d AS (SELECT DISTINCT user_id, login_date::date AS d FROM logins),
g AS (SELECT user_id, d, d - (ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY d))::int AS grp FROM d)
SELECT user_id, MIN(d) AS streak_start, MAX(d) AS streak_end, COUNT(*) AS days
FROM g GROUP BY user_id, grp HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3 ORDER BY days DESC;

Retired DBA here, tinkering for fun. I wrote an org chart query for our club's volunteer table. Cycle guard included, since people enter data badly:
WITH RECURSIVE chain AS (
  SELECT id, name, manager_id, name::text AS path, 0 AS depth FROM staff WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, c.path || ' > ' || e.name, c.depth + 1
  FROM staff e JOIN chain c ON e.manager_id = c.id WHERE c.depth < 12)
SELECT * FROM chain ORDER BY path;
What's your opinion?

Hey! Uni student, databases course. We had to get the top 3 rated films per category, and I ended up with this:

Product analyst, six years in. Here's my sessionization for web events, 30-minute timeout. Would love a second pair of eyes:
WITH f AS (
  SELECT user_id, ts,
    CASE WHEN LAG(ts) OVER w IS NULL OR ts - LAG(ts) OVER w > INTERVAL '30 minutes' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS new_s
  FROM events
  WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts)
)
SELECT user_id, ts, SUM(new_s) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts) AS session_id FROM f;

I run a small hotel and taught myself SQL from a library book. This finds double-booked rooms:
SELECT a.booking_id, b.booking_id AS conflicts_with, a.room_id
FROM bookings a
JOIN bookings b
  ON a.room_id = b.room_id
 AND a.booking_id < b.booking_id
 AND daterange(a.check_in, a.check_out) && daterange(b.check_in, b.check_out);
I'm proud of it, honestly. What do you make of it?

I'm an HR analyst and need salary stats by department that won't expose individuals. My attempt:

Daily revenue report for January, with zero-fill for days without orders. Used a half-open range so midnight orders aren't doubled:
SELECT d::date AS day, COALESCE(SUM(o.total), 0) AS revenue
FROM generate_series(date '2024-01-01', date '2024-01-31', interval '1 day') d
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.created_at >= d AND o.created_at < d + interval '1 day'
GROUP BY d ORDER BY d;

Point-in-time join against a type 2 customer dimension, so each sale gets the tier the customer had when they bought. I'm a data engineer, 10 years in, casually asking for a review:
SELECT s.sale_id, s.amount, d.price_tier
FROM sales s
JOIN customer_dim d
  ON d.customer_id = s.customer_id
 AND s.sold_at >= d.valid_from
 AND s.sold_at < COALESCE(d.valid_to, 'infinity');

Snowflake dedupe for our signups table. Emails differ by case, and ties on timestamp need a deterministic winner:

Warehouse supervisor, learning SQL at night. Stock upsert that ignores out-of-order updates from the scanners:

Pareto analysis for our catalogue: what share of revenue the top products make. I added the tie-breaker and ROWS frame deliberately.
WITH r AS (SELECT product_id, SUM(revenue) AS rev FROM sales GROUP BY product_id)
SELECT product_id, rev,
  SUM(rev) OVER (ORDER BY rev DESC, product_id ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) / SUM(rev) OVER () AS cum_share
FROM r ORDER BY rev DESC, product_id;
I'm a finance manager, not a developer. Does this look right to you?

Flattening JSON order items in Postgres. Our orders come from three vendors, so the key isn't always present:
SELECT o.id, item->>'sku' AS sku, (item->>'qty')::int AS qty
FROM orders o
CROSS JOIN LATERAL jsonb_array_elements(o.payload->'items') AS item
WHERE o.payload ? 'items';

Our invoice numbers should be sequential, and the auditors want any missing ranges. Here's my query, I'm an accountant who picked up SQL on the job:
SELECT prev_no + 1 AS gap_start, invoice_no - 1 AS gap_end
FROM (
  SELECT invoice_no, LAG(invoice_no) OVER (ORDER BY invoice_no) AS prev_no
  FROM invoices
) t
WHERE invoice_no - prev_no > 1;

7-day moving average of site visits. I used a RANGE interval frame rather than ROWS so missing days don't skew it:
SELECT day, visits,
  AVG(visits) OVER (
    ORDER BY day
    RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '6 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
  ) AS avg_7d
FROM daily_visits;

I coach a youth football league and built the table from raw match results. Ties break on goal difference, then goals scored:
WITH r AS (
  SELECT home AS team, hg AS gf, ag AS ga FROM matches
  UNION ALL
  SELECT away, ag, hg FROM matches)
SELECT RANK() OVER (ORDER BY SUM(CASE WHEN gf > ga THEN 3 WHEN gf = ga THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) DESC,
  SUM(gf - ga) DESC, SUM(gf) DESC) AS pos, team
FROM r GROUP BY team ORDER BY pos;
Thoughts?

Sales report with subtotals by region and city plus a grand total. I used GROUPING() to label the rollup rows rather than rely on NULLs:
SELECT CASE WHEN GROUPING(region) = 1 THEN 'ALL' ELSE region END AS region,
  CASE WHEN GROUPING(city) = 1 THEN 'Subtotal' ELSE city END AS city,
  SUM(amount) AS sales
FROM sales
GROUP BY ROLLUP (region, city)
ORDER BY GROUPING(region), region, GROUPING(city), city;

Job queue worker claim in Postgres. Multiple workers poll at once, so I used SKIP LOCKED:
WITH next AS (
  SELECT id FROM jobs
  WHERE status = 'queued'
  ORDER BY priority DESC, created_at
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
  LIMIT 1
)
UPDATE jobs SET status = 'running', started_at = now()
FROM next WHERE jobs.id = next.id
RETURNING jobs.*;
Staff engineer here, sharing for a sanity check. What do you think?

Funnel conversion for our checkout flow, first timestamp per step so repeat visits don't inflate the counts:
WITH s AS (
  SELECT user_id,
    MIN(ts) FILTER (WHERE step = 'view') AS v,
    MIN(ts) FILTER (WHERE step = 'cart') AS c,
    MIN(ts) FILTER (WHERE step = 'pay') AS p
  FROM funnel_events GROUP BY user_id)
SELECT COUNT(v) AS viewed, COUNT(c) FILTER (WHERE c >= v) AS carted, COUNT(p) FILTER (WHERE p >= c AND c >= v) AS paid FROM s;
Casual question: how does it look?

Monthly cohort retention for our subscription app. I'm a data scientist and wrote it in one sitting, so tell me if I've missed something.
WITH f AS (
  SELECT customer_id, MIN(date_trunc('month', ordered_at)) AS cohort
  FROM orders GROUP BY 1)
SELECT f.cohort,
  DATEDIFF('month', f.cohort, date_trunc('month', o.ordered_at)) AS months_since,
  COUNT(DISTINCT o.customer_id) AS active
FROM f JOIN orders o USING (customer_id)
GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY 1, 2;

Customers who bought a printer but never bought ink. I'm a retail manager, and I used NOT EXISTS since I'd read NOT IN breaks with NULLs:

Year-over-year revenue by month, built on LAG over a month-partitioned window so it's one pass over the table. I'm a financial analyst, 15 years in.
SELECT yr, mo, revenue,
  ROUND(100.0 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER w) / NULLIF(LAG(revenue) OVER w, 0), 1) AS yoy_pct
FROM (SELECT EXTRACT(year FROM d) AS yr, EXTRACT(month FROM d) AS mo, SUM(amt) AS revenue FROM ledger GROUP BY 1, 2) m
WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY mo ORDER BY yr)
ORDER BY yr, mo;
Your opinion?

I'm a nurse who got curious about our scheduling data. This finds nurses working more than 5 consecutive days:
WITH d AS (
  SELECT nurse_id, shift_date,
    shift_date - (ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY nurse_id ORDER BY shift_date))::int AS grp
  FROM (SELECT DISTINCT nurse_id, shift_date FROM shifts) s)
SELECT nurse_id, MIN(shift_date) AS first_day, COUNT(*) AS days_in_a_row
FROM d GROUP BY nurse_id, grp HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;

I run a small bakery and wanted to know which days each item sold zero, so I can stop baking it. Here's the query I wrote:

FROM products p
CROSS JOIN generate_series('2024-03-01'::date, '2024-03-31', '1 day') d
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM sale_items si JOIN sales s ON s.id = si.sale_id

Genealogy is my hobby, and I finally got this working. It pulls all of Hannah's ancestors with generation numbers and stops if bad data creates a loop:
WITH RECURSIVE anc AS (
  SELECT id, father_id, mother_id, 0 AS gen, ARRAY[id] AS path FROM people WHERE name = 'Hannah Moll'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT p.id, p.father_id, p.mother_id, a.gen + 1, a.path || p.id
  FROM anc a JOIN people p ON p.id IN (a.father_id, a.mother_id)
  WHERE p.id <> ALL (a.path))
SELECT p.name, a.gen FROM anc a JOIN people p USING (id) ORDER BY gen, name;
Thoughts?

I log my 5k runs in a database (nerdy, I know). This shows only the runs where I set a new personal best:
SELECT run_date, km5_time
FROM (
  SELECT run_date, km5_time,
    MIN(km5_time) OVER (ORDER BY run_date ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING) AS prev_best

WHERE prev_best IS NULL OR km5_time < prev_best
ORDER BY run_date;

Proud of this one from my SQL homework! Find students who've completed every required course:

FROM students s
JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id AND e.completed

HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c.id) = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM courses WHERE required);

I manage a tiny climbing gym and need to catch double-booked rooms. This is what I came up with:
SELECT a.room, a.id AS booking_a, b.id AS booking_b
FROM bookings a
JOIN bookings b
  ON a.room = b.room
 AND a.id < b.id
 AND a.starts_at < b.ends_at
 AND b.starts_at < a.ends_at
ORDER BY a.room, a.starts_at;

Plant nerd here. I keep a table of my 60 houseplants, and this tells me which are due for watering today:
WITH last AS (SELECT plant_id, MAX(watered_on) AS last_on FROM waterings GROUP BY plant_id)
SELECT p.name, COALESCE(l.last_on, p.acquired_on) + p.water_every_days AS due
FROM plants p LEFT JOIN last l ON l.plant_id = p.id
WHERE COALESCE(l.last_on, p.acquired_on) + p.water_every_days <= CURRENT_DATE
ORDER BY due;
Opinions welcome!

I own a small bike repair shop and wanted to know how long customers take to come back for a second visit:
WITH o AS (
  SELECT customer_id, ordered_at,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ordered_at) AS rn
  FROM orders)
SELECT AVG(b.ordered_at - a.ordered_at) AS avg_gap

Statistics student here. For my project I needed median salary by department, skipping departments that are too small to mean anything:

I own a small indie bookstore. This flags titles to reorder once stock minus open customer holds drops under 3:
-- pre-aggregate holds so multiple holds don't duplicate book rows
SELECT b.isbn, b.title, b.on_hand - COALESCE(h.held, 0) AS available
FROM books b
LEFT JOIN (SELECT isbn, SUM(qty) AS held FROM holds WHERE status = 'open' GROUP BY isbn) h USING (isbn)
WHERE b.on_hand - COALESCE(h.held, 0) < 3
ORDER BY available;
What do you think?

Birdwatching is my hobby and I keep every sighting in Postgres. This counts how many new species (lifers) I add each year, with a running total:
WITH f AS (
  SELECT species, EXTRACT(year FROM MIN(seen_on))::int AS yr
  FROM sightings GROUP BY species)
SELECT yr, COUNT(*) AS lifers, SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER (ORDER BY yr) AS life_list
FROM f GROUP BY yr ORDER BY yr;

For my data analytics class I had to split clickstream data into sessions with a 30-minute inactivity gap. Here's mine:

         THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS new_session
  FROM clicks)
SELECT user_id, ts,
  SUM(new_session) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts) AS session_no

I run a food truck and wanted each location's best sales hour, keeping ties:

FROM (

    RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY location ORDER BY SUM(total) DESC) AS rk
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY location, EXTRACT(hour FROM sold_at)) t
WHERE rk = 1;

I'm a small-time landlord with four tenants and a ledger table. This gives each tenant's running balance, with charges sorted ahead of payments on the same day:
WITH ledger AS (
  SELECT tenant_id, due_on AS d, amount FROM charges
  UNION ALL
  SELECT tenant_id, paid_on, -amount FROM payments)
SELECT tenant_id, d, amount,
  SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY tenant_id ORDER BY d, amount DESC ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS balance
FROM ledger ORDER BY tenant_id, d;
What's your opinion?

I track my D&D group's attendance. I wanted players who've made every session since they joined, so I used a double NOT EXISTS:

WHERE NOT EXISTS (

    AND NOT EXISTS (
      SELECT 1 FROM attendance a
      WHERE a.session_id = s.id AND a.player_id = p.id));

Here's a funnel query I wrote for my online shop's January traffic:
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS visited,
  COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) FILTER (WHERE event = 'add_to_cart') AS carted,
  COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) FILTER (WHERE event = 'purchase') AS bought

I kept the date range open-ended on purpose so an index could be used. Any thoughts?

I own a flower shop and Mother's Day skews everything, so I compare each month to the same month last year:

FROM monthly_revenue
WINDOW w AS (ORDER BY month)
ORDER BY month;

Library fines assignment, and I wanted unreturned books to keep accruing fines at $0.25 per day:
WITH f AS (
  SELECT member_id,
    GREATEST(COALESCE(returned_on, CURRENT_DATE) - due_on, 0) * 0.25 AS fine
  FROM loans)
SELECT m.name, SUM(f.fine) AS fines
FROM f JOIN members m ON m.id = f.member_id
GROUP BY m.id, m.name
HAVING SUM(f.fine) > 0
ORDER BY fines DESC;
What do you think?

I'm cataloguing my vinyl collection in Postgres with a tags array. Wanted live jazz albums but no Christmas ones:
CREATE INDEX albums_tags_gin ON albums USING gin (tags);
SELECT title, artist
FROM albums
WHERE tags @> ARRAY['jazz', 'live']
  AND NOT tags && ARRAY['christmas']
ORDER BY artist, title;
I'd love to know how this strikes you.

I'm a freelance designer and invoice clients in installments. This shows what each client still owes. I aggregated billed and paid separately first so the joins don't multiply rows:
WITH b AS (SELECT client_id, SUM(amount) AS billed FROM invoices GROUP BY 1),
p AS (SELECT i.client_id, SUM(pay.amount) AS paid FROM payments pay JOIN invoices i ON i.id = pay.invoice_id GROUP BY 1)
SELECT c.name, COALESCE(b.billed, 0) - COALESCE(p.paid, 0) AS owed
FROM clients c LEFT JOIN b ON b.client_id = c.id LEFT JOIN p ON p.client_id = c.id
ORDER BY owed DESC;
Thoughts?

Cleaning up my shop's mailing list. This removes duplicate emails (ignoring case and spaces), keeping the most recently updated row:
DELETE FROM contacts
WHERE id IN (
  SELECT id FROM (
    SELECT id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
      PARTITION BY LOWER(TRIM(email)) ORDER BY updated_at DESC, id) AS rn
    FROM contacts) t
  WHERE rn > 1);
I'm a bit nervous about running a DELETE. What's your opinion?

I analyze my own online chess games for fun. Here's how I score my openings as Black, counting draws as half a point and ignoring openings I've played fewer than 20 times:
SELECT opening, COUNT(*) AS games,
  ROUND(AVG(CASE result WHEN 'win' THEN 1.0 WHEN 'draw' THEN 0.5 ELSE 0 END), 3) AS score
FROM games
WHERE color = 'black'
GROUP BY opening
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 20
ORDER BY score DESC;
What do you reckon?

Hi! I'm a second-grade teacher and I finally wrote a picture book premise: A little bunny named Benny Bunny is sad because he thinks he's not special. Then he learns that everyone is special in their own way, and the whole forest has a party. The end. Can you tell me what you think? I'd love to send it to publishers soon!

Here's the pitch for my kids' book: "Sammy the Shark is scared of the water. He is a shark who lives in the ocean, but he is afraid of the ocean water. One day he learns to swim and isn't afraid anymore." My daughter is 5 and she's my target audience. Thoughts?
