Hey, I'm 16 and I wrote this for my little cousin. Premise: A 4-year-old girl named Lily inherits her late grandfather's shipping company, and must negotiate with dock unions to save it from bankruptcy, with the help of her talking hamster, Mr. Nibbles. Ages 3-5. What do you think, any feedback?

Retired accountant here, first attempt at writing for my grandkids. Premise: Penguins live in the Sahara Desert and have to find a way to stay cool. Percy Penguin builds an igloo out of sand and all the penguins cheer. I wanted it to be educational too. Would you give me your honest opinion?

I'm a nurse and I've been writing at night after shifts. My idea: Timmy the Tooth is a tooth who doesn't want to be brushed. Every page, a different food tells him brushing is good, and he says no. Then a dentist says yes. Then the book ends with a list of dental rules. Could you give me feedback? Nervous to share!

So I came up with this awesome idea for a kids book 😄 A boy named Max finds a magic pencil that draws anything real. He draws a dragon, a castle, a pizza, a robot, a unicorn, a rocket, and a swimming pool. Then he goes to bed. Thoughts? Just kinda curious what you'd say.

I'm a stay-at-home dad and I've been telling this story at bedtime for months. A princess named Princess Rosalina lives in a pink castle. A mean dragon steals her crown. A brave prince rescues it and they get married. She is so happy. Do you think I could get this published? Please be straight with me.

My book premise, for ages 6-8: "Gerald the Giraffe has a very long neck. Because his neck is long, he is tall. Because he is tall, he can see far. Because he can see far, he sees a lot of things." It goes on like this for 30 pages until he sees his friend. What's your opinion?

I'm a software engineer, new to children's lit. Here's my concept: Zara the Zebra learns about the water cycle. She meets Evaporation, Condensation, and Precipitation, who are all villains trying to steal her lake. Then Collection saves the day. Also there are 14 other characters I haven't described yet. How does it sound?

Hello! I'm 68 and this is my first book. "Once upon a time, in a land far, far away, there lived a little boy who wanted to be a hero. He went on a quest and found a sword. He was a hero. The end." I drew pictures too. Can you give me your thoughts?

I teach kindergarten and wanted a book about sharing. Premise: Two squirrels, Sam and Sue, fight over one acorn. A wise old owl appears and lectures them for six pages about sharing and the economy. They split the acorn. I'm planning to read it to my class on Monday. What do you think?

Just finished my first draft idea! A kitten named Whiskers gets lost in the city. She meets a dog who is mean, then a bird who is mean, then a rat who is mean, then a cat who is mean. Then she finds home and everyone is nice. Mom says it's cute. What would you say?

I'm a college student studying marketing and I'm self-publishing a book for kids. It's about Billy the Bee who discovers honey comes from cows. He tells all the other bees, and they start a cow farm. It's meant to be funny and teach kids about nature. Can I get your feedback?

As a pediatric dentist I wanted a book for toddlers. Premise: A creepy shadow named Mr. Cavity haunts a little girl every night, whispering that her teeth will fall out and rot, and she'll die alone unless she brushes. She brushes. He vanishes. Ages 2-4. Does this work? Interested to hear your take.

Hi, I'm a high school student and I'm writing a book called "The Adventures of Adventure Dog." It's about a dog named Adventure who goes on adventures. On his first adventure he goes to the park. On his second adventure he goes to another park. Third adventure: a different park. Could you share your opinions?

I'm a mom of three and I wrote this on my phone during naptime: A little cloud named Cloudy is sad. He rains. Then he's happy. Then he's sad again. Then happy. Then sad. Then happy. It teaches kids about feelings! I'd love to hear what you think about it.

Premise for my picture book (ages 3-6): A boy named Jake has a fight with his best friend, so he builds a time machine, travels to the Jurassic period, and is eaten by a T. rex. His friend feels sorry. The moral is to apologize. I think kids love dinosaurs! Honest thoughts welcome.

I've been a lawyer for 20 years and I'm trying my hand at a kids' book. Premise: Oliver Owl teaches woodland animals about contract law, with each page featuring a clause. Sample line: "Hereinafter, the party of the first part, Squirrel, shall share nuts." My nephew is 4. What are your thoughts on it?

Here's my idea for a chapter book! A girl named Emma finds out she is secretly a princess AND a wizard AND a fairy AND a mermaid. She goes to a school for chosen ones, where the chosen one is her. There's a dark lord who wants to destroy everything. It's totally original! What do you think?

Hi, I'm a grandma who loves to write. My story: "Daisy the Duck went to the pond. She saw a frog. The frog said, 'Hello, Daisy.' Daisy said, 'Hello, frog.' The frog said, 'How are you, Daisy?' Daisy said, 'I am fine, frog. How are you?'" This goes on for a while. Please tell me your thoughts!

I'm a freelance illustrator, and I'm writing my own story. Premise: In a world where all vegetables are alive, Carl Carrot is chopped up by a farmer and put in a stew, and his friends have to eat him in the end as a lesson about the circle of life. Preschool age. Would love your input!

I'm 10 and I wrote a book idea! It's about a boy named Jack who is the best at everything. He wins every race, every spelling bee, and every game. Everyone loves him. He never loses. The end. My teacher said to ask someone what they think. What do you think?

As a pastor, I want to write a children's book about honesty. Premise: Little Tommy tells one lie about eating a cookie, and then lightning strikes his house, his dog runs away, and his family gets sick. He confesses, and everything is fixed. Ages 4-7. Could I get your honest feedback on this concept?

Hey! I'm a first-time writer. My story is about Ollie the Octopus who has eight arms and plays eight sports. On page 1, he plays soccer with one arm. On page 2, he plays soccer with two arms. On page 3, three arms. It goes up to eight, then we start again to teach counting to 100. Thoughts?

Hi! I'm a college sophomore and wrote my first picture book premise for a class. Benny the Bunny doesn't like to share his carrots. Then he meets a sad squirrel named Sammy who has no nuts. Benny shares, and they become best friends forever. The end. Could you tell me what you think? I'm hoping to show it to my professor.

I own a small bakery and I'm writing a kids' book! Premise: Cupcake Carl lives in Sweet Dreams Bakery on 5th Street. Every day, Cupcake Carl says Sweet Dreams Bakery has the best cupcakes in town. Carl visits kids' birthday parties, and everyone says Sweet Dreams Bakery is the best. I'd love your feedback before I print copies!

Here's my idea for a kids' book, I do this as a hobby: Pepper the Penguin lives at the North Pole and loves sliding on the ice. One day his friend Paul the Polar Bear invites him over for fish dinner and they play tag with the reindeer. What do you think? Be honest-ish, haha.

I run a dental clinic and want to write a book for my young patients. Premise: Tommy eats candy every day and refuses to brush. His teeth fall out, he can't eat pizza, and all his friends laugh at him forever. Then he brushes and the teeth grow back. Lesson: always brush! Can you give me your thoughts on it?

Hello, I'm a nervous grad student writing a book for ages 2-4. Opening line: "Ephemeral Ellie contemplated the existential ramifications of her translucent wings as the iridescent twilight meandered across the melancholy meadow." She's a butterfly who learns about change. Is this a good start for toddlers? Sorry, it's my first one.

I'm a retired bus driver and I rhyme for my grandkids. Here's the start: "There was a cat named Matt, who wore a big red hat. He liked to sit and eat, a lot of tasty treat. The dog came by named Fred, and went to take a bed." I'm going to keep going like this for 30 pages. Thoughts?

Just a casual idea from my creative writing class: Lily is scared of the dark. One night a magic fairy appears and says, "Don't be scared, Lily, the dark is fine!" Lily isn't scared anymore. The fairy leaves. Lily sleeps well. I've got that as the whole story so far. What do you think, any tips?

I'm so excited to share this! My book is about Max, a boy who hates school. He struggles all year, tries lots of things, and makes no friends. Then on the last page he wakes up and realizes it was all a dream and school is actually fun. I think kids will love the twist! Feedback welcome!

Hey, I'm a high school student writing a book for my little cousin. Characters: Ollie the Owl, Fiona the Fox, Gary the Goat, Mimi the Mouse, Rusty the Raccoon, Daisy the Deer, Bruno the Bear, Wendy the Worm, and Zed the Zebra. They all go on a picnic. I'll introduce each one for two pages. Does that sound okay?

Hi, I'm a stay-at-home mom and I wrote this for my 5-year-old. Premise: 6-year-old Lucy gets lost, so she walks alone into the forest at night, picks some bright mushrooms to eat, and follows a stranger who offers her a ride home. It's an adventure about being brave! Would you say it's ready to send to publishers?

My book for preschoolers begins: "Sally was sad. She was very sad. Sad, sad, sad. Her sadness made her feel sad inside. She felt so sad that she was sad." Then Sally finds a puppy. I'm a hobby writer and this is my first draft. Nervous to hear what you think!

Hi! I make handmade stars-and-moon nursery decor and I'm writing a matching book. Premise: A little star wants to shine brighter than all the other stars. She tries and tries, and in the end she learns that everyone is special in their own way and she shines the brightest of all. Could you let me know your thoughts?

I'm a gym owner writing a children's book about fitness. Premise: Chubby Charlie gets teased by everyone at school for being round. He starts running every day and loses 30 pounds in a week. Now everyone likes him and he's finally happy! I want to promote healthy habits. How does it sound to you?

Hi, I'm in a children's lit course and this is my pitch. "Pip the Pig wakes up. Pip eats breakfast. Pip goes to the park. Pip sees a tree. Pip goes home. Pip takes a nap." It's a day-in-the-life book for ages 3-5. I tried to keep it simple. Thoughts?

I'm a hobbyist and love writing rhymes! Here's my opening: "Oh Timmy the turtle, so slow and so green, was the most slowest turtle that I've ever seen. He walked to the shop to buy a big bun, but the shop it was closed, so he didn't have fun!" How's it look so far? Open to anything!

I'm making an educational book for my homeschool co-op about dinosaurs! Premise: A T. rex and a Triceratops live in the Ice Age with cavemen Bob and Ug, who ride the dinosaurs to hunt woolly mammoths. Kids will learn real science while having fun. I'm a bit proud of it. What are your thoughts?

I'm a dog groomer writing a book. Premise: Poor Penny the Poodle lives with two mean stepsisters who make her clean all day. A fairy godmother gives her a fancy collar so she can go to the Dog Ball, where a prince dog falls in love with her. She loses a bone at midnight. I'm calling it Penny-rella! What do you think?

Writing a kids' book for a school project. Here's a bit: "Zoe felt very happy because she was happy. She smiled a big smile with her mouth, which showed she was happy. Then Zoe felt sad because her balloon popped, and she cried tears from her eyes, which meant she was sad." Does this work for kids? Any advice?

I'm a kindergarten teaching assistant making a counting book. "One duck swims in the pond. Two frogs sit on a log. Three bees buzz in the air. Five cows eat the grass. Four pigs roll in the mud. Seven hens peck the corn. Six sheep nap in the sun." Kids will learn numbers 1 to 7! Could you give me feedback?

I'm a plumber and wrote a book for my nephew! Premise: Pipe Pete is a wrench who lives in a toolbox and then he finds out about a leak and then he goes to fix it but then the toolbox falls and then Pete is stuck and then a hammer helps him and then they fix the leak and then it's night. Thoughts?

Hi everyone, I'm a student and this is the ending of my picture book. Bella the Bird spends 20 pages trying to find her lost feather, flying through storms and meeting a wise owl. On page 21, she finds it. On page 22: "And that's all." I wanted it to feel punchy. Does it work?

Hobby writer here! My book is about Buzzy the Bee, a boy bee who is the queen of the hive and lays all the eggs. He flies to the flowers, makes honey in his stomach, and stings bad guys many times, which is fun, and keeps living. Kids will love learning about bees! What's your opinion?

I run a small daycare and am writing a bedtime book. Premise: Before sleeping, Little Wolf hears monsters under his bed, in the closet, and outside the window. They chase him through the house with loud roars until he hides in the basement. He's still hiding at the end, but the book rhymes! Do you think parents would like it?

I'm a student making an alphabet book! "A is for Apple. B is for Ball. C is for Cat. D is for Dog. E is for Elephant. F is for Phone. G is for Giraffe. H is for Hat. I is for Ice cream. K is for Kween." I'm planning to finish through Z next week. Can you tell me what you think so far?

Retired bus driver here, first try at a picture book. Premise: every night, Ruth's shadow slips off to work the night shift at a bakery across town, and comes home at dawn smelling of bread and too tired to play. Ruth decides to follow it one night. The whole book is that one walk through the sleeping city. Would love your honest opinion.

I'm a pediatric nurse and I wrote this for my patients. Opening: "The machine by Tomás's bed made three sounds. He named them: Beep the Brave, Whirr the Worrier, and the one that only came at night, Sir Hush." Over the book he makes friends with each. Could you tell me what you think? I'm a little nervous showing it to anyone.

Hi! I'm 11 and I wrote a book for my little brother. It's called The Baby Is a Very Loud Potato. First page: "Mama brought home a potato in a blanket. It cried. Nobody else thought this was strange." Please tell me what you think and what I should change!

I teach second grade and I'm drafting a story. Premise: Odile the snail is the world's slowest mail carrier, so every letter arrives years late. But each one lands on the exact day its reader needed it most. Chapter one is a birthday card, forty years overdue, reaching a man on the morning he turns lonely. Curious how this lands for you.

My daughter splits her week between two homes, so I wrote her this. "Mina had two toothbrushes, one blue, one green. They had never met. Every Sunday night, zipped in the dark of her bag, they compared notes about her." They slowly learn to be a team. Does the premise work? I'm nervous to ask, but I'd like real feedback.

I'm 72 and my granddaughter doesn't speak Tagalog. So: in Lola's kitchen there's one rule, you can only ask for something by its name in the other language. "Pass the salt" becomes "asin," and soon Mari is hungry in two languages. Every page adds a word and a recipe. What's your opinion? Be honest, I've survived worse.

Illustrator here, writing my first text. This is the refrain of a bedtime book:
"Not yet," said the moon, "I'm still tucking in the sea."
"Not yet," said the sea, "I'm still rocking the whale."
"Not yet," said the whale, "I'm humming the stars their tune."
"Not yet," said the stars, "we're waiting up for you."
Thoughts on how it reads aloud?

My son stutters, so I wrote a book about a river. "The river didn't hurry past the rocks. It stopped, and tried again, and tried again, and that is why it sang." Eli watches it the whole afternoon before his class presentation. I'm a software engineer, not a writer, so I'd really value an outside opinion.

I've been a carpenter for forty years and this is my first story. The narrator is a house. "The Pattersons took the couch, the lamps, and the cat. They left me the height marks on the kitchen doorframe, which I thought was kind." Then it waits for the next family. What's your take on it?

I'm 16 and wrote this for a school project. A kid is scared of the dark, but the Dark is scared of kids: they're loud, sticky, and own flashlights. First line: "Under Jonah's bed, the Dark was practicing its brave face." They end up hiding in the same closet. Does it work? Be real with me lol.

I'm a linguist trying picture books for the first time. Barnaby the goat eats a dictionary and starts hiccuping random words. The farm learns to read them: "Marmalade" means he's lonely, "Ostrich" means a storm is coming, "Plinth" means he loves you. Then one day he hiccups a word nobody knows. How does this strike you?

Here's the ending of my picture book about Pip, a dragon whose fire is only warm enough to toast one marshmallow: "And that is why, in Hollowby, if you wait at the bus stop in January, you will find a small green dragon holding out her paws, and a line of people who are not in a hurry." What do you think? I'm a line cook, so be as blunt as you like.

I'm a geologist, and I wrote a book for my niece. "Every stone on the beach was waiting to become something. Dot only wanted to be thrown once, and touch the water seven times." She is, and she does, and then she sinks, slowly, to where the sand is made. Last page: a new beach. Would you give me your honest reaction?

Written at 2am while my twins slept. Two sisters share a room, and Dad lays masking tape down the middle. Page 6, the tape is a river. Page 9, a border with passports. Page 14, a bridge of stuffed animals. Last line: "The tape was still there in the morning. It had just gotten a lot easier to step over." Honest opinion, please?

I'm an accountant, and this is the opening of a picture book I've been playing with: "'Excuse me,' said the giant, leaning in from the edge of page three, 'would you mind turning the page? My elbow is on page four.'" The giant is too big for the story, and the other characters have to help him fit. What do you think?

I'm a school librarian and an immigrant, and I wrote this one for me too. Linh collects the wrong ways people say her name in jars: Lin, Lynn, Lean. Her grandmother says each jar is a small gift from someone who tried. On the last page, a new teacher asks Linh to say it first. I'd love your thoughts, truly.

I'm a vet tech, and kids ask me about death all the time. Premise: Gus's goldfish dies, and at the funeral each relative gives a different eulogy. Gran's is wrong, Dad's is too short, and Gus slowly realizes each of them knew a different fish. Last line: "Gus said his own, and it was the longest." Could you give me your opinion?

I'm an urban planner and I wrote this on the train. Ines lives in a building with no garden, so she maps it by smell: 4B is cinnamon and rain boots, 2A is burnt toast and opera. Mr. Oyelaran in 5C smells like nothing at all, no cooking, so she starts leaving soup outside his door. What do you make of it?

I teach maths, and I wrote this for my youngest class. "Zero was round and empty and absolutely sure she was nothing." Then One stands beside her and suddenly they are Ten, and the other numbers realize none of them can get past nine without her. I'd love to know what you think, especially as a non-teacher.

I'm a farmer, new to writing. In the town of Marl, your umbrella opens onto whatever you're feeling: Grandpa's makes drizzle, the mayor's makes hail. Nell's opens only sunshine, because she never lets anyone see her sad. The day it finally drizzles over her, the whole town comes to stand underneath. Tell me what you think, please.

I'm a paralegal who writes at lunch. Here's the first line of my chapter book: "The day Marguerite Okonkwo-Bell turned nine, she inherited a lighthouse, a debt, and a very opinionated seagull." The seagull has strong views on her accounting. I'm wondering what you'd say about the voice and where it might go.

I'm 9 and this is my first book. My tooth said, "I'm not falling out. I have a lease." Then it made friends with my tongue and they had a secret handshake, and Mom said the dentist would have to negotiate. Everybody in Room 4 already lost theirs except me. Do you like it? What would you change?

I'm a sign language interpreter, and this is my first book. Cal moves to a town where nobody signs. Each day he invents a sign for something: bread is two hands rising, rain is ten small taps. By autumn the baker, the bus driver, and one very smart dog are answering him. How does the premise strike you? Honest feedback welcome.

I'm a merchant sailor, away most of the year, and I wrote a counting book for my kids. "One compass, so you can always find me. Two socks that don't match on purpose. Three letters, to open on three Sundays." It goes up to ten, and ten is the ship coming home. I'm pretty nervous about this. What's your reaction?

I taught kindergarten for 35 years and finally wrote my own. Mr. Quill, a bear who runs a train station's lost-and-found, has one rule: he never asks what something is worth. Then a boy comes in looking for "the afternoon I was happy here with Dad." Mr. Quill starts searching the shelves anyway. What's your opinion?

This is the first time I've shown anyone this, so I'm a bit nervous. Picture book premise: Grandma's words are migrating. Each autumn a few fly south: first "colander," then "Thursday," then my character's name. Nine-year-old Ines builds a feeder from a shoebox and fills it with index cards of words. Grandma reads each one aloud slowly, as if tasting it. Could you tell me what you honestly think?

Hey! I run a bakery and wrote a story for the kids who come in on Saturdays. Gerald, a sourdough starter, sulks when he's fed late, and six-year-old Pia learns to read his bubbles like moods. On the last page she tells him she'll be late on Monday, and apologizes first. Any thoughts? I'm mostly curious how it would work read aloud.

Pretty proud of this one! "Marguerite Outgrows Her Shell." A hermit crab queues on a beach for a bigger home, in a market where a whelk shell is a status symbol and a bottle cap is "a fixer-upper." Each page she trades up and meets the tiny, delighted crab now living in her old shell. The final spread is a long line of crabs passing shells down the sand. Opinions welcome!

I wrote this for my little brother, whose dad works nights. "The House Is Wearing Its Quiet." Every afternoon Theo tiptoes through the rooms like they're a sleeping animal: cereal without crunching, cartoons on captions only. At four o'clock Dad's alarm rings, and the whole house exhales and gets loud again. How does it read to you? Be straight with me.

Nervous to share this, but here's my counting-down picture book about moving house. Ten boxes taped shut. Nine pencil marks on the doorframe, left for strangers. Eight echoing rooms. It goes down to one girl, one key, and a new door that sticks. Then the pages count back up. I'm a nursing student with no writing background. Does the structure work?

I keep two hives and wrote this for the neighbourhood kids. Odette is a bee whose waggle dance is wobbly and gives garbled directions. Her sisters follow anyway, out of pity, and find an abandoned orchard nobody had scouted, exactly where her mistake pointed. I'd love a read from someone who knows picture books. Where would you push it?

My little cousin stutters, and I wrote this for him. Caleb notices the river stutters too, tripping over every rock ("b-b-bubble, b-b-bubble"), yet it reaches the sea every single time. Nobody in the book ever says "fix." He just sits beside the water and talks back to it. I'm a bit nervous about getting it right. Would you mind giving me honest feedback?

I'm a locksmith, so keys are my thing. "The Key to Number 12": an old man still carries the key to a house that was torn down. A girl chalks a door on the empty lot, and he turns the key in the air. The neighbours, one by one, come and knock. It's for ages 5 to 8. Would love an honest opinion if you have a minute.

Our daughter cried when the snow melted, so I wrote this on my lunch breaks. "Snowman, Stored." Odile hides her snowman in the chest freezer between the peas and Dad's fish, visiting daily with a scarf. By July he's the size of a grapefruit. In December she introduces him to the first snowfall like a returning relative. I'm a plumber, not an author. Thoughts?

I own a flower shop. Idea: "The Seed Packet Said Giraffe." A boy plants a mislabeled packet and waits, measuring himself against the soil each week and building a tall fence just in case. A sunflower arrives. He isn't disappointed. He says, "It's got the neck, though." Do you think it suits ages 4 to 6? Honest feedback, please.

Casual one from a dog groomer: "Bernard Is Not a Cloud." Bernard the poodle sits on the hill all day hoping a pigeon will mistake him for weather. Nobody does. Then a kid tells him, "Clouds get to rain," and he shakes himself off all over the whole picnic. That's the ending. I know poodles very well, but picture books, not so much. What do you make of it?

I'm a hobby knitter, and this is my first story. In the town of Fenwick, a scarf grows one stitch every time somebody feels lonely. Nobody notices until it's long enough to wrap the bakery, the bus stop and a sleeping dog. The girl who follows it to the end discovers it's attached to her own cuff. I'd really like to know how it lands for a reader.

Twenty years driving Route 9, so I wrote a picture book about it. At each stop an animal boards carrying something: a heron with a folded umbrella, a bear with a whole cake, a snail with his own bus stop. The driver says "Mind the step" to every one. The last stop is a lit kitchen window where a kid has been counting headlights. Any feedback welcome, even blunt.

I'm studying literature and tried a folktale. "Tortoise Carries the News." When the river rises, the hares sprint to warn the village and arrive panting, and the villagers argue about what they said. Tortoise arrives hours later and says it once, calmly. Everyone's already packing, because he described every cracked bank he passed on the way. Does the ending earn its moral, in your view?

I'm a tailor, and my book is about trousers. "Hem" follows one pair of corduroys across three brothers. Each page the hem is let down an inch, and the pockets hold what the last boy left: a pebble, a bus ticket, a dried worm. On the final page the youngest hears the jingle and realizes he's wearing his brothers' whole childhoods. Tell me what you think!

I'm a student and a hearing child of Deaf parents, and I've drafted a picture book. The opening line: "Dinner at Mina's house is the loudest time of the day, and nobody makes a sound." It follows her first sleepover at a hearing friend's home, where the quiet table confuses her. I'd love to hear how this opening works for someone outside that world.

I'm a potter and wrote this between kiln loads. Chip is a mug with a cracked lip who gets hidden when guests come. During a power cut, small hands choose him, because the chip fits a thumb exactly. The last line: "Perfect is for looking at. Chip is for holding." I'm unsure whether to keep that ending as written. What would you do with it?

I'm a bookkeeper by trade, and this is my weird side project. "The Tooth Fairy Files Her Taxes." Each page is an itemized receipt: "Molar, lower left, one (1). Payment: two quarters. Hazard surcharge: dog." A running mystery appears in the line items: "Tooth #4 not collected: child awake, pretending." The last invoice is a thank-you note. Does it work for you? Please be candid.

I'm a hobbyist stargazer and I wrote this for my granddaughter. "Marguerite Counts Satellites." Every clear night she and her grandpa lie on their shop roof counting the moving stars. She's told to wish on the first one, but she names them instead. When one burns up and vanishes, she writes it a goodbye. I'm wondering how a six-year-old would take it. What's your reaction?

I run a little hardware store and wrote a rhyming book. Here's how it opens:
"When the owner turns the sign and the keys click twice,
the hammers call to order and the washers roll dice;
the tape measures argue about who's most long,
and the level says, 'Friends, you are all slightly wrong.'"
What do you think? I'm curious whether the rhythm holds up when read aloud.

I'm a design student working on a wordless picture book for a class. A girl walks to school, and every puddle reflects a different sky from the real one above: rain on a sunny day, night at noon. Her boots are the only constant. The last puddle shows a girl who isn't her, and who waves. Could you tell me how this would read to a child?

I'm a beachcomber, and this is my first attempt at a kids' book. "The Low Tide Library." Each low tide a library appears on the shore, with shell-books and crab librarians. You must return everything before the water comes back. Overdue books are simply taken by the sea, "which is why the ocean is so wordy." I'd love your opinion on the premise, honestly.

For my education course I wrote "Tuesday Is Late." Leo waits at the front door for Tuesday, because Mum said it was coming. Through the day the postman arrives, then rain, then Grandma with a bag of oranges. By dinner Leo decides Tuesday is made of all of them. I'm a bit worried about it being too quiet for a read-aloud. Can you give me your honest take?

I train dogs on weekends and wrote this one for fun. "The Sunbeam Clock." A dog waits for his kid to come home, measuring the day by a strip of sun creeping across the kitchen floor: "the yellow reaches the table leg: not yet. The yellow reaches the water bowl: nearly." It ends when the beam hits the door and the key turns. Is that enough to carry a whole book?

I'm sixteen and made this for my new baby sister. "A Map of Our House." It's drawn like a pirate chart: "Here Be Dragons" (the vacuum), "Safe Harbour" (Mum's lap), "The Squeaky Stair, Do Not Cross at Night." Every page adds a landmark, and the final page is blank, labeled "Yours to Chart." I'd love to know what you think, and whether I should keep the pirate theme.

I'm 68 and finally have a backyard to myself! Here's my plan for a 10x10 plot. Row 1: tomatoes. Row 2: tomatoes (a different kind). Row 3: zucchini. Row 4: zucchini. Row 5: zucchini. Center: one giant pumpkin patch. No paths, I'll just step between the plants. What do you think?

Hi, I'm 15 and this is for a school project. My 4x4 raised bed has corn in the middle, watermelon, pumpkins and squash in the corners, sunflowers along the edge, and 6 tomato plants squeezed in wherever there's space. Could you give me some feedback before I build it?

Software engineer here, first time gardening, a bit nervous. My bed is 8 ft wide by 20 ft long, in the middle of the lawn, with no paths. Carrots and onions go in the center, lettuce on the edges. I'll just lean in to reach the middle. Any thoughts?

Here's my 6x3 herb bed plan: mint, lemon balm, oregano, and spearmint all planted together in the left half. Right half: basil, dill, fennel, cilantro. Everything goes in the same soil with no dividers so it looks natural. Would love your opinion!

My backyard faces north and a tall fence shades it from sunrise to sunset. The plan: tomatoes and peppers along the fence, eggplant in the middle, melons at the front. I can't wait for the summer harvest! Does the layout look okay to you?

I'm a new homeowner, and this is my front yard plan. A weeping willow, planted 3 feet from the foundation, right above the septic tank, for shade. Next to it, a vegetable patch and a little bench. Thoughts on the layout?

My garden plan for the front bed: cacti and ferns planted in alternating rows, one after another, all watered daily with a sprinkler so they stay happy together. A gravel path runs down the middle. Be honest, what's your take?

I'm a retired mechanic and my daughter said I should ask for feedback. Plan: oak sapling 2 feet from the patio, bamboo running the whole property line with no barrier, and the rose garden under the oak. Low maintenance, set it and forget it. Opinions?

My garden is 10 ft x 10 ft. Plan: vegetable bed 6x6, flower bed 5x5, patio 4x4, pond 3x3, and the rest of the space will be lawn. I drew it on graph paper and everything fits perfectly. Can you look it over and tell me what you think?

I'm planning my garden and here's the description: it will have flowers, some vegetables, a nice seating area, a path, and various plants. The flowers go where flowers look nice, and the vegetables go in the vegetable area. Everything is arranged in a pleasing way. Thoughts?

I'm a hobby gardener and proud of this one: a black walnut tree in the center of the yard, with tomatoes and potatoes planted in a ring right under its branches to take advantage of the shade. Benches on the outside. How does it look to you?

Layout for my south-facing bed, front to back: sunflowers (8 ft tall) at the front, then corn, then lettuce and violas at the back, since they like cool conditions. Sun comes from the front so everything gets plenty! Does this seem right? Thanks!

First-time square foot gardener! My 4x4 bed has 16 squares, and each square gets one plant: 4 zucchini, 4 pumpkins, 4 watermelons, and 4 cucumbers. That way everything is perfectly organized and even. Can you give me your feedback?

I have a 4x8 raised bed and ordered 40 tomato seedlings. Plan: plant all of them 6 inches apart in rows, with no stakes because they'll support each other. I'm hoping for a huge harvest this year. What do you think of the plan?

I'm a landscaper's apprentice. For my own yard: beds in a grid of 30 flower islands, each 1 ft wide, scattered across the lawn, with the lawn mowed around each one. A 4-inch-wide stepping path connects them, and I'll use a wheelbarrow. Feedback welcome!

I'm a mom designing a dog-friendly garden for our puppy, who loves chewing. Plan: foxglove along the fence, oleander by the gate, a sago palm in the center, lily of the valley under the window, and a grassy area to play. Does this work?

Here's my herb garden plan: I'll put it in the lowest corner of the yard, where water pools for days after rain. Rosemary, lavender, and thyme go there, since they're Mediterranean. I'll water them every day to be safe. Please share your opinion!

Rainbow garden! Stripes of red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple, pink, and white, each stripe a different single plant, one of each species, 40 species in total, no repeats. It'll be so colorful and unique. What are your thoughts?

Hi! I live in Minnesota, zone 4. My outdoor plan is a tropical paradise: hibiscus, banana trees, and mango trees, planted in the ground in October and left outside all winter. I'll add a small bench. What do you think?

I'm 8! My garden has a flower, and another flower, and a unicorn statue, and a candy tree, and a lollipop bush, and a chocolate river, and a swing. The candy plants grow in one day. My mom said to ask you what you think!

Client proposal for a 20x20 yard: cover the entire area in gravel and put a single potted fern in the center, with the description "lush tropical oasis, low maintenance." I think the clean look is a good fit. Could you give me feedback before I send it?

My garden plan: compost bin directly under the bedroom window, the dining patio right beside it, and the vegetable bed 50 feet away at the end of the yard. The compost will be uncovered so it breaks down faster. How's that sound?

I'm 74 and use a walker. My vegetable plan: in-ground beds on the steep hillside behind the house, reached by 30 uneven stone steps, with a 1-foot-wide path between each bed. The watering can will be stored at the bottom. Any thoughts?

Pollinator garden plan: double-petaled hybrid roses, pansies, and petunias in neat rows, about 100 plants all the same few colors. I'll spray insecticide weekly to keep the bugs off the flowers so the bees can enjoy them. What do you think?

Hi! Here's the plan for my 10x10 ft plot for my intro horticulture class. North side: tomatoes, peppers, eggplant. South side: 6-ft sunflowers and corn. Middle: lettuce. East: mint, oregano and basil in one bed. West: three pumpkin vines. No paths, I'll just step between plants. What do you think? I have to hand it in Friday.

I'm opening a small café and designed the patio garden myself. Front wall: a row of lavender, a row of roses, a row of tulips, a row of daffodils, a row of marigolds. Middle: a 3-inch-deep pond with two koi. Tables go wherever space is left over. Could you give me your thoughts before I order plants?

Hey, I live in Phoenix (full sun, 110°F summers) and sketched my backyard. Left bed: saguaro, prickly pear, agave. Right bed, right beside it: Boston ferns, hostas, impatiens. I'll water everything daily, same amount, so it's simple. Curious what you think!

My garden plan: The garden will have flowers. Flowers will be in the front and also flowers in the back. In the middle there will be more flowers and some plants. There will be a path so you can walk on the path. I'm a bit nervous to share it. Any feedback?

Here's my plan for our 15x20 ft townhouse yard. Four oak trees, one in each corner. A weeping willow 3 ft from the foundation. A vegetable bed right under the oaks. Bamboo along the fence to fill gaps. Hammock in the center. Would love your opinion!

First raised bed ever!! It's 2x2 feet and I'm planting: 4 zucchini, 6 tomatoes, 3 watermelon, 10 carrots, 12 lettuce and 5 pumpkins. I want a big harvest for my family. What's your take on the layout?

I run a little roadside flower stand and planned the field rows. Row 1 (front): sunflowers, 8 ft tall. Row 2: pansies, 6 inches. Row 3: zinnias. Row 4: more sunflowers. Customers walk in from the front. Please let me know what you think of the arrangement.

For my landscape class I designed a Zen garden: raked gravel in a spiral, two garden gnomes, a plastic flamingo, a neon-painted rock, a bright red tulip bed, and a light-up plastic fountain. Does the layout work? Be honest, but I worked really hard on it.
Planning my herb bed, 3x3 ft: mint, lemon balm, horseradish, and bamboo, all together so it looks full fast. I'll just let them go all summer. Can you look over my plan and tell me what you think?

Our spot under the deck gets zero direct light, but I'm planning sunflowers, tomatoes, roses and lavender there, packed tight in two rows. I'll add a grow light if needed, maybe. Here's the layout idea, thoughts?

I'm making a garden for my grandma, who uses a wheelchair. Raised beds are 4 ft tall and 5 ft wide. Gravel paths are 14 inches wide, and there are three steps at the entrance. Wanted it to feel cozy! What do you think of this layout?
My pollinator garden: eight double-bloom petunias in a perfect square, all the same color, plus a plastic bee statue in the center. They'll all bloom in July. Posting here to hear what you think!

Here's my vegetable garden plan: one acre of mixed vegetables at the far back of the property, 300 ft from the tap. I'll carry buckets to water. I can only work on it one weekend a month. Hoping to sell produce by summer. What do you think?

Rose garden plan for my side yard, which faces north and sits shaded by the fence all day: 24 rose bushes, spaced 6 inches apart in three rows, no walkway so I can save space. I'm a little nervous about showing this. Thoughts?

I'm planning a backyard orchard in northern Minnesota (zone 3): two banana trees, a lemon tree, an orange tree, and a fig, all planted outside in October. Layout is a neat 2x3 grid. Does that look right to you?

Here's my yard plan in feet. Plot: 10x10. Bed A: 6x6. Bed B: 6x6. Path between them: 3 wide. Bed A holds beans, Bed B holds squash, and the rest is lawn. I think I've covered everything. Can you tell me what you think?

Tomato bed plan: I'm putting 8 tomato plants and 4 peppers directly under the big black walnut tree in my yard because the spot is already cleared. Soil is rich from the leaves. Drawing attached in words below: two rows, east to west. Thoughts?

I own a small daycare and designed a kids' garden. Plants: foxglove, oleander, castor bean, lily of the valley, and angel's trumpet in a ring around the sandbox, with a low 1-ft fence. Kids can touch everything. What do you think of the layout?

My garden is a symphony of colors where nature's tapestry unfolds in a dance of beauty. Flowers here, veggies there, a bench somewhere. Every corner whispers peace and tranquility. No measurements yet, but that's the vibe. Can you share your thoughts?

I have a big dog who runs the fence line, so I made this plan: sago palms and azaleas along the fence, lily of the valley around the dog door, and a mulch path of cocoa bean shells where he likes to dig. Does the layout seem okay to you?

Planning my balcony garden (4x6 ft, fourth floor): a 400-lb stone fountain, six full-size apple trees in clay pots, a hammock, and a raised bed of corn. Everything's placed on the left edge to leave room for chairs. Would love your feedback!

Garden plan for school project: 30 tomato plants in one straight line from the house to the fence, then 30 more in the next line, then 30 more. I'll replant tomatoes in the same spot every year because they like it. Any feedback?

Here's my backyard layout. The compost pile sits right next to the patio dining table, under the kitchen window. Tomatoes go in the shade of the shed on the north side. Flowers are along the road. A trampoline sits over the herb bed. What do you think?

Hi! I've retired from teaching and finally have time to plan our 4m x 12m back garden (Yorkshire, heavy clay, south-facing). Plan: a curved gravel path shifting sides halfway so you can't see the end; near the house, a thyme and chamomile terrace; mid-garden, a bed of Geranium 'Rozanne', Calamagrostis 'Karl Foerster' and Sedum for late structure; at the far end, a single multistem Amelanchier over a bench. Could you tell me what you think?

I'm a line cook with a 3m x 5m Brooklyn rooftop, and wind is brutal. My layout: a 1.2m cedar windbreak slat wall on the west side; behind it, 60cm-deep troughs of rosemary, sage and thyme; along the east parapet, self-watering tubs for shiso, Thai basil and chilies; one central table with a tomato 'Sungold' cage at each corner. Everything within three steps of the door so I can grab it mid-service. Honest opinions welcome!

For my landscape architecture course I designed a rain garden for a 6x8m front yard that floods at the downspout. Roof water enters via a stone swale, slows through a 25cm-deep basin planted with Iris versicolor, Joe Pye weed and switchgrass, then overflows into a higher mesic zone with asters and little bluestem. A stepping-stone path crosses on the dry berm. I'm a bit nervous about presenting it. Any feedback?

I'm 74 and gardening from a wheelchair now, so I redesigned my plot. Paths are 1.2m wide, compacted fine gravel, with a turning circle at each junction. Raised beds are 70cm high with a 30cm timber ledge to lean on, and only 80cm wide so I can reach the middle. Strawberries and herbs go at the front edge, with tall beans trained on arches at the back. A shaded seat sits beside the water butt. What do you reckon?

I'm 16 and I made a plan for our tiny 1.5m x 3m balcony to help pollinators. West-facing, so hot. Back rail: lavender in long troughs. Middle tier: a 3-step shelf with creeping thyme, borage and calendula. Floor: a shallow saucer of pebbles and water for bees. Hanging baskets along the front with nasturtiums, trailing down so there's something flowering from April to October. Do you have any thoughts?

I'm a night-shift nurse in Phoenix, and I designed a garden I can enjoy at dusk with no lawn. The layout: a decomposed granite courtyard, a central ring of boulders around a palo verde for shade, agave and red yucca on the south edge, and a night-blooming cereus and white evening primrose along the patio. A drip line runs on one timer, three zones. Total water use is under 15% of our old lawn. What's your take?

Our London courtyard is 3m x 5m, north-facing, with walls on every side. I'm planning a woodland feel. The back wall gets climbing hydrangea; beneath it, ferns (Polystichum, Dryopteris), hellebores and Epimedium. A single paved diagonal leads to a small bench, with Japanese forest grass spilling over the edge, and white foxgloves to rise through in June. Pale wall paint to bounce light. I'm a web designer, not a gardener, so I'd welcome your opinion.

I run a ten-rod allotment plot and have worked out a four-year rotation. It's divided into four 5x6m blocks: legumes, brassicas, roots, then alliums with potatoes. Between the blocks run 45cm paths that line up with a central compost bay of three bins. Perennials (rhubarb, asparagus, artichokes) sit along the north edge so they never shade anything. Flowers for the bees run along the paths' edges. How does it look to you?

I teach year 3 and designed a school garden for 28 kids. Eight 1m x 1m beds in a ring around a central 'story circle' of log stools, so every child can reach a bed and still hear me. Each bed is named for a theme: Pizza, Salsa, Rainbow, Tea, Bug Hotel and so on. A low willow tunnel connects the entrance. Paths are wide enough for a wheelchair. Does this seem workable?

I'm an occupational therapist, and this is my layout for a sensory garden in a dementia care home. A looped path, 1.5m wide, with no dead ends, so no one gets stuck. Along it, five stations: scent (lavender, rosemary), touch (lamb's ear, grasses), sound (bamboo, wind chimes), taste (raspberries, mint) and a familiar-memory corner with a washing line and a shed. Handrails run along the edges, and the seating is every 12m. Would you give me your thoughts?

I'm a software engineer and I've planned a 5m x 7m garden inspired by Japanese design, but adapted to Ohio. The idea: three clustered stones in an area of raked gravel, shaped like a dry stream. It's crossed by a flat stone bridge. A Japanese maple stands in the corner, and I've placed moss under a shaded eave. I'm keeping the plant list to nine species, and nothing is symmetrical. Here's the plan. What do you think?

I've been gardening for fifty years, and this is my cottage border plan for a 2m-deep strip along a 15m fence. I planned it by bloom calendar: March, hellebores and snowdrops at the front; May, peonies and alliums; July, delphiniums behind phlox and Echinacea; September, Japanese anemones and asters. Every clump is sized so gaps from fading plants are covered by the neighbor. Tall things at the back, but dotted forward, in threes. Care to comment?

We have a quarter acre in Oregon, and I'm designing a food forest. Canopy: four semi-dwarf apples and two pears on the north side. Understory: hazelnuts and serviceberries. Shrub layer: currants and gooseberries. Ground layer: strawberries, comfrey and chives. Vertical: hardy kiwi on the south fence. Paths follow the contour so the water slows, and a swale catches the winter rains. It's my first design, and I'm nervous about showing it.

I live on a steep slope in Cape Town, and this is my plan for terraced fynbos. Four dry-stone terraces, each 1.5m wide, with the steps offset so water never funnels down. Top terrace: proteas and leucadendrons. Middle: restios and pelargoniums. Bottom: Agapanthus and buchu near the path. No irrigation after the first summer. I'd really love your feedback on the plan!

I work nights, so I designed a moon garden for 4m x 6m. A circular lawn of pale gravel reflects light. White-flowering plants, including Nicotiana sylvestris, Moonflower, Jasmine, and silver foliage from artemisia and lamb's ear, all planted on the west edge to catch the last light. Along the path, solar-free low lanterns sit at ankle height. It's meant to be best at 10pm. Do you have any thoughts?

I'm a vet tech with two huskies, and I planned a garden that works with them rather than against them. A 1m wide dog run follows the fence perimeter in shredded cedar, so they patrol there and leave the beds alone. The beds are raised 40cm with sturdy shrubs: rosemary, lavender, and ornamental grasses. No toxic plants at all, including sago palms and oleander. A shallow digging pit with sand sits in the corner. Any thoughts?

I'm replacing my front lawn in Austin, and our HOA wants to see a neat design. Plan: a symmetrical frame of clipped germander hedge, in a rectangle 8m x 5m, with Texas sage, salvia greggii and blackfoot daisy inside. A single limestone path leads from the street. Flagstone border; no mulch visible. The neat edges are meant to make a native planting look 'intentional'. How would you rate this?

I'm a beekeeper with six hives, and I planned a 10m x 10m forage garden to support them from March to October. Early: crocus, willow, and hellebores. Spring: lungwort, borage, and fruit blossoms. Summer: lime tree, phacelia, and marjoram. Autumn: ivy, Sedum, and asters. Hives are in the southeast corner, facing away from the path, with a 2m hedge forcing bees to fly up. What do you think of it?

I live in a tiny house on a 2m x 3m patch of ground. I planned a vertical garden to make the most of it. Three cattle panel arches create a tunnel, trained with beans, cucumbers, and malabar spinach. Below, a 40cm bed holds lettuce in the shade. The south wall carries espaliered fig and pots on hooks. A seat built into the base of the arch. I'd love to hear your opinion!

I'm a textile artist, and I designed a dye garden of eight 1.2m circular beds, each one for a colour. Madder for reds, woad and Japanese indigo for blues, weld for yellow, coreopsis for orange, hopi black sunflower for grey-purple, dyer's chamomile, and marigold. Beds are arranged in a colour wheel, with a central bench and a mixed bed of dye plants in the middle. I'd like to hear your honest opinion.

I'm an architect, and this is my plan for a small formal parterre in a 9m x 9m space. A square is divided into nine cells with a 3x3 grid: the outside eight hold low box balls and clipped hornbeam, while the central cell is a still water mirror. The paths are 60cm wide gravel, with an axis aligned to the kitchen door. Plant color is limited to white and green. The only variation is a cell of tulips in April. Thoughts?

I'm a farmer, and I set aside 1 acre on the edge of my property for a wildlife pond and meadow. A 20m x 10m pond with a shallow shelf on the south side, and a deep area of 2.5m on the north. A wildflower meadow, mown only in September, surrounds it, with a hedgerow of hawthorn, blackthorn, and dog rose on the windward side. A log pile and a stone hibernaculum for amphibians sits at the east end. Do you have any feedback?

I'm a wedding florist and I just designed a cut-flower plot of 8m x 12m. Ten 1m beds, 30cm paths, planted in succession: ranunculus and sweet peas early; dahlias, zinnias, and cosmos for summer; and in the autumn, chrysanthemums. Each bed has a harvest window noted so I never run short for June weddings. Foliage, such as eucalyptus and ninebark, along the northern fence. Netting frames are collapsible. Would you share your opinion?

I'm a herbalist who wants to build a 6m x 6m tea and medicine garden. It's a mandala, with four quadrants divided by paths: calming (chamomile, lemon balm, lavender), digestive (peppermint, fennel, calendula), immune (echinacea, elderberry, thyme), and a quadrant for rotating annuals. In the center, a small sundial surrounded by holy basil. Drying racks are on the shed's south wall. What do you make of it?

I'm a retired fisherman living on the Scottish coast, and I've planned a garden for a very windy 15m x 10m plot. The first line of defence is a 3m shelterbelt of sea buckthorn and escallonia on the west. Behind it, a stone-walled kitchen garden with raised beds at 50cm for kale, leeks, and potatoes. The walls are curved so the wind doesn't eddy. A bench faces the sea, nestled in a hollow. Any thoughts?

Hi! For my landscape studio course I designed a 12x20 ft Tucson courtyard. One desert willow in the northwest corner shades the hot afternoon wall. A dry-wash path of granite fines curves through brittlebush, Parry's penstemon and a single blue agave. A rain chain empties into a sunken basin planted with sedges. Seating sits on the east side for cool mornings. No turf. I present Thursday, so what's your take?

I run a small café and I'm redoing our 4x6 m back patio as a working garden. Layout: espaliered fig and rosemary on the south wall; two cedar raised beds at counter height (60 cm) with basil, shiso and chives, so staff can snip from the pass; thyme between the pavers; lemon verbena by the seating so guests brush it walking past. Honest thoughts welcome.

Here's my hellstrip plan, 8x25 ft, Ontario zone 5, casual and just for fun. Three height bands. Front: prairie dropseed at 18 in spacing, so it reads tidy to neighbours. Middle: golden alexanders, then pale purple coneflower, then anise hyssop for a May to September bloom run. Back: New England aster and little bluestem for October colour. Seedheads stay up until March for the finches. What would you change, if anything?

For my FFA project I mapped a 24x16 ft school garden that wheelchair users can reach. Beds are 30 in tall with 36 in clear paths and a 5 ft turning circle at the centre. The corn-bean-squash trio goes in the long bed, with nasturtiums trailing over the edge. A rain barrel with a lever spigot sits at seated height. I'm a little nervous about sharing it. Does the flow make sense?

I'm nervous about this one. It's my first design: a 10x10 ft moss garden under a Japanese maple in Portland. A single weathered basalt boulder sits off-centre, with raked gravel flowing around it like a stream. Hair cap moss goes on the shaded side and cushion moss on the sunlit side. A slate stepping path bends once so you can't see the whole garden at a glance. Would you tell me what you think?

I'm a cut-flower farmer on a quarter acre. Beds run north-south, 30 in wide with 18 in paths, 100 ft long, so every stem gets even light. Block 1 is early tulips and ranunculus, followed by zinnias in the same bed. Dahlias get their own block with a 4 ft path for harvest carts. A cooler sits at the low end so buckets only travel downhill. I'd like your opinion before I order drip tape.

My small city yard is 15x30 ft, so I made a four-bed rotation plan: Bed A brassicas, Bed B legumes and peas, Bed C tomatoes, peppers and basil, Bed D roots and alliums. Each moves one bed clockwise every year, and compost goes on whichever bed is next to host the tomatoes. Cover crop of crimson clover fills any gap in winter. A 2 ft path loop keeps everything within arm's reach. Opinions?

Studying permaculture and my final assignment is a guild plan. At the centre is a semi-dwarf apple. Around it: comfrey at the drip line as a mulch source, chives and garlic to deter pests, daffodils as a grass barrier, nasturtium as a trap crop and borage for pollinators. Clover covers the ground between. The guild is 12 ft across, with a 3 ft access gap on the north side for pruning. Does this hang together, in your view?

Hi all, here's my balcony plan: 2x1 m, east-facing, 7th floor in Mumbai, so it's windy. Along the rail go sturdy pots of curry leaf and lemongrass as a windbreak. Cherry tomatoes climb a tensioned wire trellis against the wall. Hanging shelf units hold mint, coriander and Malabar spinach in graduated sizes. A drip line runs from a single 20 L reservoir on a timer. Any feedback? I'd love to hear it.

We run a six-room B&B and I've planned an evening garden outside the guest rooms. Pale flowers show up at dusk: white nicotiana, evening primrose and moonflower on an arch. Scent is layered by distance: night phlox at the path edge, jasmine at the doorway. Low solar lights sit below knee height so the stars stay visible. A gravel crunch path is the only route so guests are heard arriving. What do you think?

My clay yard floods by the downspout, so I've drawn a rain garden. It's 6x14 ft and shaped like a kidney, 8 in deep, with a stone overflow notch toward the street. The wettest zone holds blue flag iris and swamp milkweed. The middle has Joe Pye weed and cardinal flower. The rim has switchgrass and little bluestem for dry spells. A 4 in wood-chip mulch layer keeps weeds down. Would this actually work?

I'm a design student working on a sensory garden for a dementia care home. The path is a continuous loop, so no dead ends cause confusion. Every 10 m is a bench in a pool of shade, with a different scent: lavender, then mint, then rose. Raised beds of lamb's ear and grasses invite touching. All plants are non-toxic, and there's a bird feeder visible from the lounge window. I'd really value your opinion.

Here's my dye garden, 12x12 ft, arranged like a colour wheel. The centre bed holds Japanese indigo. Around it: madder (red) on the west side, weld (yellow) in the south, and woad (blue) in the east. Marigold and coreopsis fill in the oranges between. Madder is in a sunken bed with edging because it spreads, and it needs three years before harvest. I stagger the rows so I get dye every autumn. Thoughts?

I own a small brewery and want a beer garden that supports what we brew. Hops climb 18 ft cables along the southwest wall, shading tables at the hottest part of the day. Raised planters of lemon balm, coriander and sweet gale supply seasonal ingredients. Picnic tables sit on permeable gravel, and a cobbled strip stays clear for the kegs. Chalk labels on each plant let people taste the connection. Any feedback?

My side yard is a 6x30 ft wind tunnel on the Scottish coast. So the plan is a staggered hornbeam hedge at the windward end, a mix of sea buckthorn and escallonia behind it for salt spray, and then the actual garden: a gravel path zigzagging between hardy geraniums, sea kale, and thrift, with a bench tucked in the lee. Even in a gale you could drink tea there. What do you think?

For my coastal ecology class I planned a salt-tolerant dune garden for a Nova Scotia cottage. Beach pea and American beachgrass go at the front to hold sand. Bayberry and beach plum make a mid-height shrub layer. Rugosa roses at the rear give hips for birds. A boardwalk of cedar slats on posts protects the roots and bridges the dune. No fertilizer, no irrigation. I'd appreciate your thoughts before I hand it in.

My north-facing Seattle yard gets almost no direct sun, so I designed it for texture rather than flowers. Layers: Japanese forest grass and ostrich ferns in drifts, hellebores for winter bloom, epimedium under the ferns, and variegated Solomon's seal to catch light. A single silver birch at the back lifts the canopy. Paths are mossy flagstones. The 2x3 m footprint is tiny, but I tried to make it look bigger. Thoughts?

I keep bees, and I sell honey at the farmers' market, so I mapped a forage plan for my 1-acre lot. A six-foot hedge of serviceberry and pussy willow sits in front of the hives to force a high flight path. Bloom runs in order: willow in March, crocus, then lilac, then basswood, then borage and buckwheat in July. Asters and goldenrod go in for autumn. A shallow water dish with pebbles sits 10 ft from the hives. Does it look sensible?

I'm a student in California and my final project is a fire-wise native garden. Zone 0 (first 5 ft from the house): gravel and a few flagstones. Zone 1 (5-30 ft): irrigated islands of manzanita, salvia and yarrow, with 10 ft spacing and no ladder fuels. Zone 2: a meadow of deer grass mowed to 4 in in June. Boulders act as breaks. A single coast live oak stays, with the area under it cleared of litter. Any feedback would be welcome.

Hello! This is my winter-interest border for Minnesota, 10x30 ft along the garage. Red twig dogwood at the back for stem colour against the snow. Mid layer: switchgrass 'Northwind' and sedum 'Matrona', both left standing. A paper birch cluster at the east end with white bark glowing at sunrise. Hellebores are tucked in near the door, so there's something to see on the shortest days. I'd like to know what you think!

I took on a half plot at my allotment (5 rods) and this is my plan. A 3 ft path divides the plot lengthwise, with a compost bay and shed at the north end so the shade doesn't hit crops. Six 4x8 beds are laid out so I can reach the middle from the sides. Water butts catch run-off from the shed roof. Sweet peas go along the shed wall, and a rhubarb crown sits by the compost bay. How does it look to you?

I'm a market gardener on half an acre. The layout follows the workflow: harvest from the beds, then down a gravel lane to the wash station under the walnut tree, then the cooler and the pickup window. Two 20x48 ft high tunnels sit on the north edge so they won't shade anything. Field beds are 30 in wide with 12 in paths and run along the contour for drainage. I'd value an outside opinion on the flow.

For my biology project I designed a wildlife pond and bog garden for our school field. The pond is 3x4 m with a shallow sloping side so frogs and hedgehogs can climb out, and a deep end of 80 cm for winter. Bog plants at the shallow end: marsh marigold, ragged robin, and water mint. A log pile and loose stones on the north bank give hibernation space. No fish, so the tadpoles survive. Would you tell me what you think?

I work nights, so my garden is for moonlight. It's a 15x15 ft square: white-flowered plants like Nicotiana sylvestris, white foxglove, and 'Iceberg' roses, with silver foliage of lamb's ear and artemisia to reflect light. A pale gravel circle in the middle holds a single bench. Night-scented stock and jasmine run along the fence. There's no lighting except candles in a lantern. What do you think of the plan?

Here's my tsubo-niwa idea for a 2x2 m light well in our Kyoto machiya. One stone lantern on the north side. Moss in the shade, a dwarf maple in the corner to cast a shadow on the wall in the afternoon. A single line of river stones from the engawa to the lantern gives a 'stream' that is dry. A tsukubai basin with a bamboo spout stands on the west side. Please share your thoughts.

Hi! I'm a high school junior and I wrote my first logline for a film class. Here it is: "A young orphan discovers he is the Chosen One and must defeat the Dark Lord to save the world before it's too late." What do you think?

Here's the logline for my thriller screenplay: "A detective with a dark past, who is haunted by his dark past, hunts a serial killer who kills people in a series of murders." I'm planning to enter it in a contest. Any thoughts?
Hey, accountant here, first time trying screenwriting. My logline: "Two people who hate each other are forced to work together and, against all odds, fall in love." Be honest, how's it sound to you?

I'm 62 and just retired, and writing movies is my new hobby! My logline: "A lonely lighthouse keeper named Jack finds a message in a bottle, travels to Paris, meets a baker named Claire, learns to trust again, fights a corrupt mayor, and discovers his father was a pirate." Thoughts?

Logline for my sci-fi film, nervously sharing it: "In the year 3000, robots become sentient and, in a twist, humans must decide whether robots are people or machines, and it's a story about what it means to be human." Would love your feedback.

Just finished the pitch for my action movie, "Explosion Force." Logline: "Big things blow up while Mike Strong, an ex-soldier cop, runs, shoots, and punches to stop bad guys with a bomb." Can you tell me what you think?
I'm a film student and this is my thesis logline: "A girl feels sad. Over ninety minutes, she feels sadder, and then the film ends." I'd love your opinion before I submit it to my professor.

Hi, I'm a dentist who writes horror on weekends. Logline: "A family moves into a house that is haunted by a ghost who was murdered there long ago, and they must escape before the ghost gets them. The ghost is Gary." Thoughts?

Writing a historical drama set in ancient Rome in 1850 BC. Logline: "Emperor Julius Caesar must lead his legions across the Atlantic to conquer America before Cleopatra's brother can steal his throne." What's your take?

Here's my rom-com logline: "Emma, a workaholic big-city career woman, returns to her small hometown for Christmas, where she meets Jake, a rugged local carpenter, and rediscovers the true meaning of the holidays." Could you give me your thoughts? Thanks so much!

Hello, I'm a software engineer trying out screenwriting. My logline: "A hacker types really fast on a computer and hacks the entire internet in 10 seconds to stop a virus that turns all computers evil." What do you think?

So I'm 24, work in retail, and have a movie idea I'm kind of nervous to show anyone. Logline: "A man wakes up and it was all a dream, but then the dream was real, but then it was a dream again." What do you think?

Here's the logline for my animated kids' movie: "A talking dog, a talking cat, and a talking hamster go on a road trip to find their owner, learning that friendship is the real treasure along the way." Any feedback?

I wrote this logline for my war movie and I'm hoping to send it to a producer cousin: "During World War II, a soldier fights in a war, and the war is very hard on everyone, including him, his friends, and also the enemy soldiers." Thoughts?

Retired teacher here, writing a mystery. Logline: "When the butler is found dead in the library, a quirky amateur sleuth with a cat must solve the case, and the killer turns out to be the butler's secret twin." What do you think?

Hey! Logline for my superhero movie: "After being bitten by a radioactive spider, a shy teenager gains amazing powers and must learn that with great power comes great responsibility." Pitching it next week. What's your opinion?

I'm a stay-at-home dad and I wrote my first logline during nap time: "A cowboy rides into town, but the town doesn't want him there, so he has to decide whether to stay or ride out of town, and also there's a sheriff." Thoughts?

My logline, for a courtroom drama: "A brilliant young lawyer, who has never lost a case, takes on the one case he cannot win, and in the end, with a surprise twist that I won't spoil, which is that the defendant did it, justice prevails." Feedback welcome!

Here's the logline for my disaster movie, a little nervous: "When a tsunami, an earthquake, a volcano, a meteor, and a zombie outbreak hit New York on the same day, one scientist named Dr. Dave must save everyone using only a paperclip." What do you think?

I'm a 45-year-old nurse and this is my first-ever logline: "A woman discovers her husband has been lying to her about something big, and now she has to figure out what, and why, and what it means for their marriage and for her." Would you give me your opinion?

Logline for my fantasy epic: "In the magical land of Eldoria, where elves, dwarves, and wizards live in uneasy peace, a farm boy named Aric finds a mysterious sword and must journey to the Mountain of Doom with a wise old wizard to destroy an evil ring." Thoughts?

Writing a medical drama and I'm a med student, so it's accurate! Logline: "A surgeon performs a heart transplant by removing the patient's brain and putting it in a new body, and then has to deal with the hospital board." What do you think?

Hi, I'm a YouTuber moving into film. Logline: "Based on a true story, though I changed everything: a famous influencer gets stranded on an island with no wifi and has to learn to survive, and learn about herself, and also maybe find wifi." Thoughts?

My logline for a sports movie: "A struggling underdog team with a tough-but-fair coach overcomes impossible odds to win the big championship game in the final seconds." I'm hoping to turn it into a full script this summer. What do you think?

Hello from a 19-year-old college freshman! Logline for my movie: "Alex Johnson, a 28-year-old man, who is 28 years old, goes on a quest. Then something happens. It changes everything. Nothing will ever be the same." Any thoughts?

Hi! I'm a film student and this is the logline for my short thesis film: "A brooding detective with a dark past must solve one last case before he retires, but the case gets personal." Could you tell me what you think? My professor wants us to pitch next week.

Here's my logline for a movie I've been outlining on weekends: "In a world where everything is falling apart, one chosen hero must rise up and save the world from the evil darkness that threatens everyone." Any thoughts? Totally open to feedback!

I own a small bakery and I'm writing a screenplay on the side. Logline: "A baker who loves baking bread discovers a secret recipe for bread that changes his life forever, and now he must bake the bread before time runs out." What's your opinion?

Nervous to share this, but here goes. My logline: "After a teenage girl moves to a new town and is the new girl, she meets a mysterious boy who is secretly a vampire, and she must choose between him and her normal life." Does this work as a logline?

Hey, high school junior here, entering a screenwriting contest. My logline is: "When a meteor the size of Jupiter is going to hit Earth in two days, a team of ordinary plumbers must fly to space and blow it up with a single wrench." Would love your feedback!

I'm a retired hobbyist filmmaker and I just wrote this: "Set in 1850s Ancient Rome, a gladiator named Chad uses his smartphone to rally the Colosseum crowd and overthrow Napoleon." Be honest, what do you make of it?

Proud of this one! Logline for my feature script: "Sarah, a sad woman, is sad after her husband dies, and over the course of the movie she goes through grief, sadness, and then slowly becomes happy again. Then she dies at the end." Thoughts?

I run a small landscaping company and I've always wanted to make a movie. Here's my logline: "A landscaper and a rich widow fall in love over a garden, but her family disapproves, and he's secretly a prince, and also there's a murder, and a talking dog helps." What do you think?

Casual question: I wrote this logline for a sci-fi short for my YouTube channel. "Two astronauts on Mars find out that the other astronaut is actually a robot, but it turns out the first astronaut is also a robot, and so is Mars." Can you give me your take?

I'm a college sophomore taking intro to screenwriting. My logline: "A hacker who can hack anything hacks into the government's computers and hacks the truth, and they try to hack him back." I'm hoping to submit it Friday. How does it read to you?

Here's the logline for my horror movie: "Five teenagers go to a cabin in the woods for the weekend, where a masked killer picks them off one by one, and only the final girl survives." I'm planning to shoot it with my friends this summer. What do you think?

I'm a nurse who writes scripts as a hobby. Logline: "Dr. Hartman, a brilliant surgeon, performs a heart transplant in 5 minutes with no assistants, then goes home, and then the hospital is sued, but he wins by being the best doctor ever." Does this sound good to you? Please share your opinion.

Hi, I own a tiny pet grooming shop and wrote a kids' movie idea. "A poodle named Fluffy wants to be a famous dog, so she goes on a journey to become famous, and learns that being herself is the most important thing of all." Any feedback?

My friends said I should share this one. Logline: "A man wakes up with amnesia and slowly discovers he was a secret assassin all along, and the people hunting him are the very agency that trained him." I'm wondering what you'd say about it!

Student here, final project due soon. My logline: "In 2090, a robot learns to feel emotions and wonders what it means to be human, as humans wonder whether robots can be human, in a future where robots and humans are close." How's it come across?

I do wedding videography and want to try narrative film. Logline: "On the day of her wedding, a bride finds out her fiancé is cheating, but then they get married anyway and everything is fine. The end." Curious what you think of it!

Posting my first-ever logline, so be gentle haha: "Jake is a guy who plays football and is also good at math and has a girlfriend but his best friend is jealous, and Jake's dad wants him to go to college but Jake wants something else." Thoughts?

I'm a history buff making an amateur movie. Logline: "During the American Revolution of 1920, George Washington and Abraham Lincoln team up to fight the British Navy using steam-powered tanks." I'd love to know your thoughts before I start casting.

Hello! I'm a small-business owner (coffee roaster) writing a rom-com. Logline: "A barista and a customer who both love coffee fall in love over coffee, and discover that love is like coffee: sometimes bitter, sometimes sweet." What's your take?

I wrote a logline for my sports drama and my teammates are waiting to hear. "An underdog team of misfit kids with a tough but caring coach overcomes all odds to win the big championship game against their arch rivals." How would you react to it?

Here's my logline for an animated short I'm making for class: "A cloud is sad because it is a cloud, so it rains, and then the rain makes a flower, and the flower is happy, and the cloud is sad again, and it rains more, and so on." What do you think?

I'm a part-time barber and hobby screenwriter. Logline: "When a mob boss's son gets a haircut that goes wrong, the barber must flee the city, find himself, fight the mob, rescue his sister, save his shop, and learn to forgive his father." Can you give me feedback?

Quick one for you. My logline: "A time traveler goes back in time to the past to change history, but when he changes the past it changes the future, so he has to go back again to fix it, which he does by going back in time." Opinions welcome!

I'm a grad student in biology and wrote a thriller. Logline: "A scientist discovers that a deadly virus can be cured by simply boiling water, and must warn the world before the evil corporation, which is evil, silences her." Would appreciate your thoughts!

Hi! For my podcast's fiction side project, I wrote a movie logline: "Three best friends take a road trip across the country to find themselves, and along the way they learn about life, love, and each other, and nothing will ever be the same." What do you think of it?

I'm a 34-year-old home inspector, and I've been writing a horror screenplay on the side. Here's the logline: "A home inspector notices that every house in a new subdivision has one more room on the inside than on the outside, and the extra rooms are starting to be occupied." Be honest, what's your take?

Hi! I'm 16 and this is the first logline I've written for a film project in my media class: "When her father, a small-town marching band director, slowly loses his hearing, a teenage drum major secretly conducts the band from the field while he believes he's still leading it." Could you tell me what you think?

Retired court stenographer here, age 71. I've started on a screenplay, and this is my logline: "A 911 dispatcher takes a call from a woman who only whispers about her cat, and has eleven minutes to decode what the cat means before her abuser returns." I'd love an outside opinion, if you don't mind.

Okay, nervous about sharing this. I'm a line cook with zero film training. My logline: "A Greek-American wedding DJ discovers the bride's and groom's fathers are former mob rivals, and has until the garter toss to defuse a forty-year blood feud using nothing but a playlist." Thoughts? Feel free to be blunt.

Here's a logline from my thesis film at NYU, I'm 24 and about to pitch it: "In 1923 Newfoundland, a lighthouse keeper's deaf daughter must guide a lost rum-running ship to shore using only the lamp's beam, though the men aboard are the ones who drowned her father." How does it read to you?

I'm a crossword constructor, not a screenwriter, but I tried my hand. Logline: "A crossword constructor realizes that his Sunday puzzles are carrying messages from his wife, who vanished a year ago, and the editor who keeps accepting them is the last person who saw her." What's your reaction?

Hey, I'm a 45-year-old pediatric nurse, and I wrote this for a short film contest: "When a ten-year-old's imaginary friend begins aging faster than she does, she has one childhood left to keep him alive." Does it work as a logline? Any feedback welcome.

I teach high school chemistry and write screenplays on weekends. Newest logline: "In a kingdom where lying is physically impossible, the court poet is the only person permitted to say untrue things, and the king orders her to write a eulogy for a war that was lost." What would you say about it?

So I'm a 58-year-old retired rugby referee from Cardiff, and I've turned my life into a story. Logline: "A Welsh rugby referee going blind must officiate the final match of his career using only memory and the sound of boots on grass." Would you tell me what you make of it?

Hi, I'm a UN interpreter in my 40s and have always wanted to write a film. Here's my logline: "A summit interpreter mistranslates a single word to avoid an incident, then watches her small lie become the foundation of a peace treaty that one true sentence could destroy." Curious what you think!

Just a casual share from a night-shift security guard who writes screenplays on his breaks: "Three octogenarian sisters plan to steal their late father's violin back from the museum that bought it from a forger, but the only one who can authenticate it is the sister who hasn't spoken to them in thirty years." Opinions?

I'm 29, a pawnshop clerk and aspiring writer. I'd really like a fresh pair of eyes on this: "In a city where memories can be sold, a pawnbroker who specializes in buying grief discovers that a customer's sold memory is of the pawnbroker's own wedding." What do you think of it as a logline?

My grandson says I should share this with someone. I'm 77 and worked as a railway signalman. Logline: "In 1887 Montana, a Chinese laundryman is the only witness to a lynching and the one man the law won't let testify, so he decides to bring the court to his laundry." What are your thoughts?

Proud to finally share this. I'm a Mumbai-based sound editor, 52, and it's the first story I've written myself: "In 1950s Bombay, the unseen playback singer behind a film star's voice must decide whether to expose her when the star's husband falls in love with the voice and not the woman." How does it strike you?

I run a small funeral home and wrote this dark comedy logline between appointments: "A professional mourner hired to fill empty seats at a stranger's funeral realizes she is the only person present who knows the deceased was murdered." Would love to hear what you think of it.

Hi! Animation student, 20, pitching to my class on Friday. My logline: "A nearsighted lighthouse moth must persuade a fleet of fishing boats to follow her instead of the light, because the light has gone out." Could you give me your honest reaction?

I've been a newspaper copy editor for thirty years and I'm trying screenwriting. Logline: "Two obituary writers at a dying small-town paper, long at war over each other's prose, each begin secretly writing the other's obituary, the most honest work either has done in years." What do you make of it?
