Here's my logline. I'm a long-haul trucker, 50, and I write in the cab at rest stops: "With six hours to his deadline, a trucker picks up a hitchhiker who can tell him exactly how many miles he has left to live, and it's fewer than the distance to his daughter's wedding." Thoughts?

I'm a cartographer by trade and I wrote a movie idea about my own work. Logline: "On the last ferry off a Louisiana island being erased from the map, a cartographer hired to redraw the coastline must decide whether to include the home of the one woman who refuses to leave." Could you tell me your impressions?

I'm 38, a former ballet dancer turned physical therapist, writing my first script. Here it is: "At a Soviet ballet academy, a night-shift cleaner who was once its most promising dancer is asked to secretly teach a defecting star the one step that got her banned." Would you mind giving me your opinion?

Quick one from a 26-year-old barista: "A court stenographer who has silently typed every word of eleven thousand trials is subpoenaed to testify, and discovers she is the only person who remembers what was actually said." What do you think? I'm planning to enter it in a screenwriting fellowship.

I'm a hospice night nurse, 43, and my coworkers encouraged me to write this down: "When a hospice nurse notices her dying patients all ask for the same stranger in their final hour, she tracks him down and finds a lonely locksmith who has never met any of them." Tell me what you think, please.

Hello, I'm a 62-year-old widowed bank teller and I wrote a logline for a movie I'd actually like to watch: "After forty years forging signatures to keep a failing small-town bank afloat, a widowed clerk must forge her own death certificate to stop the town's pensions from disappearing." Does it grab you?

I'm a Mars-obsessed linguistics grad student, 27, working on a sci-fi screenplay. Logline: "As Earth's radio link to a Mars colony goes dark for two years, a translator learns the final transmission is her mother's goodbye in a dialect only she can understand." How would you react to this?

Writing this from my dorm. I'm 19 and have never shown anyone my work. Logline: "A pianist's hands begin to shake the week before her comeback, so she hires her estranged twin, who quit music years ago, to play behind a curtain while she mimes." Could you share your thoughts on it?

I'm a film student and this is the logline for my thesis short: "On the night the last manned lighthouse on the Maine coast is to be automated, its aging keeper must train his replacement, a software engineer who has never seen the sea, just as a ship appears that no radar can detect." Could you tell me what you think?

Hi! I run a small bakery and write screenplays on Sunday evenings. Here's my latest logline: "In a city where memories are taxed, a widowed auditor must decide whether to declare the one afternoon with her late husband that she cannot bear to hand over." Any thoughts? Be honest, I can take it.

Okay, nervous about sharing this, I've only ever shown my cat. Logline for a heist comedy I'm writing: "Three retired piano movers in Glasgow plan the perfect robbery of a concert hall by stealing the Steinway while the pianist is still playing it." What's your opinion?

I'm a hobbyist who restores old films at my local library. This idea came from work: "A deaf film restorer cleaning a lost 1927 silent reel notices a background extra signing a warning to her, and that the signs change with every restoration pass." Would love your feedback on it!

Just a casual one: I teach myself screenwriting on YouTube and wrote this logline. "In 1889, a widowed schoolteacher enters the Oklahoma Land Run on a borrowed mule, carrying her husband's ashes and a map she has just realized he forged." Thoughts? Anything you'd change?

Hey, I'm a UN-adjacent translator by day and a rom-com writer by night, so this one is personal. "For ten years, a conference interpreter has quietly softened a hardline diplomat's insults; then she falls for the opposing interpreter, who has been doing exactly the same thing." How does it read to you?

I'm a high school student making an animated short for a school contest. Here's my logline: "In a tide-pool housing crisis, a broke hermit crab tours increasingly absurd shells, including a Pringles lid, while a rival buyer keeps outbidding her." What do you think? Does it make you want to see it?

I'm a farmer's daughter studying documentary filmmaking and I'm proud of this one. "For forty years a Dutch tulip grower has mailed a single bulb each spring to a stranger in Ohio; this film follows the first year he receives no reply." Tell me your honest opinion, please!

I'm a court stenographer who writes thrillers on the side, and I've been sitting on this logline for months. "A court stenographer realizes the defendant's testimony matches, word for word, the transcript of a trial that has not happened yet." Could you give me your opinion?

I own a laundromat in Detroit and I wrote a movie idea between loads. "When a laundromat owner finds handwritten notes in the pockets of one regular's clothes, each addressed to a different stranger, she delivers them and learns he is apologizing for a fire she always believed was an accident." What do you make of it?

Posting this for a screenwriting class feedback round. Logline: "Tourists from the future keep arriving on one ordinary Tuesday in 1997 Tulsa, until the bored video-store clerk who notices them finally asks why." I'd appreciate any reactions, big or small. Thanks in advance!

My grandmother actually ran a dry cleaner, which inspired this. "A Korean grandmother who has worked in a Brooklyn dry cleaner for thirty years is the only witness who can identify a killer, but she has spent those years pretending not to speak English." Does this work for you? I'd love to hear your opinion.

I coach a running club and I'm writing my first screenplay. Logline: "A blind marathoner's guide runner begins to lose his own sight, and neither man tells the other." I'm a bit nervous putting it out there. What's your take?

I'm a tabletop RPG game master, and this started as a campaign idea. "In a kingdom where dragons are extinct, the royal dragon-slayers' guild survives by faking attacks; when a real egg hatches in the guild vault, its least competent apprentice must hide it from her own bosses." What do you think?

I'm a retired crossword constructor and I've started writing screenplays. "A retired crossword constructor realizes a killer is leaving clues in the daily puzzle, a puzzle she herself stopped writing last year." I'd value your opinion, especially on the setup.

I'm a high school junior and wrote this for a film club pitch night. "When a stroke leaves her grandfather speaking only the Cantonese he spent fifty years hiding, a sixteen-year-old who never learned it has one summer to decode his confession." How would you react to this as a pitch?

I do funeral photography and I'm starting a dark comedy. Logline: "A professional mourner who attends the funerals of the friendless finds herself at her estranged father's service, where no one else has shown up and her professional standards are on the line." Curious what you think!

Hi, I'm a community-college history student and this is for a screenwriting elective. "In 1666 London, a baker's apprentice who accidentally started the Great Fire spends four days trying to put it out before anyone learns his name." Could you share your thoughts?

My siblings and I grew up near a roadside attraction, so this is close to home. "Three siblings have one weekend to sell their late father's failing dinosaur park, but the only buyer wants it demolished, and the brontosaurus holds their mother's ashes." Any feedback?

I'm a sci-fi nerd and I run a small comic shop. Here's my movie logline: "A janitor aboard a generation ship discovers that the destination planet was reached two hundred years ago, and the officers have been circling in secret because they like being officers." What do you think?

I'm a chef who did a winter season in Antarctica and wrote this on the flight home. "At a twelve-person Antarctic winter station, the cook counts thirteen plates on the dinner table, and nobody else will admit to noticing." What's your opinion?

I run a tiny karaoke bar in Manila and I've been turning my regulars into a script. Logline: "Every Thursday for eleven years, a stranger has sung the same ballad at a karaoke bar; when he stops coming, the tone-deaf owner learns the song and sets out to find him." Thoughts?

I'm a sonar-tech student, and I tried writing a drama about it. "A submarine sonar operator realizes the whale she has tracked for years is singing her late father's navy radio call sign, and that the pattern has begun to count down." Would you mind giving me your opinion?

I make small stop-motion films in my garage and I'm drafting a feature. "When the moon starts arriving late for work, a night-shift janitor's nine-year-old daughter climbs the world's tallest crane to find out who has been quietly doing its job." What do you think of it?

Hello! I sell secondhand books and I've been writing a fantasy-western. Logline: "A ferryman on a river that only flows on Sundays must carry a gunslinger and the sheriff hunting him across, and only one will be allowed to step off the far bank." Do you have any thoughts on it?

I'm a retired English teacher and I gave this opening at our book club last night: "Webster's dictionary defines a book as a set of written pages. Books are very important. Books have been around for a long, long time. Today I want to talk about books and why books matter to all of us." Would you say it works as an opening? Be honest!

message: Our community garden club asked me to open the seed swap, and I worked on this for ages: "A seed is a very patient letter. message: I own a small bike repair shop, and the local cycling club asked me to give a maintenance talk. Opener: "Your bike is already talking to you. A squeak means thirsty. A click on every pedal stroke means something's loose. Grinding when you brake means you're a week overdue at my shop and a day from the ditch. Today I'll teach you its language, so you stop learning it at the bottom of a hill." Honest opinion please.
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: Tonight I'm opening our astronomy club's star party. Here's the speech: "The light you'll see in Andromeda left 2.5 million years ago, before anything we'd call human. It has been traveling toward this field, this telescope, this paper cup of cocoa in your hand. Please don't rush. It's waited a long time for you. Red flashlights only, and be kind to the dark." What do you reckon?
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: I'm a sophomore proposing a reusable-cup deposit to our eco club. Short version: "Our cafeteria throws out 1,100 cups a week. I counted, wearing gloves, over two Mondays. Stacked, that's about as tall as our gym. A fifty-cent deposit costs you nothing if you return the cup. Let's make forgetting expensive and remembering free." How persuasive is it? I only get ninety seconds.
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: I'm giving a short tribute at our woodworking club for my mentor Ines, who's moving away. "Ines taught me to read grain the way you'd read a face: for what it has lived through. 'The crack isn't the flaw,' she'd say. 'Pretending it isn't there is.' Every shelf in my apartment now has a visible repair, and each one is stronger than the board it began as. Thank you, Ines." Does it work?
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: Our D&D club's campaign ends Saturday after two years, and as DM I'm giving the closing words: "You started as four strangers who couldn't agree on a tavern. You end as the only people alive who know why the lighthouse went dark. The dice never decided who you became. You did, one badly timed joke and one heroic lie at a time. Roll initiative one last time." Thoughts? I'm a bit nervous!
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: I roast coffee in my garage and sell at weekend markets. Our homebrewers' club invited me to talk. "Roasting is controlled burning. First crack sounds like popcorn, second like Rice Krispies. Between them is a minute or two where a bean decides whether it tastes like blueberries or a campfire. I've ruined four hundred pounds learning that window, so you only have to ruin two." Casual talk, but how does it sound?
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: I sing alto in our community choir and I'm making the fundraising appeal at the spring concert. "We've never been a loud choir. We're forty people who hold one chord until it stops being forty voices. This hall's roof leaks directly onto the tenors. I'm not saying that explains the pitch. I'm saying fix the roof and we'll find out." Is the humor too much for an appeal?
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: At the model railroad club I'm presenting my 4x8 layout: "This layout is thirty-two square feet. It holds one town, one tunnel, and one man named Gus who has waited at the same crossing for six years. I built a world so small that every decision was a decision about Gus. Scale isn't about size. It's about how closely you're willing to look." Would you tell me how it comes across?
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: I'm introducing Tokyo Story at film club tonight and only get a minute. "This film is slow on purpose. An elderly couple visit their grown children, who are too busy for them. That's it. Watch the empty rooms after people leave them. Ozu holds the shot a beat too long, and that beat is where the film keeps its heart. If you check your phone, check it after the credits." Feedback welcome.
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: I run a small catering business, and our cooking club asked me to talk about salt. "Salt isn't a seasoning. It's a volume knob. Too low and the tomato whispers; too high and it screams. Taste, add, taste again, until the tomato sounds like itself. And salt early: pasta water should taste like a mild sea, not an insult." I'm a bit nervous. Does it work as an opening?
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: I just got elected captain of our university fencing club, and here's my acceptance speech: "Fencing is the only sport where you improve by being hit and then asking why. I've been hit by most of you. I'm grateful for every touch. My promise as captain is simple: I'll tell you the truth about your footwork, and I'll bring the good coffee. Salut." Does it sound confident enough?
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: I own a small pottery studio and I'm speaking to our makers' club about kiln failures. "Every cracked bowl I've pulled from a kiln taught me the same thing about water: it hides in clay long after you think it's gone, then turns to steam and leaves, and the clay pays. Patience isn't a virtue in pottery. It's a physical requirement. Let it dry. Then let it dry some more." Thoughts?
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: I'm a high school junior giving a lightning talk at math club tonight: "People say 0.999... is just under 1. Fine. Then there'd be a number between them. Name one. Take your time; I'll wait. You can't, because the gap would have to be smaller than every positive number, and the only such number is zero. The dots aren't an approximation. They're a promise." Is it clear enough for beginners?
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: Our beekeeping club asked me, a hobbyist with three hives, to talk about swarms. "A swarm looks like panic, but it's moving day: thousands of bees, a queen in the middle, and scouts who've already picked the new house. They hang from a branch and vote by dancing. The loudest dancer doesn't win; the best address does. If you find one, don't spray it. Call me. I'll bring a cardboard box." Be honest!
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting
